docs.title: Profile System
docs.text:
Every device HIDMaestro can emulate is a JSON file in profiles/<vendor>/<slug>.json. 337 ship in the embedded catalog across 73 vendors, counting the distinct vendor values with Logitech (Saitek), Generic/Arduino, PXN/Lite Star and Sony Interactive Entertainment under their parent brands and Generic left out (Microsoft, Sony, Nintendo, Logitech, Thrustmaster, Fanatec, MOZA, SimuCUBE, VKB, VIRPIL, WinWing, Honeycomb, Hori, 8BitDo, Razer, Steelseries, Valve, Corsair, Keychron, Cherry, and 53 more). 51 are keyboards and 52 are mice. Runtime-built profiles authored via HMProfileBuilder use the identical schema and run through identical machinery.

This page documents the JSON schema field-by-field, the three runtime architecture groups a profile can fall into, and how the SDK resolves a profile into a deployable virtual device at CreateController time.

docs.title: On-disk layout
docs.text:
profiles/
  schema.json                       # JSON Schema document for all profiles
  scraped_descriptors.json          # 22 raw descriptors recovered from real devices
  linux-kernel-fixed-descriptors.json  # patched descriptors from the Linux kernel
  microsoft/
    xbox-360-wired.json
    xbox-series-xs-bt.json
    xbox-elite-v2.json
    ...23 Microsoft profiles
  sony/
    dualsense.json
    dualsense-edge.json
    dualshock-4-v1.json
    dualshock-3.json
    ...16 Sony profiles
  nintendo/
    switch-pro.json
    switch2-pro.json
    joycon-l.json
    joycon-r.json
    gamecube-adapter.json
    n64-nso.json
    snes-nso.json
    ...12 Nintendo profiles
  thrustmaster/
    t300rs.json
    t-flight-hotas-4.json
    t16000m.json
    ...20 Thrustmaster profiles
  ...28 more vendor folders

Vendor folder names are slugs of the manufacturer (thrustmaster, 8bitdo, vkbsim). File names are slugs of the model (xbox-360-wired, t-flight-hotas-x, dualsense-edge-bt).

The full vendor list at v1.8.1: 8bitdo, amazon, asetek, cammus, ch-products, fanatec, flydigi, google, heusinkveld, honeycomb, hori, logitech, microsoft, misc, moza, nacon, nintendo, pxn, razer, sega, simagic, simucube, snk, sony, steelseries, taito, thrustmaster, turtle-beach, valve, virpil, vkbsim, winwing.

The misc/ vendor catches everything else: arcade controllers, niche racing pedals, devices the contributor couldn't slot into a clean vendor namespace.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
{
  "id": "xbox-360-wired",
  "name": "Xbox 360 Controller (Wired)",
  "vendor": "Microsoft",
  "vid": "0x045E",
  "pid": "0x028E",
  "productString": "Controller (XBOX 360 For Windows)",
  "manufacturerString": "©Microsoft Corporation",
  "type": "gamepad",
  "connection": "usb",
  "descriptor": "05010905a101a10009300931150026ffff350046ffff950275108102c0...",
  "nativeDescriptor": "05010905a101...",
  "inputReportSize": 18,
  "deviceDescription": "Controller (XBOX 360 For Windows)",
  "triggerMode": "combined",
  "driverMode": null,
  "buttonMap": null,
  "axisMap": null,
  "triggerButtons": null,
  "notes": null
}

docs.title: Required fields
docs.text: Field Type Meaning id string Unique slug, e.g. "xbox-360-wired". Used by HMContext.GetProfile, case-insensitively. The filename need not match: most vendor folders prefix the id with the vendor slug, so profiles/logitech/g29.json carries "id": "logitech-g29". name string Human-readable display name shown in UIs. vendor string Manufacturer name. Doesn't need to be a slug. vid string USB Vendor ID as a 4-digit hex string with 0x prefix. pid string USB Product ID, same format. productString string The string returned by IOCTL_HID_GET_STRING (HID_STRING_ID_IPRODUCT). This is what joy.cpl and games see. Match the real device exactly. SDL3's controller database keys off this. See when revisions disagree. type string Device category. One of: gamepad, wheel, joystick, flightstick, hotas, arcadestick, pedals, keyboard, mouse, other. A keyboard or mouse profile takes SubmitKeyboard, SubmitMouse and SubmitConsumer (see Keyboards and Mice). connection string Connection type the profile represents. One of: usb, bluetooth, wireless-adapter.

docs.title: Optional fields
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning manufacturerString string | null null The string returned for manufacturer query. Defaults to vendor if null. descriptor string | null null HID report descriptor as a continuous hex string. Null = profile is a placeholder, not deployable. Spaces and dashes are ignored. A string with any other character that is not a hex digit, or an odd number of digits, refuses the file at load, and a profile built in code at create with HMProfileException (v2.0.0). inputReportSize int | null derived Length on the wire of the input report a data-only frame fills, in bytes, the report ID's byte included. The driver sends that report at this length. When null, the report's own length in the descriptor. dataReportId string | null null v2.0.0. The input report a data-only frame fills, as a hex byte such as "0x01", for a device where the SDK's own choice is wrong. Must name an input report the descriptor declares, and is refused beside an always-armed extendedReport. See The report a data frame fills. nativeDescriptor string | null null The original physical device's descriptor before any HIDMaestro-side modifications. Kept as a record; not used at runtime. deviceDescription string | null productString The Device Manager display name (FriendlyName PnP property). Some catalog profiles (Logitech F310) carry a curated deviceDescription distinct from productString. triggerMode string | null null Profile-level annotation describing the descriptor's trigger encoding: combined (descriptor declares one Z axis carrying LT - RT), separate (descriptor declares independent Z + Rz), or null for non-gamepad. Note: every Xbox profile surfaces in DirectInput as 5 axes with combined Z regardless of this annotation: the velocity-usage trick + xinputhid synthesis collapse separate-trigger descriptors into the canonical xusb22.sys 5-axis shape. WGI / browser see separate triggers via Vx/Vy + GameInput registry mapping. driverMode string | null null "xinputhid" binds Microsoft's xinputhid filter for GIP-over-HID profiles like Xbox Series BT, One BT and Elite v2 BT. As of v2.0.0 it is the alias of the xinput block's "via": "xinputhid", and "xusb22" an alias for the same path. A profile carries its xinput block, its driverMode, or neither. xinput object | null null v2.0.0. How the device reaches XInput, the presentation group of the device model. via is "xusbCompanion", an XUSB companion devnode beside the HID device as xusb22 presents a wired Xbox 360 pad, or "xinputhid". subType, flags, battery, information and capabilities set what the companion answers. An empty block means no XInput. See XUSB Companion. bluetoothTransport string | null "classic" v2.0.0. For a Bluetooth profile, the hardware and compatible IDs of a real device of that transport: "classic" gives BTHENUM\{00001124-...} IDs, "le" gives BTHLEDevice\{00001812-...} IDs. See Cross-API Coverage. bluetoothVendorIdSource string | null "usb" v2.0.0. Who assigned the VID in the Bluetooth IDs: the USB-IF ("usb", source 2) or the Bluetooth SIG ("bluetooth", source 1, as the Luna's _Dev_VID&010171 carries). driverPid string | null null PID override for hardware-ID matching only. The driver's INF-bind process matches against this PID; applications still see the real pid field via HidD_GetAttributes. Used for xinputhid-bound profiles where the real PID would be claimed by GameInput / HIDAPI: a sentinel like 0x0001 here makes those backends skip the device so SDL3 falls through to its XInput backend with the correct identity. buttonMap int[] | null identity Optional remapping table. Index = HMButton bit position; value = descriptor button index. Sony profiles use this to swap A/B/X/Y ↔ Cross/Circle/Square/Triangle. -1 means "abstract bit not in this descriptor" (the bit is dropped, never identity-mapped). Values at or past the declared button count address the contiguous 1-bit vendor run continuing the button array, where the DualSense Edge's paddles and Fn buttons live on real hardware (v1.5.1, issue #48). axisMap object | null heuristic Axis semantic override. Keys are hex HID usage codes ("0x32" for Z); values are semantic names ("leftStickX", "rightTrigger"). Sony profiles override Z/Rz → rightStick. sdlMapping string | null null v1.5.0+. SDL gamepad mapping body, everything after the GUID and name, trailing comma included. Set it for pads SDL reaches through DirectInput and has no database entry for, which SDL would otherwise expose as roleless joysticks. See SDK Reference for the consumer side. triggerButtons int[] | null null Two-element array [LT_button_index, RT_button_index]. When triggers are nonzero, the corresponding buttons engage automatically (DS4/DualSense L2/R2 digital buttons). extendedReport object | null null v1.3.5+. Vendor-blob input layout. When present, HMController.SubmitState packs reports per the field list rather than via the descriptor-driven encoder. Used for profiles where the descriptor declares a single opaque vendor-defined field (Sony BT 0x31, future profiles with similar shape). See section below. extendedOutputReport object | null null v1.3.5+. Vendor-blob output layout. When present, the SDK decodes incoming output reports of the declared report ID and surfaces parsed-field events via HMController.OutputDecoded. Pairs with HMOutputEncoder.Encode for the inverse direction. deviceModelFrom string | null null v2.0.0. The device model the profile takes for the groups its own keys leave empty: a catalog profile's id, a model this release holds, or a model in the loaded directory's models folder. See Device models. deviceModel string | null null v2.0.0. "none" takes no model, by name or by identity. No other value is accepted. featureStubs, valueSources object | null null The answers the device gives to GET_REPORT(Feature), with the value sources their patches read. On UMDF2, v2.0.0 compiles them into the controller's FeatureAnswers value. See Composite USB Personas. protocol object | null null v2.0.0. A USB/IP device's registers, commands, replies and clock. See protocol. stateBlock, inputReports, liveFeatureReports object | null null v2.0.0. A device that builds its reports from its own state. See Report programs. stream object | null null v2.0.0. The idle repeat: the last frame sent again at the device's period while the consumer is quiet. See stream. axisCenters object | null null v2.0.0. The wire value a descriptor-path axis carries at the SDK's 0.5, keyed by HID usage name, such as {"X": 127}. See Report field parameters. extendedReport.ports, extendedOutputReport.ports object | null null v2.0.0. A report that carries several controllers, one block per port. See Devices with ports and protocols. backend string | null null "usbip" runs the profile on the USB/IP transport instead of the UMDF2 driver, with usbConfiguration describing the whole USB device. See Composite USB Personas. notes string | null null Implementation notes, descriptor provenance, quirks. Free-form.

The full JSON Schema lives in profiles/schema.json.

docs.title: When hardware revisions disagree
docs.text:
"Match the real device exactly" stops being a complete instruction when a manufacturer changes a string mid-life and leaves nothing on the wire to tell the revisions apart. A DualSense sold in 2020 reports Wireless Controller. One sold today reports DualSense Wireless Controller. Both report bcdDevice 0x0100 and the same 054C:0CE6, so no field a profile could branch on distinguishes them, and a profile serves one string or the other.

HIDMaestro's rule for that case is that the current revision wins, since a consumer keyed to a retired string is already broken against real hardware a user can buy. As of v1.4.5 dualsense and dualsense-composite serve DualSense Wireless Controller. The launch string remains available on dualsense-bt, whose dualsense-bt-full sibling carries the current one, so both are reachable from the catalog and a consumer that needs the older identity can ask for it by profile id.

Write the reasoning into notes when you make this call in a profile of your own. The next person to compare the profile against a descriptor dump will find the mismatch and needs to know it was a decision.

docs.title: The report a data frame fills (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
A data-only frame, from SubmitRawReport or from SubmitState through the descriptor-driven encoder, goes out from the UMDF2 driver as one input report at one length. The SDK picks that report from its own parse of the descriptor: the first input report with game pad fields, or for a keyboard or mouse the descriptor's first input report. inputReportSize, when set, is that report's whole length on the wire, its ID byte included. The SDK writes the report ID and length into the controller's configuration, and the driver uses them only when they match the descriptor and length in use.

When the SDK's choice is not the report the real device sends, dataReportId names the right one. A create refuses a dataReportId that names no input report of the descriptor, and one beside an extendedReport with alwaysArmed, whose report the data frames fill instead, before anything machine-wide. HMProfileBuilder.FromProfile copies it. microsoft-designer-keyboard sets "0x01". Its descriptor declares a vendor report 0x27 as its first input report, and the real keyboard sends its keys as report 0x01 of 12 bytes: "Press A" is 01 00 04 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 in Android CTS's microsoft_designer_keyboard_keyeventtests.json, beside the register file the profile's descriptor comes from.

Through v1.12.0 the driver took the first Report ID item of the descriptor's first Application Collection, whatever kind of report it named, and the SDK measured that report with a walk that kept no Push and Pop stack. Sixteen catalog profiles now send a different data report on a UMDF2 controller:

Profile v1.12.0 v2.0.0 logitech-wingman-formula-gp 0x00, 3 bytes 0x00, 5 bytes gamecube-adapter-hid 0x11 (an output report), 1 byte 0x21, 38 bytes joypad-gc-adapter 0x11 (an output report), 1 byte 0x21, 37 bytes microsoft-designer-keyboard 0x22 (a feature report), 1 byte 0x01, 12 bytes, by its dataReportId genesis-nso, n64-nso, snes-nso, joycon-l 0x21, 49 bytes 0x3F, 12 bytes joycon-charging-grip 0x21, 49 bytes 0x3F, 12 bytes switch2-pro-controller 0x05, 64 bytes 0x09, 64 bytes joypad-steam-input 0x02, 64 bytes 0x01, 64 bytes ps3-remote 0x00, 17 bytes, the driver's default 0x00, 12 bytes circuitpython-gamepad 0x05, 6 bytes 0x05, 7 bytes pxn-vd6 0x01, 62 bytes 0x01, 63 bytes thrustmaster-t16000m 0x00, 10 bytes 0x00, 9 bytes vader-4-pro 0x00, 32 bytes 0x00, 9 bytes

The last four carried inputReportSize values that disagreed with their own descriptors. circuitpython-gamepad and pxn-vd6 counted the data bytes without the ID, one byte short of the declared report, which HID class rejects. thrustmaster-t16000m and vader-4-pro sent a report longer than any their descriptors declare. switch2-pro-controller sends every frame whole on its extended lane, so its change does not reach the wire. Two rows still do not match the device. gamecube-adapter-hid's descriptor gives each of its ten Application collections Usage 0, as the real adapter's does, so Windows' HID parser refuses it (HIDP_GETCOLDESC_TOP_COLLECTION_USAGE, which S37 checks) and the device fails with Code 10 either way. joycon-charging-grip carries the Bluetooth Joy-Con descriptor, and a wired grip never sends 0x3F. switch-pro keeps 0x21 at 362 bytes, and every other UMDF2 profile keeps its report and length. A driver older than v2.0.0 ignores the SDK's choice, so these profiles keep their old reports on a 1.x driver, which a running 1.x program's InstallDriver puts back.

Four catalog descriptors held main items of tag 0, which HID 1.11 does not define, and now hold their sources' bytes:

  • ps3-remote: hid-sony.c ps3remote_rdesc, which the profile names as its source, with two items given a data byte (below). The catalog copy had 90 bytes, with bytes doubled.
  • saitek-x52: the 119 bytes of Launchpad bug 492056 comment 14. One byte was missing and three were changed.
  • thrustmaster-t80: byte 79 is 09, so Rx and Ry follow as in the T-Flight HOTAS 4 and T300RS descriptors the profile says it shares. No dump of a T80's own bytes is published.
  • joypad-steam-input: joypad-os sinput_descriptors.h. The copy had lost the three report ID values its macros stand for.

Windows' own HID parser refused three catalog descriptors. HID class runs it at the device's start, so each of these devices failed its start with problem code 10:

  • ps3-remote: hid-sony.c writes its Usage Minimum and one Input item with no data byte, which Windows refuses. HID 1.11 gives such an item the value 0, so the profile writes both with a data byte of 0: 69 bytes and the same 12-byte report.
  • tinyusb-generic-gamepad: its reports were not whole bytes. It now serves TinyUSB's TUD_HID_REPORT_DESC_GAMEPAD with its report ID 2: a 12-byte input report of six 8-bit axes, an 8-bit hat and 32 buttons, and no output or feature report.
  • nacon-bigben-ps4: Linux's fixed descriptor, whose Feature item has no usage. It now serves the descriptor the pad serves (hid-bigbenff.c): a 27-byte input report with X, Y, Z and Rz and with L2 and R2 as buttons 7 and 8, beside 8-byte vendor output and feature reports. 146B:0902 is BigBen's wired game pad for the PS3, so the profile is now "BigBen Game Pad for PS3", with "Bigben Interactive" and "Bigben Game Pad" as its USB strings. Its id is unchanged.

gamecube-adapter and gamecube-adapter-hid stay refused, as the real adapter's descriptor is: each of their ten Application collections carries Usage 0, which hidparse refuses as a top-level collection without a usage (STATUS_COULD_NOT_INTERPRET, HIDP_GETCOLDESC_TOP_COLLECTION_USAGE). joypad-gc-adapter parses.

Every descriptor walker in the SDK keeps HID 1.11's global item stack, Push and Pop. Battery scenario S37 checks the input, output and feature lengths the SDK reads for all 243 catalog report descriptors against hid-tools', and runs every one through the machine's own hidparse.sys, as HID class does at a device's start.

docs.title: Vendor-blob fields (extendedReport / extendedOutputReport)
docs.text:
Some controllers' descriptors declare their input as a single opaque vendor-defined field: Sony BT (DualSense, DualSense Edge, DS4 BT) is the canonical example, but Switch Pro and various wheels follow the same pattern. The descriptor doesn't say which bytes carry sticks vs buttons vs gyro vs CRC; the wire format is firmware convention.

Pre-v1.3.5 the SDK couldn't pack these: it would fall back to whatever simpler input report the descriptor declared first (Sony BT: Report 1, 9 bytes), which Steam Input misclassified and parsers like dualsense-tester couldn't read. v1.3.5 makes the byte layout data: profile JSON describes every field's type, position, and bit range; the SDK walks the field list as a generic codec.

"extendedReport": {
  "reportId": "0x31",     // hex string; emitted as the report ID byte
  "size": 78,             // total bytes including report ID at byte 0
  "fields": [
    { "byte":  1, "type": "uint8-rolling", "semantic": "btSeqTag", "initial": 0 },
    { "byte":  2, "type": "uint8-axis",    "semantic": "leftStickX",  "center": 128 },
    { "byte":  3, "type": "uint8-axis",    "semantic": "leftStickY",  "center": 128 },
    { "byte":  6, "type": "uint8-trigger", "semantic": "leftTrigger" },
    { "byte":  9, "bits": "0-3", "type": "hat-octant", "semantic": "hat", "neutralValue": 8 },
    { "byte":  9, "bits": "4-7", "type": "button-mask", "buttons": ["X","A","B","Y"] },
    { "byte": 10, "type": "button-mask",
      "buttons": ["LeftBumper","RightBumper","_","_","Back","Start","LeftStick","RightStick"] },
    { "bytes": "74-77", "type": "crc32-le",
      "scope": { "prefix": [161, 49], "from": 1, "to": 73 } }
  ]
}

docs.title: Field types
docs.text:
Type Direction Semantics uint8 both Plain byte. Encode writes initial, or the touch report's packet counter for touchpadPacketCounter. Decode returns the byte uint8-rolling both Per-controller counter that advances by stride each report (input). Plain byte (output) uint8-axis both Stick axis. Encode takes the SDK's 0..1 stick (0.5 centered) to min..max, or center - 127..center + 127 when center is not 128. Decode returns a signed float about center uint8-trigger both Trigger, 0..1 to min..max. Decode returns 0..1 uint8-pressure input A button's pressure, 0 to 255, from the Pressure* fields uint8-battery input BatteryLevel in the declared bit range, fullValue while full uint8-level-map input The battery byte from an 11-entry levels table, with fullValue ahead of chargingValue (v2.0.0) int16-le both A motion word: the raw Gyro* and Accel* shorts, or with scale the calibrated AccelG* and GyroDps* values. center writes offset binary int16-axis input Signed 16-bit stick axis, min..max int16-pad, int16-pad-or-stick input A Valve trackpad coordinate from the touch fingers. int16-pad-or-stick sends the stick while the finger is up, as the 2015 Steam Controller does uint16-le, uint32-le input sensorTimestamp: the consumer's stamp, divided by divisor in the 16-bit form, or with clock: "accumulate" elapsed time over divisor uint16-trigger input 16-bit trigger, min..max. max is required uint16-pressure input Pad pressure: max while a finger touches, min otherwise. max is required uint10-be input A 10-bit big-endian motion value about center, rescaled by resolution over sourceResolution uint32-rolling input 32-bit packet counter that advances every report touchpad-finger input Sony's 4-byte touch finger: lifted bit, tracking ID, 12-bit X and Y bitfield input Status flags named in buttons: batteryCharging, batteryFull, micMuted, headphonesConnected, cableConnected hat-octant both 4-bit hat in the declared bit range. HMHat.None is neutralValue (typically 8), 1..8 are 0..7 button-mask both Named-button bitmask. buttons is an ordered list of HMButton names or "#n" for bit n (LSB first within the declared bit range). "_" is a placeholder slot stick12-pair input Two 12-bit stick axes packed in three bytes, a Switch 2 stick rgb24 output 3 contiguous bytes packed as R, G, B packed-uint output Bit groups gathered across frames of a stride and reduced to one value (v2.0.0) crc32-le both CRC-32/ISO-HDLC (poly 0xEDB88320) over scope.prefix + report bytes [scope.from..scope.to], stored LE in the declared 4-byte range bytes-passthrough both Opaque byte slice. parsed[semantic] is byte[] of the declared range length bytes-zero encode Explicit zero-fill (default for unmapped bytes)

An unknown type, or an input semantic the type cannot read, refuses a profile file at load and a profile built in code at create, with the profile and the field's JSON path.

docs.title: Report field parameters (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
As of v2.0.0 a field's wire form is set by parameters, never by a type named for a device. A parameter on a type that ignores it is refused.

Key On Meaning min, max every type that carries a normalized value The wire values at the SDK's 0 and 1. The type's full range by default. min equal to max is refused invert every axis and trigger type The wire grows the other way center int16-le The wire value of a zero reading, 0 to 65535. 32768 writes offset binary, as the PS Move's motion words are. The word clamps to 0 to 65535 scale, negate, repeat int16-le of a calibrated source, accelGX to gyroDpsZ Counts per g or per degree a second, as a number or an exact ratio such as [13371, 936], and [count, stride] for a report that carries several samples dpad: "resolved" button-mask, hat-octant The d-pad from HatDegrees, HatHundredths, HatRaw or Hat, the first one set "#n" in buttons button-mask HMButton bit n levels, chargingValue, fullValue uint8-level-map The battery byte as an 11-entry table, fullValue ahead of chargingValue clock: "accumulate", divisor, holdWhile uint16-le, uint32-le of sensorTimestamp Elapsed time in the 1/3 microsecond ticks of SensorTimestamp, from the controller's clock until the first nonzero consumer stamp and from the consumer's stamps after. A repeat of the last state adds nothing, and a stamp that runs backward adds one idle interval. holdWhile names a protocol register under which the clock holds still, as steam-controller-2's does while the host has its IMU off parts packed-uint Bit groups over frames of a stride, reduced by max, scaled and clamped to a byte, as the Switch Pro's and Switch 2 Pro's rumble is

ps-move writes its motion with them:

{ "byte": 13, "type": "int16-le", "semantic": "accelGX",
  "scale": [8723, 2], "center": 32654, "repeat": [2, 6] },
{ "byte": 12, "type": "uint8-level-map", "semantic": "batteryLevel",
  "levels": [238, 238, 238, 238, 238, 238, 238, 238, 238, 238, 238],
  "chargingValue": 238, "fullValue": 239 }

A profile can also set axisCenters at the top level, outside any report block. It gives a descriptor-path axis, named by its HID usage, the wire value it carries at the SDK's 0.5. amazon-luna-usb sets {"X": 127, "Y": 127, "Z": 127, "Rz": 127} and amazon-luna-ble 32767 on the same axes, because SDL's Luna driver reads 0x7F and 0x7FFF as zero.

docs.title: Keys 2.0.0 requires
docs.text:
Where a profile written for 1.x left a key out and got a behavior from code, 2.0.0 requires the key, so no such profile changes its bytes unseen:

  • A uint16-trigger or uint16-pressure input field needs max. 1.x wrote a full pull or press as 32767: add "max": 32767 for that, or "max": 65535 for the full width.
  • An int16-axis, int16-pad or int16-pad-or-stick field of a Y semantic needs invert. 1.x negated every int16 Y: add "invert": true for that, or "invert": false for a wire that grows downward.
  • The ds3-battery type is gone. Write it as uint8-level-map with levels [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5], chargingValue 238 and fullValue 239.
  • An output field refuses min, max and dpad, invert on any type but uint8-axis, and center on int16-le, since its decoder ignores them.

A profile file that breaks one is refused at load and listed in HMContext.ProfileLoadIssues, with the JSON path and the value that keeps 1.x's bytes. A profile built or changed in code is refused at create with HMProfileException, before anything machine-wide:

JsonPath  $.extendedReport.fields[3]
Reason    extendedReport.fields[3] ('uint16-trigger').max is required. v1 wrote a full pull or press as 32767: add "max": 32767 for that, or "max": 65535 for the full width.

Battery scenario S91 checks these refusals beside its golden reports.

docs.title: Values on the wire (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
Every normalized value the SDK writes, on the descriptor path, the XUSB slice, the codec, both Switch packers and the output encoder, is min + RoundHalfEven(v' x (max - min)) in double, where v' is the clamped input, or 1 minus it for an inverted field. Ties go to the even value. Through v1.12.0 the SDK truncated or multiplied in float, which sent a value a consumer normalized from a raw count back one count low on 32,895 of the 65,536 values of a 0..65535 axis and on 252 of 256 XInput trigger bytes. Now every raw value comes back as it went in, except on a 16-bit centered stick, where a consumer that normalizes in float gets 64 or 65 values just above the center back one count low.

  • A NaN writes the field's resting value, 0.5 for a stick or a centered axis and 0 for a trigger, on every path.
  • A stick the consumer leaves unwritten rests at its center. Axes the profile's layout names as sticks rest at 0.5, and every other axis as before, 0.5 when signed and 0 when not.
  • An axis with an axisCenters entry takes two slopes, computed at create, and rounds its distance from the center once, so 0.5 and a consumer's 32768 / 65535 both land on the center.

Battery scenario S90 sends every raw value of every catalog conversion through the SDK's own code and requires it back.

docs.title: Catalog profiles whose bytes changed (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
• ps-move presents the 178-byte descriptor a real Move serves over USB: a Game Pad with three top-level collections, so Windows creates three HID children, and its HID child's usage hardware ID is UP:0001_U:0005. Its input report is the Move's own. Cross is HMButton.A, Circle B, Square X, Triangle Y, Select Back, Start Start, PS Guide and Move Misc1, and the T trigger is the left trigger. Motion goes in AccelGX/GY/GZ and GyroDpsX/Y/Z. Its battery byte is 0xEE, or 0xEF with BatteryFull, and its manufacturer string is "Sony Computer Entertainment".
  • xbox-360-flight-stick presents the 127-byte joystick descriptor its notes cite: 8-bit Z and Rz ahead of its 16-bit axes, a 12-byte report. Its HID child's usage hardware ID is UP:0001_U:0004.
  • The nine Xbox 360 profiles whose manufacturer string was mangled read "©Microsoft Corporation". Nothing on the wire changes.

Battery scenario S96 checks these against their sources. A program that stored the HID child path of ps-move or xbox-360-flight-stick sees a new device once. See Moving from 1.x.

semantic is the dictionary key consumers see in OutputDecoded.Fields and pass to HMOutputEncoder.Encode. Pick names per your domain.

docs.title: Field positioning syntax
docs.text:
• "byte": N: single byte at offset N (0-indexed; byte 0 is the report ID)
  • "bytes": "N-M": inclusive range [N..M] (used by crc32-le, rgb24, bytes-passthrough)
  • "bits": "L-H": sub-byte bit range [L..H] within the byte/byte-range

docs.title: CRC32 scope
docs.text:
"scope": {
  "prefix": [161, 49],   // two bytes for Sony BT input: [0xA1, 0x31]
  "from": 1,             // first byte covered (after report ID)
  "to":   73             // last byte covered (before CRC field)
}

Sony's wire-format prefixes: - Input report CRC: [0xA1, reportId] - Output report CRC: [0xA2, reportId] - Feature report CRC: [0x53, reportId] (per dualsense-tester reference impl)

docs.title: Arming: armOn and alwaysArmed
docs.text:
A vendor blob is not always what the controller emits first. Sony BT pads power up on the short legacy report and only switch to 0x31 / 0x11 once a host reads feature 0x05, 0x09 or 0x20, which is the same handshake real firmware uses. armOn lists those triggers, and until one fires the SDK takes the descriptor-driven path so joy.cpl and RawInput still see structured axes.

"armOn": [
  { "type": "featureRead", "reportId": "0x05" },
  { "type": "featureRead", "reportId": "0x09" }
]

Trigger types are featureRead, featureWrite and outputWrite.

Some controllers have no handshake to wait for. A Switch 2 Pro streams its structured report 0x09 from power-on and leaves it only when a host asks for the vendor blob instead, so waiting would be wrong in both directions: nothing would ever arm, and the descriptor's first declared report is the opaque 0x05 blob with no buttons or axes in it. Those profiles set alwaysArmed and emit the vendor report from the first frame.

"extendedReport": { "reportId": "0x09", "size": 64, "alwaysArmed": true, "fields": [ ... ] }

A profile with neither armOn nor alwaysArmed never runs the codec on the input direction, which is the correct default for every USB Sony profile and every plain-HID gamepad. The output direction ignores both fields.

docs.title: When to use extendedReport vs leave it unset
docs.text:
Set extendedReport only when the descriptor's first declared input is an opaque vendor blob and the wire format requires firmware-convention byte placement. For controllers whose descriptors fully describe the input report (Xbox 360 wired, DualSense USB, Switch Pro, every plain-HID gamepad), the descriptor-driven encoder packs correctly without an extendedReport block: leave it null/unset.

extendedOutputReport is independent: even when the input descriptor is fully self-describing, declaring an extendedOutputReport lets consumers use HMOutputEncoder.Encode(profile, fields) to produce wire-format bytes for driving real devices without inline byte-packing. v1.3.5 ships output blocks for DS5 USB (Report 0x02), DS5 Edge USB, DS4 v1/v2 USB (Report 0x05), in addition to BT output blocks for the DS5 family (Report 0x31) and DS4 BT (Report 0x11).

When extendedReport is set, the descriptor should declare the matching report ID first so the kernel HID stack delivers the right ID to consumers. The Sony BT profiles in v1.3.5 reorder their descriptors to put Report 0x31 (DS5 family) or Report 0x11 (DS4 family) INPUT before Report 1.

docs.title: Devices with ports and protocols (v2.0.0)
docs.text: Some devices carry several controllers in one report, and some answer commands a host must send before they report at all. A profile describes both as data, and the SDK holds only mechanisms any profile can use. The Wii U GameCube adapter is built this way, and nothing in the SDK names it. See Wii U GameCube Adapter for the device and profiles/nintendo/gamecube-adapter.json for the whole profile.

docs.title: extendedReport.ports
docs.text:
A report that carries several controllers, one block per port: a multi-port adapter, a multitap, a receiver with several pads.

Key Meaning count, offset, stride How many blocks, where port 1's starts, and how far apart they are. Byte 0 is the report ID, so an input report with an ID, and every output report, start their blocks at byte 1 or later status The block's status byte: its byte offset, the connections a port can hold with the value each sets (the first is the empty port, the second the default, at least two, each with a value of its own), and device-wide flags every status byte carries while on data The block's data bytes, such as "1-8". An empty port's are zero snapshots Copies of a block the device keeps, taken on: "connect" from the first report in which the port holds something fields The block's fields in the extendedReport field vocabulary, offsets relative to the block 
"extendedReport": {
  "reportId": "0x21", "size": 37, "alwaysArmed": true, "fields": [],
  "ports": {
    "count": 4, "offset": 1, "stride": 9,
    "status": {
      "byte": 0,
      "connections": [
        { "name": "empty", "value": "0x00" },
        { "name": "wired", "value": "0x10" },
        { "name": "wireless", "value": "0x22" },
        { "name": "wirelessNotCommunicating", "value": "0x20" }
      ],
      "flags": [ { "name": "rumblePower", "value": "0x04", "default": true } ]
    },
    "data": "1-8",
    "snapshots": [ { "name": "origin", "on": "connect" } ],
    "fields": [
      { "byte": 1, "type": "button-mask", "buttons": ["A","B","X","Y","DPAD_LEFT","DPAD_RIGHT","DPAD_DOWN","DPAD_UP"] },
      { "byte": 2, "type": "button-mask", "buttons": ["Start","RightBumper","RightTriggerClick","LeftTriggerClick"] },
      { "byte": 3, "type": "uint8-axis", "semantic": "leftStickX" },
      { "byte": 4, "type": "uint8-axis", "semantic": "leftStickY", "invert": true },
      { "byte": 7, "type": "uint8-trigger", "semantic": "leftTrigger" }
      // ...the C-stick at bytes 5 and 6 and the right trigger at byte 8
    ]
  }
}

extendedOutputReport.ports describes an output report's blocks the same way. Its fields are whole numbers, uint8, uint8-axis, uint8-trigger, uint16-le and int16-le, and each is reported under its semantic: HMPort.GetOutput("rumble"), and port1.rumble in OutputDecoded. Its port count must match the input report's.

docs.title: protocol
docs.text:
How a USB/IP device behaves beyond its descriptors. As of v2.0.0 protocol sits at the profile's top level. usbConfiguration.protocol is refused at load with its path. The full grammar is mechanism 3 of the data-driven design note.

Key Meaning state Registers of 1 to 32 bits with initial values, restored at attach and at a port reset unless keepOnPortReset. At most 64 counters Counts of reports, frames, reads or clock periods, each written into replies and reports memory Images a reply reads from and a rule writes into, filled, with constant segments and value segments such as the serial input The interrupt IN endpoint, the condition under which a poll gets a report (while, such as ["polling", "!stalled"]), and its clock. For a device that sends the SDK's report, the clock is the device's own controller poll in sourcePollMs, with sourcePollRules that change it while exactly the listed ports hold something. For a device that builds its reports, it is a period, an origin and a missed-tick rule commands The interrupt OUT endpoint, whose packets are each a command. setReport makes a SET_REPORT(Output) one command too, its whole data stage, report ID first. setReportStripsId, with setReport only, drops a leading byte that matches wValue's report ID, when that ID is not 0, from a data stage longer than one byte, as tinyusb does. A reply prefix and status, then rules, tried in order: the first that matches applies, and a command no rule matches is ignored. A rule matches a command's bytes, with .. for any byte, and its length, then sets, stores, ORs or clears registers, writes memory, decodes or raises an output report, and queues a reply built from the registers before the rule ran: constant bytes, echoed command bytes, a register, a counter, memory, a bitmap, a layout's bytes, a value or a snapshot's bytes for every port. Each part can take a while, and is zeros when it does not hold replies The channel replies go out on (the input endpoint, or a bulk IN endpoint), pending, how many can wait (1 when absent), and overflow, which one a reply past them drops decoders Output reports decoded into named values that OutputDecoded carries halt The registers under which the device answers nothing, at least one, and the status transfers fail with until a port reset: EPROTO, the default, or EPIPE setProtocol "ack", or "stall", the default getStatus "descriptor": the self-powered bit the configuration declares getReport The GET_REPORT answer. "input", the default, answers the input report as it stands for its own ID, another declared input report with its ID and zeros, and stalls an ID the descriptor does not declare. "reportId" answers the requested report ID alone and stalls report ID 0 or a one-byte request, for every report type, as tinyusb does for a firmware that supplies no report. "deviceReport", for a device that builds its reports, answers the layout that would go out now log How many commands the device keeps, raw, for a consumer to read 
"protocol": {
  "state": [ { "name": "polling" }, { "name": "stalled" }, { "name": "halted" } ],
  "input": {
    "endpoint": "0x81",
    "while": ["polling", "!stalled"],
    "clock": { "sourcePollMs": 1.19971, "sourcePollRules": [ { "portsConnected": [1, 2], "periodMs": 0.9995 } ] }
  },
  "commands": {
    "endpoint": "0x02",
    "setReport": true,
    "setReportStripsId": true,
    "rules": [
      { "match": "11", "minLength": 5 },
      { "match": "11", "set": { "stalled": true } },
      { "match": "12", "reply": [ { "hex": "22" }, { "snapshot": "origin", "bytes": "3-8", "while": ["polling"] } ] },
      { "match": "13", "set": { "polling": true, "stalled": false } },
      { "match": "14", "reply": [ { "hex": "24" }, { "state": "polling" } ], "set": { "polling": false } },
      { "match": "15", "set": { "halted": true, "polling": false } }
      // ...0x16 and 0x17 set stalled too
    ]
  },
  "replies": { "pending": 1, "overflow": "dropNewest" },
  "halt": { "while": ["halted"], "status": "EPROTO" },
  "setProtocol": "ack",
  "getStatus": "descriptor",
  "getReport": "reportId"
}

The device runs the protocol on a modeled host poll. A host polls an interrupt endpoint every period while a transfer is queued, on a grid that starts at attach and again at a port reset, and fills a transfer one packet per poll. The period is the one Windows gives the endpoint descriptor's bInterval: 8 ms for bInterval 0 to 15, 16 ms for 16 to 35 and 32 ms beyond at low speed, bInterval ms rounded down to a power of two, at most 32, at full speed, and 2^(bInterval-1) microframes, at most 32, at high speed. usbConfiguration.busSpeed takes "low", "full" or "high", the default. A low-speed device is held to an 8-byte control endpoint, interrupt endpoints of at most 8 bytes, and no bulk or isochronous endpoints. HMController.DeviceProtocol.HostPollInterval models a faster host and takes only a period Windows schedules at the device's speed. It throws InvalidOperationException on a device that builds its reports, which sends them on its own clock, and on one whose protocol names no input endpoint. A command, its reply, a report and a GET_REPORT answer allocate nothing, which battery scenario S95 checks over 100,000 of each. A device with a sourcePollMs has a new report for a host poll only once it has read its controllers since its last report, as real hardware does.

docs.title: usbConfiguration.winUsb and sharedSerial
docs.text:
winUsb.interfaceGuid is the DeviceInterfaceGUIDs value a WinUSB binding registers, which libusb needs to open a WinUSB device. HMController.BindWinUsb() builds the driver package from it and the device's descriptors. The device must have one interface and bDeviceClass 0. See Dolphin, Slippi and SDL for where the binding goes and what it leaves on an instance a real adapter can take.

sharedSerial: true serves the profile's serialString unchanged for every identity key, for a device whose every unit carries the same serial. Other USB/IP personas fold the identity into their serial.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
A profile file's device model is checked when it loads, and a mistake refuses the file into HMContext.ProfileLoadIssues with its JSON path. CreateController compiles the whole model again before it takes anything machine-wide, so a profile built or changed in code is refused with HMProfileException naming the profile, the JSON path that holds it and the limit it breaks. Both refuse:

  • ports that do not fit their report, or that start on the report ID byte
  • a status block with fewer than two connections, or two connections that share a value
  • input report fields beside ports, and output report fields that overlap the port blocks
  • a field outside a block's data bytes, or wider than its block or report by its type's own width
  • an unknown field type, an input semantic that names no SDK value, or a button name the SDK cannot express
  • a report ID that does not parse, or an armOn type other than featureWrite, outputWrite and featureRead
  • an output port count that differs from the input's, or more than 32 ports under a protocol
  • an input report over the 80-byte extended lane, or an output block or field past the output ring's 256 data bytes
  • output ports or fields past one OUT packet on a protocol whose SET_REPORT loses its report ID
  • a command rule whose match or minimum length is longer than the OUT endpoint's packet
  • a register a rule names that state does not declare, replies.pending outside 1 to 1024, setReportStripsId without setReport, or a getReport other than "input", "reportId" and "deviceReport"
  • usbConfiguration.protocol, which moved to protocol at the top level
  • an endpoint the configuration descriptor lacks or of the wrong type, and a reply on a device with no input endpoint
  • a low-speed device over its packet limits, an endpoint whose transfer type differs between alternate settings, an interrupt or bulk endpoint whose descriptors differ between them, or an isochronous endpoint declared in more than one
  • a WinUSB GUID that does not parse

The descriptor checks run at that point only for a profile with protocol or winUsb, whose descriptors the device model compiles. Every other USB/IP persona meets them when its device is built, after its transport index is taken. Every catalog profile compiles, which battery scenario S79 checks.

docs.title: Report programs and stream (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
A device that builds its reports at send time splits into data. Four catalog profiles work this way: switch-pro, switch-pro-usb, dualshock-3-full and switch2-pro-controller-composite.

  • stateBlock: a field list in the codec's vocabulary that SubmitState encodes. A raw submit on such a device is the state block itself, verbatim and of its size, and any other length throws ArgumentException. HMProfile.BuildsItsOwnReports says which profiles work this way.
  • inputReports: layouts, each with a report ID, a size, a while condition on the protocol's registers, a send rule and a program over the state block. A program is built from copy, bits, const, xor, swap16, field, lookup, hat8, pack12, counter and when blocks.
  • liveFeatureReports: the same programs, for a feature report whose answer is the current state.

The build turns every catalog program and decoder into straight-line C#, and the SDK binds it once at create. A program from outside the catalog runs on an interpreter compiled from the same validated form, with no rebuild. A catalog program the build cannot validate fails the build with KG0001, its file and its JSON path. Battery scenario S94 runs every program three ways: generated, interpreted and through a naive evaluator written from the design note.

docs.title: stream
docs.text:
stream gives a device's idle repeat: the consumer's last frame sent again one period after the last frame went out, as the real device reports at rest.

Key Meaning periodMs The period, fractions allowed, such as 1.25 for a DualSense over Bluetooth periodRegister A period a host sets, from a protocol register, with periodMs while the register holds 0 while When the device streams, on the protocol's registers. Absent streams from creation timestamps "hold", the default, repeats the consumer's last sensor timestamp. "advance" moves it on by the time since the frame it repeats

extendedReport.idleFrameIntervalMs still loads as a stream of that period. 21 catalog profiles repeat at rest: the DualSense family at 1 ms (Edge), 1.25 ms (Bluetooth) and 4 ms (USB), the DualShock 4 USB family and steam-deck at 4 ms, openffboard at 101 ms and five Thrustmaster wheels at 250 ms, none of which repeated anything before 2.0.0, and steam-controller-2, steam-deck-composite and steam-controller-composite, which already did. A consumer that counts frames sees the repeats.

docs.title: Device models (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
A profile's device model is the behavior it gives beyond its reports, in three groups, each resolved at load on its own:

Group Keys Answers featureStubs, valueSources Protocol protocol, stateBlock, inputReports, liveFeatureReports Presentation xinput, driverMode as its alias, driverPid

Within a group the first of these that applies wins, and no two merge:

  1. The profile's own keys in the group.
  2. deviceModelFrom, naming a catalog profile, a model this release holds or a model loaded from the profile's directory.
  3. A name nothing loaded holds, or a model that does not fit the profile's descriptor: the identity default, and HMProfile.DeviceModelProblem says why.
  4. No keys and no name: the identity default whose entry matches the profile, or nothing.
  5. "deviceModel": "none": no model.

The identity defaults are data, profiles/models/identity-defaults.json, written from the vendor and product checks 1.x kept in code: the Switch Pro over USB and over Bluetooth (057E:2009, the models switch-pro-usb and switch-pro), a sixaxisCompatible profile (dualshock-3-full), Sony's VID 054C by product and connection, each Sony entry naming one of the six Sony models (sony-dualsense, sony-dualsense-bt, sony-dualsense-edge, sony-dualsense-edge-bt, sony-dualshock4, sony-dualshock4-bt), and VID 045E with "xbox" in the id, name or product string, which gives xbox-360-wired's presentation, an XUSB companion. The 16 Sony catalog profiles name theirs with deviceModelFrom, the ten Xbox 360 profiles carry their xinput block and the twelve xinputhid profiles their driverMode, and no catalog profile takes a group from an identity default, which battery scenario S92 checks. The defaults exist so a profile from HMProfileBuilder, HMDeviceExtractor or your own JSON keeps the behavior its identity got from 1.x.

HMProfile.HasDeviceModel, DeviceModelSource (per group: own, named:<id>, identity:<entry> or none) and DeviceModelProblem report the result. HMDeviceExtractor.Extract writes the deviceModelFrom its identity gives, and HMDeviceExtractor.ResolveDeviceModel returns a copy with that name for a profile that has none.

A file from a directory gets every check at load. The embedded catalog's files had their model groups checked at build, where a program that does not compile fails the build with KG0001, and S92 loads the same files with every check, so the catalog's own load reads their groups without checking them again.

A directory loaded with LoadProfilesFromDirectory can carry a models folder at its top: named models and an identity-defaults.json in the catalog's formats, which load with no rebuild. Its models resolve by name for its profiles and later loads, and its identity defaults are tried before the catalog's, for profiles outside the catalog, as identity:<file>#<entry>. A keyedHexFile value source is refused on UMDF2, where the driver answers without calling the SDK.

On UMDF2 the SDK compiles a profile's answers into the controller's FeatureAnswers value, and the driver answers from it only for a 2.0.0 SDK's controller. A 1.x program's controller on the 2.0.0 driver gets no feature answers.

docs.title: Three runtime architecture groups
docs.text: The profile fields determine which of three architecture groups the runtime instance lands in. USB/IP profiles ("backend": "usbip"), the composite personas and the GameCube adapter, are none of the three: see Composite USB Personas. Disposal speed, device-tree shape, and downstream API mechanics all vary by group. See Lifecycle and Teardown for the per-group teardown latency table. The create and dispose times in the headings below were measured before v2.0.0.

docs.title: 1. Plain HID (~200 ms create, ~80 ms dispose)
docs.text:
Profiles on HIDMaestro's UMDF2 driver with no XInput presentation. The parent is ROOT\HIDClass\<token>. As of v2.0.0 that includes the nine Microsoft profiles that are no XInput device, the SideWinder Force Feedback 2 and eight keyboards and mice, which carry no IG_ and no XUSB compatible IDs, so SDL now lists them.

Includes DualSense, DualShock 4, all Logitech wheels, Thrustmaster HOTAS, flight sticks, pedals, arcade sticks, every keyboard and mouse, and most of the 337-profile catalog (307 profiles).

ROOT\HIDClass\<token>               ← UMDF2 driver (mshidumdf host)
  └─ HID\VID_054C&PID_0CE6\...       ← raw HID PDO, no upper filter

Lightest stack. One DIF_REMOVE on the ROOT parent tears down the entire tree. No XUSB companion device, no Microsoft upper filter.

docs.title: 2. Non-xinputhid Xbox (~200-700 ms create, ~135 ms dispose)
docs.text:
Profiles whose xinput block names "via": "xusbCompanion", the Xbox 360 family. XInput is delivered via a separate SWD-enumerated XUSB companion device running HMXInput.dll. WGI dispatch also runs through that companion, admitted by the xinputhid UpperFilter tripwire.

Includes Xbox 360 Wired (xbox-360-wired), Xbox 360 Type 2, Xbox 360 Wireless, Xbox 360 dance pad, Xbox 360 Arcade Stick, Xbox 360 Wheel V1/V2, Xbox 360 Guitar V1/V2 and the Xbox 360 flight stick: a 10-profile group. Xbox Adaptive is not in it. It sets driverMode: xinputhid and belongs to the group below.

ROOT\VID_045E&PID_028E&IG_00\NNNN    ← UMDF2 driver (main HID device)
  │                                    UpperFilters += "xinputhid" per-instance
  │                                    (SDK-written; blocks WGI from synthesizing
  │                                    a duplicate HID-backed Gamepad)
  └─ HID\VID_045E&PID_028E&IG_00\... ← HID child (raw PDO, input.inf)
SWD\HIDMAESTRO\<sid>_NNNN            ← XUSB companion (HMXInput.dll)
  │                                    SwDeviceCreate, System class, explicit
  │                                    per-controller ContainerID (shared with main HID).
  │                                    UpperFilters = "xinputhid" from INF
  │                                    (admits the companion to WGI's XUSB
  │                                    dispatch; xinputhid.sys does not actually
  │                                    attach: wrong device class).
  └─ XUSB interface → XInput slot + WGI Gamepad

Medium stack, fast on both sides post-v1.3.2. Two device trees to tear down. The XUSB companion runs its own WUDFHost instance hosting HMXInput.dll, which needs its own PnP release cycle.

docs.title: 3. xinputhid Xbox (~150-600 ms create, ~500 ms dispose)
docs.text:
Profiles with driverMode: "xinputhid". These match xinputhid.inf [GIP_Hid] by hardware ID (HID\VID_045E&PID_0B13&IG_00), which binds Microsoft's xinputhid.sys as an upper filter on the HID child. xinputhid provides XInput delivery and 16-button HID descriptor synthesis natively: no XUSB companion needed, single Device Manager entry.

Includes the whole Xbox One / Series / Elite family, wired and Bluetooth: xbox-series-xs, xbox-series-xs-bt, xbox-one-s, xbox-one-s-bt, xbox-one-s-bt-full, xbox-one-original, xbox-one-rev1, xbox-elite-v1, xbox-elite-v2, xbox-elite-v2-bt, xbox-elite-v2-bt-v2 and xbox-adaptive. Twelve profiles using Microsoft's GIP-over-HID protocol.

SWD\HIDMAESTRO_VID_045E_PID_0B13&IG_00\<sid>_NNNN
  │                                  ← UMDF2 driver via SwDeviceCreate
  │                                    (mshidumdf host). Explicit non-sentinel
  │                                    ContainerID closes the slot-1-skip
  │                                    bit-2 path in xinput1_4!FUN_18000de2c.
  │                                    Underscore between VID and PID avoids
  │                                    the `VID_*&PID_*&IG_*` PnP edge case;
  │                                    `&IG_00` retained for HIDAPI/SDL3/Chromium.
  └─ HID\HIDMAESTRO_VID_045E_PID_0B13&IG_00\...
        │                            ← HID child (xinputhid.inf, xinputhid
        │                              upper filter)
        ├─ xinputhid.sys              ← Microsoft inbox kernel filter
        ├─ XInput delivery (internal)
        └─ 16-button HID synthesis

Both sides fast post-v1.3.2. xinputhid is a Microsoft inbox kernel filter driver; we don't ship it. The SwD-first removal ordering in v1.3.1 closes the SwD parent first, and the children cascade automatically.

The 16-button synthesis is a known trade-off. Win11's xinputhid replaces the source descriptor's button declaration with a 15+ button Xbox One layout. This is incompatible with profiles that need the Xbox 360's 10-button fidelity through DirectInput (btnfix.c exists in the repo as an experimental approach but is incomplete: the trade-off stands as of v1.3.4). For Xbox 360 Wired the catalog profile uses driverMode=null + XUSB companion to keep 10 buttons through DI; for Xbox Series BT it accepts 16 buttons because the source descriptor already has 12 and the +4 are dead bits.

docs.title: How CreateController resolves a profile
docs.text:
1. Index allocation. Linear scan from 0; first free index wins. Locked.
  2. Architecture group selection. Branch on the presentation, the xinput block or the one the profile takes from a model:
  3. no XInput → plain HID
  4. "via": "xusbCompanion" → non-xinputhid Xbox (XUSB companion)
  5. "via": "xinputhid", or driverMode: "xinputhid" → xinputhid Xbox
  6. Container ID assignment. Per-controller GUID {48494430-4D41-4553-5452-4F00...<idx>} (ASCII "HIDMAESTRO" + 16-bit index). Shared by the main HID and any companion so xinput1_4 and Settings dedupe them. See SwDevice and PnP.
  7. Per-instance registry write. Writes ControllerIndex, Vid, Pid, ProductString, ManufacturerString, DeviceDescription, ReportDescriptor (REG_BINARY), the compiled feature and XUSB answers, etc. to HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro\Controller<index> and the device's HW key. The driver reads these at EvtDeviceAdd.
  8. Device creation. Plain HID via SetupDiCreateDeviceInfoW; SWD profiles via SwDeviceCreate (called through hmswd.exe to bypass a .NET P/Invoke incompat).
  9. PnP wait. Polls the HID child for DN_STARTED. Up to 10 s on slow machines; typically <100 ms.
  10. XInput slot-claim wait for Xbox profiles. Capped at 500 ms post-v1.3.2 to avoid 13-14 s freezes when xinputhid's allocator is in a stuck state.
  11. UpperFilter writes for non-xinputhid Xbox profiles. INF carries it on the companion; SDK writes per-instance on the main HID device.
  12. Friendly-name application. Best-effort; finalize via HMContext.FinalizeNames after all controllers are created.

The full per-archetype sequence lives in DeviceOrchestrator.cs's SetupController (~390 lines). See Lifecycle and Teardown for the disposal counterpart.

docs.title: Loading the catalog
docs.text:
// Embedded catalog (337 profiles)
ctx.LoadDefaultProfiles();

// Custom directory of JSON profiles
ctx.LoadProfilesFromDirectory(@"C:\my-profiles");

// Mix both. An id already loaded refuses the later file.
ctx.LoadDefaultProfiles();
ctx.LoadProfilesFromDirectory(@"C:\my-extra-profiles");

// What a load refused, and why
foreach (var issue in ctx.ProfileLoadIssues)
    Console.WriteLine(issue);   // file at $.json.path: reason

// Lookup
HMProfile? p = ctx.GetProfile("xbox-360-wired");

// Enumerate
foreach (var profile in ctx.AllProfiles)
    Console.WriteLine($"{profile.Id}: {profile.Name}");

Profiles are loaded into the context's catalog. As of v2.0.0 they load strictly. A file that does not parse, a key the schema lacks, a key written twice, a value a check refuses, a removed spelling (steamFirmwareStamp, the ds3-battery type, usbConfiguration.protocol) and an id already loaded each refuse the file. None of them throws from the load. Each becomes an HMProfileLoadIssue in HMContext.ProfileLoadIssues, with File, ProfileId, JsonPath (as the file writes it, such as $.protocol.rules[3].reply[1].length), Reason and Kind: Refused, NotAProfile for a file with no id, or ModelProblem for a profile that loaded with a model problem. Files load in ordinal path order, and a repeated id refuses the later file and names the earlier one, so an edited copy of a catalog profile needs an id of its own. Schema files (schema.json) and the directory's top-level models folder are not read as profiles.

docs.title: Checking a profile before you ship it
docs.text:
HIDMaestroProfileCheck, in the release ZIP beside the profile extractor, loads the catalog and then a profile file or directory as the SDK does. It prints each issue of the named files as <file> at <JSON path>: <reason>, and each loaded profile with its DeviceModelSource:

HIDMaestroProfileCheck [--cost [--launches N] [--runs N] [--reports N] [--register name=value ...]] <file or directory> ...

It exits 0 when every named file loads clean, 1 when one has an issue or a measurement fails, and 2 on a usage error. --cost runs each of the file's report programs and decoders on the interpreter, as a profile from outside the catalog runs them: 30 hidden launches at high priority by default, each the median of 10 runs of 100,000 reports, printing p50 and p95 with the runtime, tiering, CPU and instruction set, and each program's compile and the whole model's. Registers start at the protocol's initial values, so a block a host's command turns on runs only with --register setting it, as featureEnabled=0x04 turns on the Switch 2 Pro's motion in report 0x05.

A consumer that wants to ship a subset of the catalog (e.g. only racing wheels) loads just that subset:

ctx.LoadProfilesFromDirectory(@"C:\my-app\racing-wheels-only");
// Don't call LoadDefaultProfiles

Consumers that want to modify a built-in profile clone via HMProfileBuilder.FromProfile:

var modded = new HMProfileBuilder()
    .FromProfile(ctx.GetProfile("dualsense")!)
    .Pid(0x9999)
    .ProductString("Modded DualSense")
    .Build();

using var ctrl = ctx.CreateController(modded);   // not loaded into ctx.AllProfiles

The modded profile isn't registered in the catalog: it's used directly for one CreateController call. See Custom Profiles for the full clone / build / spoof patterns.

docs.title: A verbatim profile dissected: Xbox 360 Wired
docs.text:
{
  "id": "xbox-360-wired",
  "name": "Xbox 360 Controller (Wired)",
  "vendor": "Microsoft",
  "vid": "0x045E",
  "pid": "0x028E",
  "productString": "Controller (XBOX 360 For Windows)",
  "manufacturerString": "©Microsoft Corporation",
  "type": "gamepad",
  "connection": "usb",
  "descriptor": "05010905a101a10009300931150026ffff350046ffff950275108102c0a10009330934150026ffff350046ffff950275108102c0a1000932150026ffff350046ffff950175108102c0a10009400941150026ffff350046ffff950275108102c005091901290a950a7501810205010939150125083500463b10660e00750495018142750295018103750895028103c0",
  "nativeDescriptor": "05010905A1018501093009311500270000000075109502810209330934810209320935810205091901290A150025017501950281027506950181010501093915012508350046C03C660E007504950181428503060046ED01950E091001110050B5",
  "xinput": { "via": "xusbCompanion" },
  "inputReportSize": 18,
  "deviceDescription": "Controller (XBOX 360 For Windows)",
  "triggerMode": "combined"
}

descriptor is the HIDMaestro-emitted descriptor. nativeDescriptor is the original from a real Xbox 360 controller. They differ because the catalog version uses Vx/Vy velocity usages to carry separate trigger values without DirectInput recognizing them as axes. The native descriptor declares Z + Rz directly; HIDMaestro's emitted version uses Z (combined trigger) + Vx + Vy (separate triggers) so DirectInput sees 5 axes (matching real xusb22.sys behavior) while WGI / browsers see separate triggers via the GameInput registry mapping. See Cross-API Coverage.

inputReportSize: 18 is the whole report on the wire. The descriptor declares no Report ID, so there is no ID byte: 144 bits of axes, buttons, hat and padding.

triggerMode: "combined" annotates the descriptor's trigger encoding for this profile. The HIDMaestro-emitted descriptor declares one Z axis carrying LT - RT per real xusb22 DI semantics. All Xbox profiles present as 5 axes with combined Z in DirectInput regardless of triggerMode value: on profiles where triggerMode == "separate" (e.g. Xbox Series BT), xinputhid's synthesis layer collapses the descriptor's separate Z + Rz back into combined Z by the time DI reads the preparsed data. WGI and browser see separate triggers through the Vx/Vy + GameInput-mapping path.

xinput names "via": "xusbCompanion", so this profile lands in architecture group 2 (non-xinputhid Xbox + XUSB companion), and the companion answers as a wired gamepad.

buttonMap is not present: identity Xbox layout (HMButton.A → descriptor button 0, etc.).

docs.title: Catalog statistics
docs.text:
As of v2.0.0:

Metric Count Total profiles 337 Keyboards and mice 103 (51 keyboards, 52 mice) Vendor folders 59 Plain HID profiles 307 Non-xinputhid Xbox profiles 10 xinputhid Xbox profiles 12 USB/IP profiles 8 (seven composite personas and the GameCube adapter) With FFB descriptors 14 (SideWinder Force Feedback 2, the Xbox One / Series / Elite family, Amazon Luna BLE) Bluetooth profiles 26 Wireless-adapter profiles 4

The largest vendor folders are Logitech (46), misc (32, the catch-all), Microsoft (31), Razer (22), Thrustmaster (20), and Sony (17).

docs.title: Technical Reference
docs.text:
Every layer of HIDMaestro from the C# SDK down to the kernel-side HID stack. Read the first five in order for the full picture.

  • Architecture Overview: the stack diagram from SDK to driver, per-controller WUDFHost processes, and the three architecture groups.
  • UMDF2 Driver Internals: driver.c, the IOCTL dispatch table, the device context, and the event-driven worker.
  • XUSB Companion: how Xbox-family profiles get XInput without a kernel driver.
  • SwDevice and PnP: device creation, container IDs, and the XInput slot-0 story.
  • Shared Memory Protocol: the five sections per controller, the seqlock, and the named events.
  • Cross-API Coverage: how DirectInput, XInput, SDL3/HIDAPI, the browser Gamepad API, and WGI are each satisfied.
  • Multi-Controller: verified mixed-type operation and per-API ordering.
  • Lifecycle and Teardown: create paths, removal ordering, and round-trip latencies by archetype.
  • Driver Install and Signing: the embedded payload, certificate generation, and the idempotent install.
  • Build and Release: the dual-architecture build, the build settings, NativeAOT and the release recipe.
  • Testing and Verification: scripts/verify.py and the 99-scenario regression battery.
  • References: authoritative sources for every load-bearing claim in these docs.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text:
The 30,000-foot view of HIDMaestro: every component, what it owns, and how data flows from a consumer's SubmitState call to a game seeing input. Use this page as the starting point for the architecture chapter; the deep-dive subpages cover one component each.

docs.title: 1. HIDMaestro.Core.dll: the SDK
docs.text:
Lives in the consumer process. Exposes HMContext, HMController, HMProfile, etc. (see SDK Reference).

Responsibilities:

  • Embed the driver payload (driver DLLs, INFs, signing toolchain, hmswd.exe) and stage it, as of v2.0.0, under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging in directories only Administrators and SYSTEM can write, checking each file's SHA-256 before it runs.
  • Generate a self-signed certificate, sign the binaries, run pnputil /add-driver. Deploys take the machine-wide deploy lock, HIDMaestro.Admin\Deploy, a mutex in a namespace only elevated programs can open. They never downgrade an installed driver. They install the 2.0.0 driver over any older one, a full deploy with nothing on it or this build's packages added beside it when another program's devices hold it.
  • Claim ownership machine-wide (v2.0.0): the process, each controller's transport index and each identity are named pipes created with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE under the pipe prefix ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\, where only an elevated program can create one, and a record under HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOwners names the process and its controllers. Sweeps remove only what exited programs left.
  • Allocate per-context slots and machine-wide transport indices, and orchestrate SetupController (registry write → SwDeviceCreate or SetupDiCreateDeviceInfoW → PnP wait → XInput slot-claim wait).
  • Compile a profile's device model at create (v2.0.0): ports, the USB/IP device protocol and the WinUSB binding are JSON, and the SDK refuses a profile that declares them wrongly before it takes anything machine-wide.
  • Provide the abstract HMGamepadState → HID descriptor encoding.
  • Run the per-controller output-reader background thread that drains the shared output ring at ~125 Hz.
  • Manage HID PID 1.0 force-feedback shared state.
  • Manage joy.cpl OEM-name overrides with crash-safe restore.
  • Embed and load the 337-profile catalog, through source-generated JSON, so the SDK also runs in NativeAOT and trimmed single-file apps (v2.0.0).

Lines of code: ~5,300 in public surface (HMContext / HMController / HidDescriptorBuilder / HMProfileBuilder / HMDeviceExtractor / HMOemNameOverride / value types) plus ~16,600 in Internal/ (DeviceOrchestrator, DeviceManager, SwdDeviceFactory, DriverBuilder, HidDescriptorReconstructor, HidReportBuilder, SharedMemoryIO, OemNameOverrideStore, PnputilHelper, etc.).

docs.title: 2. HIDMaestro.dll: the UMDF2 driver
docs.text:
Lives in a per-controller WUDFHost.exe instance. Compiled from driver/driver.c (2,782 lines). Acts as a UMDF2 lower filter under mshidumdf.sys: the standard pattern from Microsoft's vhidmini2 sample. The HID class stack sees a real HID device; HIDMaestro is the user-mode component that:

  • Synthesizes the descriptor from the per-controller registry key written by the SDK at create time.
  • Owns a worker thread (WorkerThread) that opens the per-controller shared input section and signals on Global\HIDMaestroInputEvent<N> to wake on each new frame.
  • Handles IOCTL_HID_READ_REPORT synchronously when there's new data (seqno gate); otherwise pends in ManualQueue and completes from the worker thread.
  • Handles IOCTL_UMDF_HID_GET_FEATURE / _SET_FEATURE / _SET_OUTPUT_REPORT for HID PID 1.0 and for vendor output reports. Output IOCTLs publish into the shared output ring with OutputLock serialization.
  • Handles HID string queries (HID_STRING_ID_IPRODUCT / IMANUFACTURER / ISERIALNUMBER) from per-instance fields.
  • Writes its half of Global\HIDMaestroVersion<N> each time it opens the input section (v2.0.0), so the SDK can read the driver's version and protocol.

INF: hidmaestro.inf. Class GUID: {745a17a0-74d3-11d0-b6fe-00a0c90f57da} (HIDClass). LowerFilters = WUDFRd. UmdfHostProcessSharing = ProcessSharingDisabled so each instance gets its own host process.

Detail: UMDF2 Driver Internals.

docs.title: 3. HMXInput.dll: the XUSB companion
docs.text:
Lives in a separate per-controller WUDFHost.exe. Compiled from driver/companion.c (957 lines). Acts as a UMDF2 function driver under the System setup class. Created only for non-xinputhid Xbox profiles (Xbox 360 Wired family). Responsibilities:

  • Register the XUSB device interface ({EC87F1E3-...}) for xinput1_4.dll discovery.
  • Run an 8 ms WAIT_FOR_INPUT pump that drains pended IOCTL_XUSB_WAIT_FOR_INPUT requests with 29-byte XUSB-state replies. Required for WGI's async input pump (XusbDevice::QueueInputBuffer).
  • Translate the 14-byte GIP-format buffer the SDK packs in shared memory into XINPUT_GAMEPAD wire format on IOCTL_XUSB_GET_STATE.
  • Capture IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE 5-byte vibration packets and publish them into the output ring as HMOutputSource.XInput.
  • Answer IOCTL_XUSB_GET_BATTERY_INFO and IOCTL_XUSB_GET_LED_STATE. Both replies carry a two-byte version word before the payload, and the battery reply is 00 00 01 03, wired and full.
  • Carry a registry-string UpperFilters = "xinputhid". This does not load the kernel filter, because the System class is not a filter target. It passes WGI's IsDeviceOrAncestorFilteredBy wcsncmp check, which admits the device to WGI's XUSB dispatch path.

INF: hidmaestro_xusb.inf. Class GUID: {4D36E97D-...} (System). Created via SwDeviceCreate with explicit per-controller ContainerID (shared with the main HID device).

Detail: XUSB Companion.

docs.title: 4. hmswd.exe: the SwDevice helper
docs.text:
Standalone native executable (~299 lines C). Created only because .NET 10's P/Invoke to cfgmgr32!SwDeviceCreate returns 0x8007007E ERROR_MOD_NOT_FOUND on Win11 26200, while the identical C call succeeds. Neither CoInitializeEx, preloaded DLLs, UnmanagedCallersOnly function pointers, nor explicit function-ptr marshaling fix it. Rather than ship a broken managed migration path, the SDK invokes this small helper via Process.Start.

Args: create | remove <enumerator> <suffix> <container-guid> <hw-ids> <compat-ids> <description>. Returns the resulting instance ID on stdout for the SDK to record.

Lifetime: SWDeviceLifetimeParentPresent so the device persists past process exit. remove reconnects to the previously-created device by re-SwDeviceCreate-ing with identical args (the docs guarantee this returns a fresh handle to the existing device), downgrades lifetime to Handle, then SwDeviceClose.

Detail: SwDevice and PnP.

docs.title: 5. The 337-profile catalog
docs.text:
Embedded as a JSON resource inside HIDMaestro.Core.dll. 73 vendors across 59 folders, 1 to 46 profiles each, 103 of the profiles keyboards and mice. See Profile System for the schema and runtime classification.

A profile can describe more than a report. As of v2.0.0 extendedReport.ports describes a report that carries several controllers, the top-level protocol describes the commands a USB/IP device answers and when it sends input, stateBlock and inputReports describe a device that builds its reports from its own state, and usbConfiguration.winUsb names the interface GUID a WinUSB binding registers. The SDK checks them when a file loads and compiles them once at create. The Wii U GameCube adapter and the Switch 2 Pro composite use them, and no SDK code names either device. A profile takes the feature answers, protocol and presentation it does not carry itself from a model it names with deviceModelFrom, or from the identity defaults. See Device models. See Wii U GameCube Adapter and Profile System.

docs.title: Process / privilege model
docs.text:
Process Privilege Purpose Consumer process Admin (or non-admin for read-only operations) Hosts HIDMaestro.Core.dll. Drives SubmitState from any thread. Several consumer processes can run on one machine (v2.0.0). WUDFHost.exe (main HID, per-controller) LocalService Hosts HIDMaestro.dll. Spawned by WUDFRd.sys per device instance. WUDFHost.exe (XUSB companion, per-controller) LocalService Hosts HMXInput.dll. Only spawned for non-xinputhid Xbox profiles. hmswd.exe (helper, transient) Inherits caller's privilege (admin) Calls SwDeviceCreate, returns instance ID, exits. Lifetime <1 s per invocation.

UmdfHostProcessSharing = ProcessSharingDisabled in both INFs ensures per-controller hosts. With 6 controllers running you'll see 6-12 WUDFHost.exe instances depending on which profiles are active. ~8 MB RSS, ~10 threads each.

This was a deliberate fix. Default (ProcessSharingEnabled, the WDF directive defined in INF [...NT.Wdf] sections) funnels every instance into one shared WUDFHost; at 6 controllers that host accumulates 9+ minutes of CPU time vs ~2 seconds per per-instance host. The contention is between writer threads and concurrent XInputGetState reader threads when 2+ virtuals coexist with a real xinputhid device in the same host. See docs/investigations/issue3-dual-xinputhid-saturation-2026-04/ for the full investigation.

docs.title: Several programs on one machine
docs.text: Windows sees devices, so two programs that embed HIDMaestro share one driver, one XInput slot table and one set of machine-wide object names. As of v2.0.0 each program keeps its own part of that: an owner claim, a transport index and an identity per controller, and a record naming them. A sweep removes a device only when its program's claim is gone. The driver is deployed by one program at a time, never downgraded, and installed over any older driver whatever runs on it. A program built on v1.12.0 is judged live by its owner pipe. While such a program runs, transport indices start at 64, out of its way. It still removes every HIDMaestro device on the machine at its InstallDriver and its first create, so programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0. See Programs Side by Side.

docs.title: Data flow: input
docs.text:
A consumer's HMController.SubmitState(state) call arrives at every downstream API in this order:

Consumer thread
  ↓ HMController.SubmitState(state)
SDK encodes state → HID native bytes via HidReportBuilder
  ↓
Writes Data[] + GipData[] + SeqNo to Global\HIDMaestroInput<N>
  ↓ SetEvent on Global\HIDMaestroInputEvent<N>
─────── shared memory boundary ────────
Driver worker thread wakes (WaitForMultipleObjects on Stop+Input events)
  ↓ ProcessSharedInput
Reads SeqNo, Data[], DataSize
  ↓ WdfRequestComplete on pended IOCTL_HID_READ_REPORT (if pending)
HidClass.sys delivers to:
  ├─ DirectInput consumers (dinput8.dll)
  ├─ HIDAPI consumers (Chromium RawInput, SDL3 HIDAPI fallback)
  └─ WGI (Windows.Gaming.Input.dll)
        └─ Browser Gamepad

For profiles with an XUSB companion, in parallel:
GIP buffer is read by the XUSB companion on IOCTL_XUSB_GET_STATE
  ↓ companion translates 14-byte GIP → XINPUT_GAMEPAD wire format
XInput consumers (xinput1_4.dll → XInputGetState)
  └─ via XUSB device interface {EC87F1E3-...}
WGI also reads from the XUSB path (admitted via xinputhid UpperFilter tripwire)

End-to-end latency from SubmitState to a DirectInput GetDeviceState poll seeing the new bytes: typically <2 ms. The shared-memory write is ~250 ns, the event signal is ~5 µs, the worker wake is ~50 µs, the IOCTL completion is ~100 µs, the consumer's poll cycle is whatever rate they run at.

docs.title: Data flow: output
docs.text:
Game / DInput PID FFB / Browser put_Vibration / XInputSetState
  ↓ IOCTL_UMDF_HID_SET_OUTPUT_REPORT (or IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE on XUSB companion)
Driver / companion captures bytes
  ↓ takes OutputLock
  ↓ increments Head, writes Slots[(Head-1) % 64]
─────── shared memory boundary ────────
SDK output reader thread on next poll (~8 ms cadence)
  ↓ TryReadOutputFrame: Head moved, drain new slots in seqlock-safe order
Raises HMController.OutputReceived(packet) on poll thread
  ↓ Consumer handler decodes per (Source, ReportId)

Multiple OutputReceived invocations per poll iteration are normal: PID FFB writes Set Effect → Set Constant Force → Effect Operation Start within 1-3 ms and all three drain on the next poll.

docs.title: The three architecture groups (recap)
docs.text:
Group Profiles Device tree Notes Plain HID DualSense, Logitech wheels, Thrustmaster HOTAS, and everything outside the Xbox families ROOT\HIDClass\<token> Lightest stack. No companion. Non-xinputhid Xbox Xbox 360 Wired family (~6) ROOT\VID_045E&PID_*&IG_00\<token> + SWD\HIDMAESTRO\<token> Two device trees. XUSB companion. xinputhid Xbox Xbox Series BT, Xbox One BT, Xbox Elite v2 BT (~4) SWD\HIDMAESTRO_VID_045E_PID_*&IG_00\<token> xinputhid kernel filter binds upstream. SwD-enumerated parent.

<token> is the controller's identity token, the same on every life of that controller: see SwDevice and PnP.

See Profile System for the runtime classification and Lifecycle and Teardown for per-group create/dispose latencies.

docs.title: What HIDMaestro is not
docs.text:
For symmetry with PadForge's wiki, here's what's deliberately out of scope:

  • A polling engine. No internal pump thread for input. Consumers drive cadence.
  • A controller mapper. No deadzones, sensitivity curves, button remapping at runtime: that's the consumer's job. PadForge handles the mapping; HIDMaestro just creates the virtuals.
  • A standalone app. No UI, no settings, no config files of its own. The catalog is JSON in a DLL; the SDK is an API.
  • A kernel driver. Everything is user-mode. UMDF2 + self-signed cert + TrustedPublisher. No EV cert, no bcdedit /set testsigning, no reboot.
  • A bus driver. UMDF2 cannot publish PDOs. The XUSB companion is a peer device under the System class, not a child PDO of the main HID.
  • An anti-cheat bypass. Virtual devices are detectable. HIDMaestro doesn't try to hide.
  • A force-feedback synthesizer. The SDK delivers raw decoded packets. Effect mixing and condition synthesis are the consumer's job.
