• HID Usage Tables 1.5: Vx/Vy usage codes (Generic Desktop §4). Download from usb.org/document-library.
  • W3C Gamepad API: STANDARD_GAMEPAD mapping bucket.
  • Chromium gamepad backend: &IG_ skip semantics in RawInput.
  • HIDAPI: the Windows backend at windows/hid.c has bus type detection (the BTHENUM and BTHLEDEVICE compatible ID checks).
  • SDL3: XInput / RawInput / HIDAPI fallback hierarchy under src/joystick/windows/.
  • XInput documentation: search Microsoft Learn for "XInput Game Controller APIs". 4-slot cap, XInputGetState semantics.
  • docs/investigations/wgi-silent-sink-2026-04/: Ghidra decomp of WGI's OnPnpDeviceAdded classifier and IsDeviceOrAncestorFilteredBy.
  • References: full source bibliography for every claim in this wiki.

docs.title: Driver installation and signing
docs.text: Standard profiles use HIDMaestro's UMDF2 DLLs and a locally trusted signing certificate. Composite profiles use bundled Microsoft-signed USB/IP kernel-driver packages.

docs.title: Native payloads
docs.text:
The AnyCPU SDK selects native files from the operating system architecture, including when an x64 consumer runs under emulation on ARM64 Windows.

Resource Purpose HIDMaestro.dll Main HID driver HMXInput.dll XInput companion hmswd.exe Device creation and USB/IP root helper hidmaestro.inf, hidmaestro_xusb.inf Architecture-specific, stamped INFs signtool.exe and dependencies Signing tools for the selected OS Inf2Cat.exe and dependencies Catalog generation Profile JSON files Controller identities and report layouts

Official releases embed the drivers, helpers and signing tools for x64 and ARM64. A build from source can leave out the ARM64 payload or the USB/IP transport, and HMBuildInfo reports what a build carries (see Build and Release). One Inf2Cat serves both architectures. It is an x64 .NET program, which Windows 11 on ARM64 runs under its x64 emulation. Catalog generation uses 10_X64 for x64 and 10_RS3_ARM64 for ARM64.

docs.title: Local certificate
docs.text:
The installer creates CN=HIDMaestroTestCert if it is absent from the machine certificate store. It uses RSA-2048, SHA-256, PKCS#1 signing, and the Code Signing EKU. The certificate expires ten years after creation.

The private key is persisted in LocalMachine\My. The certificate is also installed in LocalMachine\Root and LocalMachine\TrustedPublisher.

The installer signs HIDMaestro.dll and HMXInput.dll, generates catalogs for their INFs, signs those catalogs, and adds the packages through PnP. It does not enable Windows test-signing mode.

docs.title: Staging
docs.text:
As of v2.0.0, everything the elevated SDK runs or hands to pnputil is staged per version and per operation under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging\<version>-<hash>\<operation>, where the hash is the first 16 hex characters of the embedded driver payload's SHA-256. The operations are driver (the embedded driver binaries, both INFs, signtool and Inf2Cat), package (one deploy's binaries and INFs, signed and cataloged), swd (hmswd.exe), usbip (the usbip-win2 installer), usbip-ude (the host controller package forced onto an older transport) and winusb-<profile id> (one profile's WinUSB package). A deploy stages the binaries fresh into package and checks their SHA-256 again just before signing, so another process staging the payload cannot put unsigned bytes under a package being signed. Through v1.12.0 the payload went to %TEMP%, which a process of the same user that is not elevated can write.

Program Files grants Users read and execute and nothing else, so no program without elevation can create a folder there before HIDMaestro does. %ProgramData% lets Users add folders, which is why staging moved, before release, from %ProgramData% to %ProgramFiles%. Every directory from %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro down is created with its security descriptor in the same call, O:BAG:BAD:P(A;OICI;FA;;;SY)(A;OICI;FA;;;BA), so none exists with an inherited ACL.

Each use checks every directory on its path. A directory passes when it is not a reparse point, its owner is Administrators or SYSTEM, and no allow entry grants a write-class right (write data, append data, write attributes or extended attributes, delete, delete child, change permissions, take ownership) to anyone but SYSTEM, Administrators and TrustedInstaller. %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro is reset in place when SYSTEM or Administrators own it and nobody else may change its permissions or owner or delete it or its entries, and refused with InvalidOperationException otherwise, since a hostile one there is another program's. Staging, a version or an operation directory that fails is moved aside to <name>.untrusted-<guid> and created again. One that cannot be moved is refused when it is hostile in the same sense, and reset in place when only its permissions are wrong. A moved-aside tree is left where it is and never deleted. A directory another program creates between the check and the create is refused too.

Every elevated use of a staged file runs inside a pin. Staging and each directory below it down to the one in use are held open without delete sharing, which no rename or delete of them can get past. Each staged file is held for reading with read sharing only, which no write, rename or delete gets past, and checked against its SHA-256 through that hold: the embedded bytes, or the pinned release hash for the usbip-win2 files. A driver binary is checked right before signtool rewrites it and held once signed. The pin lasts until the use is over: the driver package's sign, catalog and add, hmswd's runs, the usbip-win2 installer's run, the host controller package's install and each WinUSB package's catalog and add. A file is written under a temporary name, verified, then renamed into place, and reuse trusts no file size. hmswd.exe always comes from the embedded resource, never from beside the assembly.

An elevated child gets a protected TEMP. hmswd, the usbip-win2 installer, signtool and Inf2Cat run with their own staging directory as working directory, TEMP and TMP. pnputil and devcon get %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\childtemp\<process id>-<start time>, a folder per process with the staging descriptor. An elevated tool that cannot have one does not run with the user's %TEMP%: the operation fails with InvalidOperationException, and a cleanup that only tries skips the tool and logs it. reg.exe and sc.exe, run from System32, keep the caller's TEMP.

The diagnostic logs, teardown_diag.log under HIDMAESTRO_DIAG=1 and setup_timing.log under HIDMAESTRO_TIMING=1, stay in %TEMP%\HIDMaestro and are written with the user's own rights: the elevated half of a split UAC token writes them through a medium-integrity token of the same user. So is the USB/IP read log at the path HIDMAESTRO_DIAG_READS names. hmswd's exit code and output go into teardown_diag.log when diagnostics are on. The per-create hmswd_<enumerator>_<suffix>.log is no longer written, and hmswd.exe keeps no self-log at all, run by the SDK or by hand, so hmswd_self.log is never written.

The staging directory is reused across launches. A deploy deletes the staging of every version that no running program's owner record names, and the childtemp folder of every process that no longer runs. A moved-aside directory is never pruned. The installed-manifest check avoids repeating deployment when this build's driver packages are already installed, and on that path nothing is staged at all.

The OpenVR driver is the one exception and stays under %ProgramData%\HIDMaestro\openvr\hidmaestro. SteamVR loads the driver name hidmaestro from one registered path, and a v1.12.0 program running beside this one registers that path again, so a driver moved anywhere else would be registered twice. Nothing the elevated SDK runs, loads or hands to a tool lives there. See VR Controllers.

Installing and creating virtual devices requires administrator privileges. Reading the profile catalog does not.

docs.title: Which driver a machine runs
docs.text:
Several programs that embed HIDMaestro 2.0.0 can share a machine. Every driver deploy holds the machine-wide deploy lock, HIDMaestro.Admin\Deploy, for one call, and re-reads the installed state once it holds it. The lock is a mutex in a private namespace that only an elevated program can create or open, so no other program can take it first. The USB/IP transport's install holds a lock of its own, HIDMaestro.Admin\Transport (see USB/IP transport). Programs Side by Side lists every lock. The installed version is the newest DriverVer among the hidmaestro.inf packages in the driver store. Stamps compare by release version first, then build date, then build number.

Installed driver InstallDriver HMContext.LastDriverInstall none installs this SDK's Installed this SDK's payload nothing AlreadyCurrent this SDK's stamp, both packages present, its record missing restores the record, reinstalls nothing AlreadyCurrent this SDK's stamp, a package missing adds the missing package and moves no device onto it Installed newer keeps it: a driver is never downgraded KeptNewer older, from 1.x or an older 2.0.0 build, nothing on it a full deploy that removes the old packages Upgraded older, devices or a create of another program on it adds this build's packages beside the old ones and updates no present device Upgraded

The 2.0.0 driver takes precedence over every older one, and nothing is refused because another program's devices hold an older driver. The add beside it updates no present device, so those controllers keep the driver their host loaded until their device restarts, while every device a 2.0.0 program creates binds the newest package. Programs built on 1.x must move to 2.0.0: see Moving from 1.x.

A create installs the driver on its own devnode only, with DiInstallDevice. With no driver named, DiInstallDevice searches the driver store for the best match, and that search was about half of a DualShock 4 create's time. Since v2.0.0 the SDK keeps the INF the search chose for a set of hardware and compatible IDs, with the state of the driver store it chose in: the installed-payload record every deploy rewrites and the last write of the store's FileRepository folder. While both are unchanged, a create builds the driver list from that one INF (DI_ENUMSINGLEINF), takes the best rank and passes that driver to DiInstallDevice. The choice is kept in the process and under HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro\StoreDriverChoice, one value per set of IDs, so a program's first create skips the search too, and the key goes with SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro when the packages are removed. A failure, a tie of ranks or a missing INF forgets the choice, and the create searches as before. Through v1.12.0 a create used UpdateDriverForPlugAndPlayDevices with the profile's hardware ID, which installs the package on every present device of that ID.

docs.title: WinUSB binding packages
docs.text: HMController.BindWinUsb() generates a driver package per profile from its descriptors, hmwinusb_<profile id>.inf, signs its catalog with the same local certificate, and adds it to the driver store without installing it anywhere. The add runs under the deploy lock, and the devnode work under HIDMaestro.Admin\WinUsb. The INF includes and needs winusb.inf and registers the profile's interface GUID. It matches only the vendor-scoped compatible ID USB\COMPAT_VID_vvvv&Class_cc&SubClass_ss&Prot_pp, behind fifteen IDs no device carries, so it ranks below input.inf for every real device. The bind confirms that another driver outranks the package on the devnode, then installs it there alone with DiInstallDevice. No driver is ever installed on a present devnode after that. Once the binding's last holder lets go and the devnode is gone, it gets CONFIGFLAG_REINSTALL, so its next arrival installs by rank. The uninstall-grade cleanup removes no devnode, and keeps a WinUSB package that a gone devnode still uses. A package it keeps is noted by INF name in HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroPackagesLeft, value WinUsb (REG_MULTI_SZ), and the first sweep of each later program that finds the note removes the noted packages no devnode, present or gone, still uses, and keeps the rest noted. See Wii U GameCube Adapter.

docs.title: USB/IP transport
docs.text:
The SDK contains the unmodified usbip-win2 0.9.8.1 installers, one for x64 and one for ARM64. The x64 one is the release asset. The ARM64 one is the same tag's build from the project's signing service, posted in usbip-win2#13, since the release page carries x64 only. Their Microsoft driver signatures are retained. Each is checked against its pinned SHA-256 at build time, and the extracted copy is checked again before it runs. A copy that fails the hash is replaced from the embedded bytes and never executed.

Deployment has four cases. If the host controller that answers is one HIDMaestro installed, 0.9.7.7 or 0.9.7.5, and nothing has used it in this Windows session, the SDK moves it to 0.9.8.1: it stages the embedded usbip2_ude INF, SYS and CAT, verified against their pinned hashes, and the hmswd.exe helper forces that INF onto the controller with UpdateDriverForPlugAndPlayDevices under a time limit. The filter is not touched, and the old package is deleted only once the 0.9.8.1 image is the one the service loads. If any other usbip-win2 host controller answers, the SDK uses it as it is, in whichever of the 0.9.7.x, 0.9.8.0 and 0.9.8.1 request layouts it speaks. If usbip-win2 is in the driver store and its host controller is not answering, the SDK restarts that device through CfgMgr and does not reinstall, because reinstalling would first remove the filter bound to every USB root hub. Only when no usbip-win2 exists, neither in the driver store nor as an installer record under {199505b0-b93d-4521-a8c7-897818e0205a}_is1, in any of the three places the installer itself looks, whose uninstaller file is still there, does the SDK run the installer for the machine's architecture and wait for the host controller to appear. It never runs the vendor uninstaller, and it never runs the installer over an existing copy, which would uninstall that copy first.

The install, the restart of a host controller that stopped answering, and the move off an older one run on a thread of their own under the machine-wide lock HIDMaestro.Admin\Transport, and read the machine again once they hold it. Of two programs whose first composites arrive together, one installs and the other finds the host controller. A UMDF2 create never waits for this lock. A restart whose PnP work outlives its time limit keeps the lock until that work returns, for as long as its program runs. The installer declares no setup mutex, so before it starts one the SDK waits up to five minutes for any usbip-win2 installer still running, such as one a killed program left. An installer that ends with an error does not fail the create on its own: the SDK waits for every usbip-win2 installer to end and reads the machine. With the driver package in the store, a host controller that answers counts as installed. A machine with nothing of usbip-win2 on it gets the installer once more. Anything between fails the create. InstallUsbipBackend's progress callback runs on the caller's thread with no machine-wide lock held, and an exception it throws is dropped. pnputil runs from System32 by its full path.

As of v2.0.0 the installer runs with the smallest set it allows:

/VERYSILENT /SUPPRESSMSGBOXES /NORESTART /COMPONENTS=main,client /TASKS=vcredist /NOICONS

That leaves out the GUI, the SDK headers, the debug symbols, the desktop icon and the Start menu folder. main and client cannot be deselected. client is the drivers. The VC++ runtime stays, because devnode.exe and the libusbip.dll it loads need it. /NORESTART is required, since the installer restarts the machine without asking otherwise. What the installer leaves and its command line cannot remove: usbip.exe, devnode.exe, libusbip.dll, resources.dll and Readme.md under Program Files, the uninstaller and its Apps entry, the scheduled task "USBip Detach All On Reboot Or Shutdown", and the VC++ runtime. Battery scenario S73 runs the install in Windows Sandbox and finds no Start menu folder, desktop shortcut, GUI, SDK or debug file afterward, the VC++ runtime in place, and a composite persona carrying input. It also checks that a machine holding the installer's record and its uninstaller file, without its driver, gets a refusal instead of an uninstall.

See platform support for the version choice and validation limits.

docs.title: Lifecycle and Teardown
docs.text:
The full create / dispose orchestration. Per-archetype create budget, the three wait gates (WaitForHidChild, WaitForDeviceStarted, WaitForXInputSlotClaim), the SwD-first removal ordering, the PnP lock and removal test (v2.0.0), batch teardown, and the sweep InstallDriver runs first, which since v2.0.0 removes only what programs that have exited left behind.

The mechanics here are what make multi-controller create / dispose / live-swap responsive enough for real consumer apps. The README's "Startup and Hot-Plug Timing" table summarizes the latencies; this page is the why.

For the SDK-side API, see SDK Reference. For the underlying PnP machinery, see SwDevice and PnP. For the multi-controller scenarios, see Multi-Controller.

docs.title: Create: SetupController orchestration
docs.text:
HMContext.CreateController(profile, identityKey) takes a slot in its context, then a machine-wide lease, then runs Internal.DeviceOrchestrator.SetupController(transportIndex, profile, identity). The sequence:

1. Device model compiled and payload checked, before anything machine-wide
   (ports, protocol and WinUSB blocks, and the driver or USB/IP payload this build carries)
2. Once-per-session sweep (first create only): devices and ledger holds
   of programs that have exited. A running program's devices are never touched.
   Also starts the once-per-process phantom cleanup on a background thread
3. Lease (v2.0.0), holding the phantom cleanup off until the last record write:
   census of owner records and present devices,
   identity claim for a keyed create (waits up to 120 s while no live record
   lists the key and another program's sweep holds it),
   transport index claim (from 64 while a v1.12.0 program runs),
   owner-record entry for the controller
   identity: token, ContainerID, ParentIdPrefix, serial, all from the identity key,
   or from the transport index when the caller passed none
   {48494430-4D41-4553-5452-4F00 + 16-bit index} for the index identity
4. Per-instance owner pipe, shared sections and events, N = transport index
   (HMController.SectionNames lists them), in this order:
   \\.\pipe\HIDMaestroOwner<N> first: a v1.12.0 program that took the index
     meanwhile holds it, and the create is refused before any section is written
   Global\HIDMaestroInput<N>, CompanionInputEvent<N>, InputAck<N>,
   InputAckEvent<N>, Version<N>, then InputEvent<N>, then Output<N>
   PID state section is lazy: only created on first PublishPidPool
   Global\HIDMaestroStopEvent<N> and OutputEvent<N> are the driver's, created
     in EvtDeviceAdd (a USB/IP persona's OutputEvent<N> is the SDK's)
5. Per-instance registry write
   HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro\Controller<N>:
     ReportDescriptor (REG_BINARY)
     VendorId / ProductId / VersionNumber (REG_DWORD)
     ProductString (REG_SZ)
     InputReportByteLength (REG_DWORD)
     InputReportId (REG_BINARY, v2.0.0): report ID, 32-bit length, descriptor
     FeatureAnswers (REG_BINARY, v2.0.0): the compiled feature answer table
   HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro\Identity\<token> (v2.0.0): the controller's index,
     which the driver reads before its first start
     [profile-specific extras]
     VendorId and ProductId are written first. DeviceInstanceId, which no
     driver read, is no longer written (v2.0.0)
6. Driver-store check (UMDF2 creates): a missing driver package deploys under
   the deploy lock, HIDMaestro.Admin\Deploy
7. Registration gate (v2.0.0), per devnode: rivals for the ParentIdPrefix and a
   prior life of the id removed, each removal under the PnP lock and its removal
   test, up to 30 s for Windows' pending installs (CMP_WaitNoPendingInstallEvents),
   then HIDMaestro.Admin\Pnp taken and one more look, up to three rounds
8. Device registration under the PnP lock, instance name = the identity token:
   plain HID profiles:    SetupDiCreateDeviceInfoW ROOT\HIDClass\<token>, ParentIdPrefix written before DIF_REGISTERDEVICE
   xinputhid profiles:    hmswd.exe create SWD\HIDMAESTRO_VID_*_PID_*&IG_00\<token>, ParentIdPrefix reconciled, then the restart
   non-xinputhid Xbox:    SetupDiCreateDeviceInfoW (main HID) + hmswd.exe create SWD\HIDMAESTRO\<token> (XUSB companion)
   the lock is let go after each registration, and the driver goes onto the new
   devnode alone with DiInstallDevice (v2.0.0)
9. WaitForHidChild       (10 s budget)
10. WaitForDeviceStarted  (5 s budget)
11. WaitForXInputSlotClaim (500 ms budget post-v1.3.2)
12. Per-instance UpperFilter writes (xinputhid-companion-XOR-tripwire profiles only)
13. Friendly-name application (best-effort, FinalizeNames runs the polled re-apply)

The driver wakes on PnP binding and reads its configuration from the registry written in step 5. The shared sections from step 4 are opened lazily by the driver (LocalService can't CreateFileMapping(Global\), only OpenFileMapping what the SDK already created).

If any step fails after the lease, TeardownController is run as a best-effort cleanup, then the lease is released, so the transport index and identity go back to the machine only once the devices are gone, and the exception reaches the consumer. A create refused with HMResourceInUseException, because a v1.12.0 program took its index or a running program's device holds its ParentIdPrefix, has made no device yet. It releases only what it made, its sections, ledger holds and configuration key, and leaves the index's devices to the program that owns them. Since v2.0.0 a create also throws InvalidOperationException when its device's prior life is still there after its removal, when a gamepad or XUSB companion is not made, and when another program holds the PnP lock for ten minutes. See Creates that now fail.

docs.title: Three wait gates
docs.text: After SwDeviceCreate (or SetupDiCreateDeviceInfoW) returns success, the device isn't fully usable yet. Three wait gates ensure we only return to the consumer when downstream APIs can read the device.

docs.title: Gate 1: WaitForHidChild (10 s)
docs.text:
PnP creates the HID child node under the parent we just created. Polls CM_Locate_DevNodeW for the expected child instance ID. Typical: <100 ms warm. Slow machines (Atom Z8350): up to 2 s. Cap at 10 s.

If this times out, SetupController throws InvalidOperationException and best-effort cleanup runs. Cause: usually a corrupt INF or DriverStore inconsistency: run HIDMaestroTest cleanup (or RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, false)), then InstallDriver, to repair.

docs.title: Gate 2: WaitForDeviceStarted (5 s)
docs.text:
Polls the HID child's DEVPKEY_Device_DevNodeStatus for DN_STARTED. The driver isn't fully bound until this status flips. Typical: <50 ms warm. Cap at 5 s.

Without this gate, an immediate SubmitState after CreateController returns could land before the driver has opened the shared section: the seqno never increments and no input reaches the consumer.

Both gates end within one 25 ms poll when the driver sets its error word, or when the devnode reports a failed start (problem 10, 31, 37, 39 or 43) while Windows has no device installation pending, and the create fails naming the device and the code. As of v2.0.0 a failed start is held while an installation is pending: a full cleanup removes the driver package, Windows flags each record that named it for reinstall, and a software parent revived from that record reports problem 18 and then 10 until the install Windows queued restarts it. A gate whose time runs out fails the create on any problem the devnode shows, 28 for a queued install that failed and 18 for one Windows put off included. The XUSB companion gets three waits for its interface, with a restart after each one that ends without it.

docs.title: Gate 3: WaitForXInputSlotClaim (500 ms post-v1.3.2)
docs.text:
For Xbox-family profiles only. Polls XInputGetState to confirm the controller has been assigned an XInput slot.

This gate was 15 s pre-v1.3.2 and was the dominant cost. Distribution is bimodal:

  • Healthy claim: <100 ms.
  • Stuck case: never publishes (kernel state issue, prior-session residue).

The 15 s budget burned the full duration on every stuck case. PadForge users observed 13-14 s freezes on a single Xbox Series BT create.

The 500 ms cap (post-v1.3.2) sits ~5x above the slowest observed healthy claim. Stuck cases now degrade to a near-imperceptible pause. Controller stays functional via DI / HIDAPI / Browser / WGI when XInput doesn't pick it up; XInput consumers see the slot appear lazily on their next poll cycle.

For non-Xbox profiles this gate is skipped entirely.

docs.title: Per-archetype create latency
docs.text:
Warm-start (driver already in DriverStore), measured before v2.0.0. The registration gate v2.0.0 adds before each devnode registration has not been timed on a live create:

Profile group Median Worst Notes Plain HID ~200 ms ~400 ms One device, no companion, no XInput Non-xinputhid Xbox ~300 ms ~700 ms Two devices (main HID + XUSB companion). XInput slot-claim wait ≤500 ms post-v1.3.2 xinputhid Xbox ~250 ms ~600 ms One SwD device; xinputhid kernel filter binds. XInput slot-claim wait ≤500 ms post-v1.3.2

Multi-controller (sequential), measured before v2.0.0:

Configuration Total 1 plain HID ~200 ms 4 mixed (2 BT + 2 wired) ~2.2-2.8 s 6 mixed ~3.5 s

Cold-start (first run on machine, includes cert generation + signing + install): ~18 s for the install + create-1 step, measured before v2.0.0. Subsequent creates are warm-start cost.

docs.title: Per-step install breakdown
docs.text:
Visible in stdout when HMContext.InstallDriver runs. The figures were measured before v2.0.0:

Step Cost Stage the embedded payload under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging and verify each file's SHA-256 not measured for v2.0.0 Remove old packages (idempotent guard) ~100 ms Sign DLLs and INFs ~130 ms Generate .cat catalogs (largest single step, AV-sensitive) ~840 ms pnputil /add-driver ~580 ms Total ~1.7 s

On corporate workstations with hundreds of devices in the PnP tree, total install can stretch to 5-20 s. HIDMaestro deliberately doesn't run pnputil /scan-devices (it's a no-op for our INFs and was the largest variable contributor in profiling).

docs.title: Self-healing on init
docs.text:
HMContext.InstallDriver sweeps first thing, before the deploy:

public void InstallDriver()
{
    ThrowIfDisposed();
    HMBuildInfo.ThrowIfMissing(HMPayload.Driver);
    Internal.OwnerSweep.ReclaimDeadOwners();       // what exited programs left
    LastDriverInstall = Internal.DriverDeploy.Run();
}

Since v2.0.0 the sweep removes only the devices of programs that have exited, and the deploy installs the 2.0.0 driver over any older one, beside it when another program's devices hold it, and never downgrades a newer one. The first InstallDriver of a process also starts the once-per-process phantom cleanup on a background thread, unless a create or RemoveAllVirtualControllers() started it first. See Programs Side by Side.

Without the sweep, when a prior process crashed or was force-killed (Dispose never ran), its virtual controllers + HIDMAESTRO PnP entries stay live and remain bound to the old INF. On the next launch:

  • DriverBuilder.FullDeploy calls pnputil /delete-driver /uninstall /force.
  • That fails with "One or more devices are presently installed using the specified INF" and leaves the old INF + stale DLL bytes in DriverStore.
  • The subsequent /add-driver then sees package-already-present + "Needed repairing" and restores the stale bytes from pnputil's internal cache rather than installing the fresh extracted binary.
  • Net effect: every launch since the first one serves the stale driver forever, the v1.1.5 self-heal code never actually loads, input keeps hanging, and the only escape is manual devcon + TrustedInstaller takeown of the FileRepository subdirectory (which users do not have).

Running the sweep here FIRST removes the bound devices via devcon (returning "Removed on reboot" is sufficient: the INF becomes eligible for package deletion immediately), so the deploy's /delete-driver call actually succeeds and the fresh staged binary replaces the DriverStore contents.

The same removal is exposed publicly as HMContext.RemoveAllVirtualControllers() for consumers who want explicit defensive cleanup. It never touches a running program's controllers, the caller's own included. In normal operation, individual HMController.Dispose() is sufficient, and a program that exits normally without disposing has its devices removed as it exits.

docs.title: Dispose: TeardownController orchestration
docs.text:
HMController.Dispose() runs Internal.DeviceOrchestrator.TeardownController(index, instanceId). Sequence:

1. Cancel the output reader thread, join (5 s timeout)
2. Dispose the output cancellation token
3. Notify the context (HMContext.OnControllerDisposing)
   A ROOT device whose driver serves protocol 5 (v2.0.0): capture its HID
   children, signal Global\HIDMaestroRemoveEvent<N>, and wait up to 2 s for
   the driver to fail its device, which Windows then removes by surprise
   removal
4. Per-archetype removal:
   plain HID:           DIF_REMOVE on the ROOT\ device
   non-xinputhid Xbox:  hmswd.exe remove (XUSB companion) + DIF_REMOVE (main HID)
   xinputhid Xbox:      hmswd.exe remove (SwD parent) + cascade waits
5. Removal test per device (v2.0.0): out of the tree, the record gone for an
   uninstall, then CM_NOTIFY_ACTION_DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED within 2 s more.
   A HID child removed with its parent counts on the parent's notification.
   Each removal holds HIDMaestro.Admin\Pnp from its call through its test
6. Close shared memory mappings
7. Free per-controller registry path
8. Release the index back to the context's free pool

For SwD-enumerated devices, step 4 uses the SwD-first ordering (see below). For plain HID devices, DIF_REMOVE and the per-device removal test are sufficient.

Since v2.0.0 each removal holds the machine-wide PnP lock from its call through its removal test, so removals run one at a time, in a program and across programs, and no program of this release registers a device while another removes one. The test ends Removed, GoneWithoutRemoved (logged, never refused) or NotGone (the next registration of that id is refused). A parent removed with SetupDiRemoveDevice or SwDeviceClose gets its caller's budget, and every removal whose call finishes its work before it returns gets 2 s. See Registrations and removals.

docs.title: A removal no program can refuse (v2.0.0)
docs.text:
A queried removal asks every program that has the device open, and one refusal stops it. Steam holds the PlayStation pads' HID children open, and through v1.12.0 its refusal (PNP_VetoOutstandingOpen) stopped a Dispose halfway: the class installer had already deleted the HID child's driver and service, Windows marked the record as needing a reboot, and every later HID child on that path failed its start with problem code 19.

Since v2.0.0 a Dispose of a ROOT device first makes that query itself, as Safely Remove Hardware does (CM_Query_And_Remove_SubTreeW), before any record is touched. Every program that watches the device lets go: Windows' input stack for a keyboard or mouse, and a vendor's service that opens its own devices, such as Logitech's lighting service. A refusal changes nothing. Only when a program refuses does the Dispose ask the driver to fail the device, through the remove events of driver protocol 5 (UMDF2 Driver Internals). Windows then removes the device and its HID children by surprise removal, which asks no one, and the removals that follow find the children gone. A program that keeps reading the child sees its read fail, as after an unplug. Against one that never reads, Windows waits about 5 s before it refuses the query, the Dispose returns in about 7.5 s with no record left, and Windows finishes the removal when that program closes its handle. A watcher lets go later after a surprise removal than after a query, and a create of the same identity in that moment would get the old devnode back, which is why the query comes first. A driver older than protocol 5 does not answer, and the removal is queried as before. Software devices under SWD\, the xinputhid parents, keep the queried removal, and a USB/IP persona is not asked.

A create at an identity whose previous device a program still holds open gets that devnode back, marked for removal and never started (DN_WILL_BE_REMOVED). The create stops waiting on that flag and fails within about 2 s, saying that a program still holds the device, and a create after the program lets go starts normally.

A ROOT create also reads the HID child records under its identity's prefix. When one is out of the tree, names HIDMaestro and has no driver, as the refusal above left records through v1.12.0, the parent takes the next prefix of the identity, 1&hash&1 to 1&hash&3, the counter Windows raises when it mints one, and its HID child starts on a path with no such record. The rival guard and the ParentIdPrefix written to the parent use the prefix taken, and sweeps count every identity's alternates as HIDMaestro's.

docs.title: SwD-first removal ordering (v1.3.1)
docs.text: Two of the three architecture groups own a SwDevice-enumerated parent: Xbox 360 Wired (XUSB companion is SwD) and Xbox Series BT (main HID is SwD). SwDevice lifetimes are anchored to the HSWDEVICE handle, not the PnP devnode: children of a SwD parent cannot fully unwind their query-remove cascade until the parent's handle drops its kernel refcount.

docs.title: Pre-v1.3.1: HID-children-first (broken)
docs.text:
1. DIF_REMOVE on every HID child first
2. WaitForDeviceRemoval per child (2,000 ms timeout each: always times out
   because the parent is still holding the lifetime lock)
3. Finally close the SwDevice handle

Net cost: ~5,700 ms for Xbox 360 Wired
          ~11,000 ms for Xbox Series BT

PadForge users with Xbox Series BT virtuals saw 11+ second "Disposing controller..." pauses. Unacceptable for live profile-switching.

docs.title: v1.3.1+: SwD-parent-first (fast)
docs.text:
1. Close the SwDevice handle FIRST via hmswd.exe remove
2. Block on CM_NOTIFY_ACTION_DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED for the parent
3. Mop up any HID children that survived the cascade
   (usually zero: the SwD parent's release fires its children's removal in one cascade)

Net cost, measured at v1.3.1:
          ~135 ms for Xbox 360 Wired
          ~500 ms for Xbox Series BT

CM_NOTIFY_ACTION_DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED says the cascade has propagated, where a returned close says only that the handle closed. Critical for callers that immediately follow with a recreate (live profile switch: the new controller's SetupController would race the old one's cleanup if we returned too early). Through v1.12.0 the wait also ended as soon as a locate no longer found the devnode, without the notification. Since v2.0.0 the removal test waits for it, up to 2 s past the devnode's leaving, and logs a removal whose notification never comes.

A second optimization in the same change: when a HIDMAESTRO sweep walks registry entries that exist only as PHANTOM (registry residue from prior sessions, no live devnode), skip the hmswd.exe SwDeviceCreate-reconnect roundtrip entirely. Saves ~50-75 ms per stale entry and prevents creep across same-process recreation cycles.

docs.title: Per-archetype dispose latency
docs.text:
Measured at v1.3.1, before v2.0.0. The 2.0.0 release notes compare 2.0.0's create and dispose times with 1.12.0's.

Profile group Pre-v1.3.1 Post-v1.3.1 Plain HID ~80 ms ~80 ms Non-xinputhid Xbox ~5,700 ms ~135 ms xinputhid Xbox ~11,000 ms ~500 ms

The plain HID path was already fast pre-v1.3.1 because there's no SwD parent. The two SwD-bearing groups got the dramatic improvement.

Round-trip (dispose + recreate) latencies, measured before v2.0.0:

Profile pair Latency DualSense ↔ DualShock 4 ~280 ms DualSense ↔ Xbox 360 Wired ~350-850 ms DualSense ↔ Xbox Series BT ~650-1100 ms Xbox Series BT ↔ Xbox 360 Wired ~750-1300 ms

Down from ~6.4 s and ~11 s respectively pre-v1.3.1. PadForge users reported create and swap as instantaneous on the v1.3.1 path, before v2.0.0.

docs.title: Batch teardown: DisposeControllersInParallel
docs.text:
public void DisposeControllersInParallel(
    IEnumerable<HMController> controllers,
    Action<HMController, long>? perControllerCallback = null);

Disposes a set of controllers from parallel threads, with the per-controller HID orphan sweep suppressed and run once at the end instead of per-controller. Since v2.0.0 every devnode removal holds the machine-wide PnP lock, so the removals themselves run one after another, and the batch takes about the sum of the controllers' removals, where it took about the longest one. The time the callback reports for each controller includes the time its removals waited behind the others'.

ctx.DisposeControllersInParallel(
    new[] { ctrl0, ctrl1, ctrl2, ctrl3 },
    perControllerCallback: (c, ms) => Logger.Info($"  {c.Profile.Id}: {ms} ms"));

Internal sequence:

1. Set _batchDisposing = true
2. Parallel.ForEach: each controller's Dispose runs on its own thread,
   and their removals take HIDMaestro.Admin\Pnp one at a time
3. Set _batchDisposing = false
4. RemoveOrphanHidChildrenBatch: single sweep

The per-controller Dispose checks _batchDisposing; when set, it skips the per-controller orphan sweep that would otherwise run inside each TeardownController.

A perControllerCallback that throws stops nothing (v2.0.0). Every controller is disposed, the orphan sweep runs, and the exceptions come out afterward in one AggregateException, with one controller as with many. Through v1.12.0 a set of two or more left the controllers not yet started undisposed once a callback threw, and with one controller the exception came out bare.

Before v2.0.0, with the removals overlapping, 4-6 mixed controllers took 1.5-4 s end to end. No figure for v2.0.0 exists.

HMContext.Dispose() itself uses an equivalent path internally: consumers don't need to call DisposeControllersInParallel explicitly unless they want the per-controller wall-clock telemetry.

docs.title: Single-element / empty input
docs.text:
Single-element inputs degrade to a plain serial dispose on the calling thread. Empty inputs are no-ops. The implementation:

if (arr.Length == 0) return;
if (arr.Length == 1)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    try { arr[0].Dispose(); } catch { }
    // Wrapped as the set path wraps it.
    try { perControllerCallback?.Invoke(arr[0], sw.ElapsedMilliseconds); }
    catch (Exception ex) { throw new AggregateException(ex); }
    return;
}
// ... two or more: each Dispose on its own thread, removals one at a time

docs.title: Live profile switch
docs.text:
Switching a slot's profile mid-session (HMController.Dispose() then HMContext.CreateControllerAt(index, newProfile)) is synchronous by design. Slot-allocation determinism requires the old devnode fully gone before the new one is created: otherwise the new device would race the old one's removal and might land in a slot the old one hasn't released yet.

Round-trip latencies are the dispose + create numbers above. PadForge's user-perceived "switch slot 1 from DualSense to Xbox 360 Wired" was ~850 ms, measured before v2.0.0.

docs.title: Hot-plug API
docs.text:
Each controller is independently disposable. Removing one does not disturb the others:

using var ctx = new HMContext();
ctx.LoadDefaultProfiles();
ctx.InstallDriver();

var ctrl0 = ctx.CreateController(ctx.GetProfile("dualsense")!);
var ctrl1 = ctx.CreateController(ctx.GetProfile("xbox-360-wired")!);
var ctrl2 = ctx.CreateController(ctx.GetProfile("switch-pro")!);

ctrl1.Dispose();    // dispose middle one: others stay live, slots renumber
// ctrl0 still works at index 0
// ctrl2 still works at index 2
// indices 1 is free; next CreateController fills it

Slot indices don't compact automatically. If you want sparse-to-dense compaction (after disposing index 1, want index 2 to become index 1), you have to dispose index 2 and recreate at index 1. The XInput user-index allocator handles this on its side independently: an XInput slot-N controller becoming slot-1 means a brief disconnect/reconnect at the XInput level for slot 2 consumers.

PadForge does this compaction explicitly via the "bubble-up cascade" in its Step 5 InputManager: see PadForge's wiki for the consumer-side implementation. The SDK doesn't enforce a particular scheme.

docs.title: Force-kill recovery
docs.text:
If the consumer process crashes without disposing controllers, the next sweep of any program on the machine removes them: the sweep at the start of InstallDriver, the one a program runs on its first create, or RemoveAllVirtualControllers(). The crashed program's ownership claim died with it, so its owner record proves it is gone. The sweep holds each dead group's index and identity claims until its devices, and the orphaned HID children it removes after them, are out of the device tree, so a restarted program cannot create over a device on its way out. A group whose claims another program holds is skipped, and a group the sweep cannot confirm gone keeps its configuration and its dead record for the next sweep. Typically:

// Process A creates 3 controllers, then crashes
// Process B starts:
using var ctx = new HMContext();   // constructor doesn't sweep yet
ctx.InstallDriver();   // ← the sweep runs here and removes process A's devices
ctrl0 = ctx.CreateController(...);   // fresh state

A program that exits normally without disposing has its devices removed by the SDK's own exit handler, which waits at most 10 seconds for the phantom cleanup and a create in flight, then removes them to the end, as Dispose does. When that wait runs out, a device does not leave, or another program holds the PnP lock past what is left of the 10 seconds, the devices stay until the next sweep, as a crashed program's do. A keyless program restarted after a crash gets its old transport index, and so its old identity, back only when no other program holds that index, and while a program built on v1.12.0 runs, only when the index is 64 or more.

The regression battery's S12_ForceKill_Recovery and S17_ForceKill_MidCascade scenarios validate this end-to-end. See Testing and Verification.

docs.title: Composite personas are swept by a separate route (v1.4.5)
docs.text:
The sweep walks the ROOT and SWD enumerators removing devices whose hardware IDs carry the HIDMAESTRO token. A composite persona carries no such token by design, because the USB Audio Class driver binds against an exact Sony identity, so the enumerator walk cannot reach one. Before v1.4.5 an orphaned persona survived the self-heal: a USB DualSense stayed enumerated with nothing left running to feed it.

RemoveAllVirtualControllers detaches personas from the emulated host controller first, then walks the enumerators. Two consequences worth knowing:

  • As of v2.0.0 it detaches only the personas of programs that have exited, matched by the server port each program's owner record names, and any import on the SDK's port ranges whose server no longer listens, which covers a v1.12.0 program that has exited. RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, preserveInstall) detaches every one, another live program's included.
  • The detach runs before the walk, and before it detaches anything it disposes this process's own emulated devices to join their input pump threads. Those pumps map the shared input sections directly and take no part in the stop-event drain, so a pump still running when the sweep unmaps its section is an access violation on a background thread, not a leak. Consumers calling the public API get this ordering for free.

Sweeping with a live controller is safe as of v1.4.6. Until then it was not: the sweep released every shared-memory mapping the process held without stopping a live HMController, whose output poll loop is canceled only by Dispose. The loop kept reading a view that had just been unmapped and the process died with 0xC0000005 on a thread unrelated to the call that was made (#45).

Poll threads now register with the shared-memory layer, and every unmap path cancels and joins them first, so this is handled inside the SDK rather than being a rule callers have to remember. Disposing controllers before a sweep is still the tidier shape, and on older versions it is the only safe one.

For deliberate cleanup (e.g. uninstalling HIDMaestro entirely), use:

HIDMaestroTest.exe cleanup

Which calls RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, preserveInstall: false): every HIDMaestro device and import on the machine, then the driver packages. Don't reach for raw pnputil /remove-device or devcon: the cleanup command is the right interface.

docs.title: Anti-pattern: pnputil /delete-driver /uninstall /force on the active driver
docs.text:
Don't. Leaves devices in Code 14 ("restart required"). Always:

  1. HIDMaestroTest cleanup (or HMContext.RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, false)) FIRST to evict the devices.
  2. Plain pnputil /delete-driver (no /uninstall) if a package delete is even needed.

InstallDriver is idempotent across version bumps: manual uninstall before reinstall is almost never the right move.

The cleanup command does the right thing because:

  • It walks every HIDMaestro PnP entry by enumerator name (SWD\HIDMAESTRO*, ROOT\VID_*&PID_*&IG_00).
  • It calls hmswd.exe remove for SWD entries (the only documented teardown for SWDeviceLifetimeParentPresent).
  • It calls DIF_REMOVE for ROOT entries.
  • After the sweep, if a driver-package delete is desired, it runs pnputil /delete-driver (no force flags).

docs.title: Multi-Controller
docs.text:
Up to N virtual controllers running simultaneously. Verified working with 6 mixed (2× Xbox Series BT + 2× Xbox 360 Wired + 2× DualSense) on a Ryzen 9955HX3D dev box and on an Intel Atom Z8350 fixture. The SDK supports unlimited; downstream APIs cap variously.

This page covers the mechanics that make multi-controller work: slots and transport indices, the friendly-name re-application race, per-instance WUDFHost, ordering across APIs, and what each downstream consumer caps at.

For per-controller PnP machinery, see SwDevice and PnP. For the underlying driver design, see UMDF2 Driver Internals.

docs.title: SDK-side: slots and transport indices
docs.text:
CreateController takes the lowest free slot in its context, first-fit with no upper bound. Slots are dense in normal operation: 0, 1, 2, 3 for four sequential creates, and after the controller in slot 1 is disposed, the next create lands in slot 1. For deterministic slots, use CreateControllerAt(index, profile), which keeps its contract of one controller per slot per context.

As of v2.0.0 a controller also holds a machine-wide transport index, HMController.TransportIndex. It is the slot number when no other program uses that index, and otherwise the lowest free one, so a program running alone gets the numbers every earlier release gave it, except that a keyed create whose identity a dead program's device still carries lands on that device's index, and an index whose names another program took first is skipped. While a program built on v1.12.0 runs, every create starts at index 64, slot 0 on 64 and slot 1 on 65, and a keyless controller's paths and container id, and every controller's HID serial and MAC bytes, move with the index. See Programs Side by Side. Through v1.12.0 the slot was the only index, and two programs that each created a first controller both got index 0 and wrote each other's sections and keys. Two contexts in one process collided the same way.

The transport index drives:

  • The shared memory section names (Global\HIDMaestroInput<N>, etc.), listed by HMController.SectionNames.
  • The per-instance registry path (HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro\Controller<N>).
  • The ControllerIndex the driver reads from its device key, and the serial number string (HM-CTL-<N> zero-padded to 4 digits).
  • The default identity of a controller created without an identity key, and with it the ContainerID GUID's last 16 bits ({48494430-...-4F00<idx:X4>}).

The devnode instance names and the ContainerID derive from the identity key when the caller passes one, and from the transport index otherwise, so a controller created with a key comes back at the same paths across processes. A keyless controller can land on another transport index, and so another identity, when another program holds its slot's index. See SwDevice and PnP and Programs Side by Side.

docs.title: Friendly name re-application
docs.text: There's a Windows PnP race where the first controller's friendly name gets overwritten by the second controller's driver-bind activity. Symptom: 4 controllers all show "Game Controller" instead of their per-profile names like "Controller (XBOX 360 For Windows)" / "DualSense Wireless Controller".

docs.title: Fix: HMContext.FinalizeNames
docs.text:
Call once after creating ALL controllers:

using var ctrl0 = ctx.CreateController(profile1);
using var ctrl1 = ctx.CreateController(profile2);
using var ctrl2 = ctx.CreateController(profile3);
using var ctrl3 = ctx.CreateController(profile4);
ctx.FinalizeNames();   // re-apply friendly names after PnP settles

The method polls each HID child for DN_STARTED (driver fully bound) before re-applying. On fast machines exits in <100 ms; on slow machines adapts up to 5 s rather than failing from an insufficient fixed sleep.

The proven pre-SDK test app (~v0.x) called this as "Phase 1.5: Finalizing device names". The functionality moved into the SDK; consumers should call it as their final create step.

docs.title: Per-instance WUDFHost
docs.text:
Both INFs (hidmaestro.inf and hidmaestro_xusb.inf) carry:

[..._Install.NT.Wdf]
UmdfHostProcessSharing = ProcessSharingDisabled

Each device instance gets its own WUDFHost.exe process (~8 MB RSS, ~10 threads). With 6 controllers running, expect 6-12 WUDFHost.exe processes: one per main HID instance plus one per XUSB companion (companions only exist for non-xinputhid Xbox profiles).

docs.title: Why per-instance hosts
docs.text:
Default (ProcessSharingEnabled) funnels every UMDF2 instance into one shared WUDFHost. At 6 controllers, the shared host accumulates 9+ minutes of CPU time vs ~2 seconds per per-instance host. Empirically traced in 2026-04 (docs/investigations/issue3-dual-xinputhid-saturation-2026-04/).

Root cause: contention between writer threads (HIDMaestro virtual instances) and concurrent XInputGetState reader threads when 2+ virtuals coexist with a real xinputhid device in the same host. Per-instance hosts run their I/O paths in parallel, idle CPU stays near zero, and peak throughput scales with controller count.

docs.title: Detecting regression
docs.text:
If a future change accidentally drops the ProcessSharingDisabled line, the symptom is exponential CPU saturation under multi-controller load. Detection:

Get-Process WUDFHost | Measure-Object -Property Count
# Expected: N main HID instances + M XUSB companion instances
# Regression: 1-2 hosts regardless of controller count

docs.title: XInput's 4-slot cap
docs.text:
xinput1_4.dll hard-caps at 4 slots regardless of how many Xbox-family virtuals exist. With 6 Xbox-family controllers, only 4 are visible through XInputGetState. Slots 0..3 fill in creation order.

Non-Xbox profiles don't claim XInput slots. A 6-controller config of (4× Xbox Series BT + 2× DualSense) sees 4 XInput slots (the 4 Xbox controllers) plus 2 controllers visible through DI / HIDAPI / WGI / Browser. Non-Xbox profiles can run beyond 4 simultaneously through every other API.

If your consumer needs more than 4 XInput-visible controllers, that's a Microsoft-side limit; no user-mode workaround.

docs.title: Browser cap
docs.text:
Chromium's gamepad API caps at 4 connected gamepads on Win10/11. With 6 mixed controllers, browser sees 4 in a deterministic order (alphabetical by GUID, not by creation order: see Cross-API Coverage).

Restart Chromium to clear stale slot caching when adding/removing controllers during a session.

docs.title: SDL3 / DirectInput / HIDAPI: no cap
docs.text:
These APIs see every controller HIDMaestro creates. 6 mixed = 6 visible. PadForge's bench tests have run 8+ controllers simultaneously through DI/HIDAPI without issue.

The SDK side scales linearly: each additional controller adds one shared memory section (~17 KB), one WUDFHost process (~8 MB), and proportional cost to SetupController / Dispose / FinalizeNames. As of v2.0.0 a create also takes its ownership claims and a census of the owner records and present devices, and a dispose releases them.

docs.title: Several programs
docs.text: Controllers from several programs that embed HIDMaestro share the XInput, Browser and ordering behavior above, since Windows sees devices, not programs. Each program's controllers keep their own transport indices, identities and sections, and a program's cleanup removes only what exited programs left. The XInput cap of 4 slots above counts every Xbox-family controller on the machine, whichever program created it. See Programs Side by Side.

docs.title: Ordering across consumers
docs.text:
Game enumeration anchors to creation order across most APIs:

API Order XInput Sequential user-index 0, 1, 2, 3 in creation order. Slot allocator skips dead slots. DirectInput IDirectInput8::EnumDevices returns in Windows-internal order (typically creation order). HIDAPI hid_enumerate returns in PnP enumeration order (creation order). Browser Gamepad (Chromium) Alphabetical / lexical GUID ordering. Match to creation order is coincidental. WGI Creation order via Gamepad::Gamepads. joy.cpl Creation order. SDL3 Creation order via SDL_GetJoysticks.

For UI flows where the user expects "Controller 1 = first one I created", every API except Chromium gets it right. Chromium reorders: the consumer needs to sort or remap if browser ordering matters.

docs.title: Don't parallelize CreateController
docs.text:
A consumer might be tempted to parallelize multi-controller creation:

// DON'T DO THIS
await Task.WhenAll(profiles.Select(p => Task.Run(() => ctx.CreateController(p))));

The creation order anchors every downstream API. Parallel creates produce non-deterministic order across XInput, WGI, joy.cpl, browser, RawInput, SDL3 simultaneously: the user-visible game enumeration becomes a coin flip per launch.

Always create sequentially. Multi-controller perf comes from making each step faster (the v1.3.x latency improvements), not from parallelism. Verified at the SDK level: CreateController takes the context lock for index allocation but otherwise serializes through SetupController's registry-then-PnP-create path.

docs.title: DisposeControllersInParallel
docs.text:
Disposal can run from parallel threads because the user-visible ordering is already broken when controllers are gone. Since v2.0.0 the removals themselves run one at a time, because each devnode removal holds the machine-wide PnP lock:

ctx.DisposeControllersInParallel(
    new[] { ctrl0, ctrl1, ctrl2 },
    perControllerCallback: (c, ms) => Logger.Info($"  {c.Profile.Id} disposed in {ms} ms"));

The per-controller HID orphan sweep is suppressed during the batch and run once at the end instead of per-controller. A batch of several controllers takes about the sum of their removals, where before v2.0.0 it took about the longest one, so what the batch path saves is the repeated orphan sweep.

Before v2.0.0, with the removals overlapping, 4-6 mixed controllers took 1.5-4 s end to end. No figure for v2.0.0 exists. See Lifecycle and Teardown and Registrations and removals.

docs.title: Per-controller serial number for SDL3 disambiguation
docs.text:
Two virtual DualSense with the same VID:PID:ProductString get bucketed by hid_enumerate into a single device unless they have different serial numbers. HIDMaestro generates a per-instance serial:

// Driver-side, in InitInstancePaths
WCHAR serial[64];
RtlCopyMemory(serial, L"HM-CTL-", sizeof(L"HM-CTL-") - sizeof(WCHAR));
AppendUlongDecimal(serial, ControllerIndex, /* zero-pad to 4 */);
// e.g. serial = "HM-CTL-0001"

Returned by IOCTL_HID_GET_STRING / HID_STRING_ID_ISERIALNUMBER. SDL3 / HIDAPI use this string as a per-device disambiguator; identical VID:PID/ProductString controllers get distinct GUIDs derived from the serial.

The exact format (HM-CTL-<index>) isn't part of any contract: consumers are expected to treat the string as opaque. Don't parse the index out and use it for ordering; use creation order instead.

docs.title: Verified configurations
docs.text:
The regression battery (regression_battery.ps1) exercises multi-controller configurations:

Scenario Configuration What it tests S07_Multi_CreateAll_Idle 4 mixed, idle, quit Baseline multi-slot teardown via clean process exit S08_Multi_SwapOneSlot 4 wired, swap slot 1 Single-slot swap doesn't leak across siblings S09_Multi_SwapAllSlots 4 wired, swap each slot to a different family Concurrent live-swap of every slot S10_Multi_RemoveOne 3 mixed, remove 1 HMController.Dispose without replacement leaves no residue S11_Multi_MultipleXinputhid 3 different xinputhid profiles + swap xinputhid INF-match handling under multiple concurrent xinputhid binds S15_Multi_SixControllers 6 mixed (beyond XInput's 4) + swap slot 5 Slot-allocator skip + ContainerID encoding for high indices. The HM "6-controller baseline" use case. S19_Multi_RapidMultiSlotSwap 4 controllers, swap each slot's profile back-to-back, no settle Closest stdin proxy for PadForge's ApplyAscendingIndexPreemption async-dispose path S20_Multi_HeterogeneousCascade 4 controllers, every family in one batch, then quit DisposeControllersInParallel correctness with all four families simultaneously S23_Multi_CustomInMix 5 mixed: 360 + Series BT + DualSense + Switch Pro + Custom + swap custom slot Real PadForge-shape consumer config S71_Coexistence Programs that embed HIDMaestro as separate processes, with peers built on v1.12.0 and v1.11.0 Transport indices, identity claims, sweeps and deploys across programs, with an XInput slot, WGI and Raw Input entries left alone

See Testing and Verification for the harness mechanics.

docs.title: Performance at scale
docs.text:
Measured before v2.0.0. The registration gate v2.0.0 adds before each devnode registration has not been timed on a live create.

Configuration Cold start (1st run) Warm start (subsequent) Idle CPU 1 plain HID ~18 s (cert + sign + install + create) ~200 ms ~0.04% 1 Xbox 360 Wired ~18 s ~200-700 ms (slot-claim wait dominates worst case) ~0.04% 1 Xbox Series BT ~18 s ~150-600 ms ~0.04% 4 mixed (2 BT + 2 wired) ~20 s ~2.2-2.8 s ~0.16% (4× ~0.04%) 6 mixed (sequential creates) ~22 s ~3.5 s ~0.24%

Cold-start cost is dominated by certificate generation, signing, and pnputil /add-driver. After the first run the driver is in the DriverStore and subsequent creates skip the install entirely.

Idle CPU is the per-controller WUDFHost measurement. Each per-instance host has its own thread pool sleeping on the input event; it spends most of the time in kernel WaitForMultipleObjects. Linear scaling means 6 controllers consume ~0.24% of one CPU core at idle, well within the noise floor.

docs.title: Atom Z8350 fixture (slow-hardware validation)
docs.text:
The regression battery also runs on an Intel Atom Z8350 (4 cores @ 1.44 GHz, 4 GB RAM, Win10 IoT LTSC 19044). Slow-hardware target for validating the event-driven harness without time-based settles.

It runs the full battery at HIDMAESTRO_TIMEOUT_SCALE=2. Its last full run, the 57-scenario v1.7.3 battery, passed 57/57, as on Ryzen-class hardware. The slow-hardware result is the reason the harness is pure ACK-driven instead of fixed-sleep timed: a fixed sleep that's "enough" on a fast machine isn't enough on Atom. ACK-driven waits scale with the machine.

See Testing and Verification.
