  • vJoy reference descriptor: in github.com/njz3/vJoy under driver/sys/hidReportDescFfb.h. The four-feature variant that triggers the pid.dll AV.
  • HIDMaestro issue #16: the empirical pid.dll AV report.
  • HIDMaestro issue #6: the Chromium phantom-axis trap that motivates AddButtons round-up and AddTrigger byte-alignment validation.
  • References: full source bibliography.

docs.title: Keyboards and Mice
docs.text:
New in v1.12.0, a profile can be a keyboard or a mouse. The catalog holds 51 keyboards and 52 mice from 32 vendors. Each is the report descriptor of one interface of a real device, taken from public dumps: usbhid-dump output posted in project issues, libinput recordings and the Linux kernel's HID selftests. It answers issue #67.

Source: the profiles under profiles/ whose type is keyboard or mouse, the packers in Internal/KeyboardMousePacker.cs, the descriptor parser in Internal/HidReportMap.cs, and the probes that verify them, test/probes/kbm_offline_check and test/probes/kbm_live_check.

docs.title: What Windows sees
docs.text:
A keyboard or mouse profile is created like any other plain HID profile and reaches Windows as the device its descriptor describes. Windows' keyboard and mouse class drivers open its collections and Raw Input lists each one as its kind. A Scroll Lock pressed on a virtual keyboard turns Scroll Lock on, and the mouse moves the cursor.

A profile carries one interface of the real device. Its other interfaces, including the ones vendor configuration tools talk to, are not emulated. Keyboard and mouse profiles get no GameInput mapping and no joy.cpl name.

docs.title: Driving one
docs.text:
using var mouse = ctx.CreateController(ctx.GetProfile("logitech-g502-hero")!, "mouse-1");
mouse.SubmitMouse(new HMMouseState { X = 25, Y = -10, Buttons = HMMouseButtons.Left });
mouse.SubmitMouse(new HMMouseState());

using var keyboard = ctx.CreateController(ctx.GetProfile("keychron-q6")!);
keyboard.SubmitKeyboard(HMKeyModifiers.LeftShift, new[] { HMKey.A });
keyboard.SubmitKeyboard(HMKeyModifiers.None, ReadOnlySpan<HMKey>.Empty);
Method What it sends SubmitMouse(in HMMouseState) Buttons, relative X and Y, Wheel and Pan. A movement larger than the descriptor's field is split across as many reports as it takes. SubmitKeyboard(HMKeyModifiers, ReadOnlySpan<HMKey>) The modifiers and every key held down. A report without a key releases it. More keys than the report holds report ErrorRollOver, as a real keyboard does. SubmitConsumer(ReadOnlySpan<ushort>) Consumer-page usages such as volume and media keys, on a profile that declares a consumer collection.

Each packs into the reports the profile's descriptor declares, with or without report IDs, so a mouse whose buttons and motion sit in separate reports gets both. A method throws InvalidOperationException when the descriptor declares no collection of that kind.

docs.title: Every report arrives
docs.text:
A gamepad reports state, so only the newest report matters. A mouse reports movement, which adds up, and a keyboard reports presses and releases, which must all arrive. For keyboards and mice the driver confirms each report once HID class has stored it, and the SDK sends the next only after that, at most one per millisecond, the interval of a full-speed USB device. On a busy machine a report cannot overtake the one before it. A burst of 600 one-count moves lost nothing, and neither did four mice driven from four threads at 250 Hz each. With every core busy, four mice each sending as fast as the SDK allows delivered every report, in order, across 800 runs.

A wait for the confirmation gives up after 200 ms. After three misses in a row the controller stops waiting until a confirmation arrives again, so a device Windows has stopped reading does not hold up the caller. DeliversEveryReport says whether a controller works this way. It is false on a gamepad and on a driver older than v1.12.0.

Windows merges consecutive mouse moves into one WM_INPUT message, so a reader that counts messages sees fewer than were sent. The movement adds up to the same total.

docs.title: Buttons past five
docs.text: Raw Input's RAWMOUSE carries five buttons. A mouse built with HidDescriptorBuilder.VendorButtons gets a second, vendor-page collection, and SubmitMouse sends buttons six and up there. Raw Input lists that collection as a HID device of its own.

docs.title: Absolute pointers
docs.text: HidDescriptorBuilder.Mouse(absolute: true) builds a pointer that takes 0 to 32767. It reaches Raw Input flagged MOUSE_MOVE_ABSOLUTE, on Windows' 0 to 65535 scale.

docs.title: Keyboard LEDs
docs.text: Windows sends a keyboard its LED state when it arrives and on every change, and resends it to the keyboards already present when another arrives. KeyboardLedsChanged raises each state as HMKeyboardLeds flags (NumLock, CapsLock, ScrollLock, Compose, Kana), and KeyboardLeds holds the latest. The arrival state comes while CreateController is still running, before a handler can be attached, so attach the handler and then read the property.

docs.title: Stable paths and timing
docs.text: Four mice with one VID and PID are four Raw Input devices, and each identity key gets the same device path back on every life, as with every other profile. Creating a mouse took 386 to 458 ms and Dispose 87 to 196 ms.

docs.title: When the consumer goes away
docs.text:
If the consuming process ends with a key or button down, however it ends, the driver lets go of it: keys and buttons go up, relative motion stops, and an absolute pointer stays where it was. Without that, Windows repeats a held key until the device is removed, 32 times in 1.5 s as measured. The SDK holds one end of a named pipe for each controller and the driver keeps a read pending on it, so the driver learns of the exit when the pipe closes. Dispose sends the same release itself before teardown, and ReleasesOnConsumerExit says whether the driver watches.

The devices a dead consumer leaves are removed by the next session's cleanup, or by RemoveAllVirtualControllers. Windows will not disable a keyboard, and while one is up it will not disable the device above it either, so the cleanup removes a keyboard with SetupDiRemoveDevice, children first, the order Dispose uses.

docs.title: Building one in code
docs.text:
HidDescriptorBuilder has starters:

Starter Builds Mouse(buttons = 5, absolute = false, wheel = true, pan = true, reportId = 0) A relative 16-bit mouse, or an absolute pointer Keyboard(keys = 6, leds = true, reportId = 0) The boot keyboard layout KeyboardNkro(leds = true, reportId = 0) A keyboard with a bit for every key ConsumerControl(slots = 1, reportId = 0) Consumer-page usages VendorButtons(count, reportId) The second collection for buttons six and up

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
Battery scenario S69 runs with no device. It checks that builder recipes from before v1.12.0 build the same bytes, the new starters and their guards, the packers against bytes worked out by hand, and every catalog keyboard and mouse parsed, packed and read back.

Battery scenario S70 runs through Raw Input:

  • Four mice with one VID and PID get four paths, and the same four come back when they are created again in reverse order.
  • A 600-report burst and four threads at 250 Hz lose no counts.
  • An absolute mouse arrives flagged MOUSE_MOVE_ABSOLUTE, and buttons six and eight arrive through the vendor collection.
  • Two keyboards, one without report IDs and one with Report ID 2, each hold the LED state Windows sent on arrival, and a Scroll Lock pressed on one reaches both as the new state.
  • A consumer usage arrives as a HID report, and output and feature reports reach OutputReceived split at their first byte.
  • Every catalog keyboard and mouse starts, reaches Raw Input as its kind and confirms delivery.
  • A consumer killed while it holds a key, a mouse button and an absolute pointer leaves the key and button up and the pointer where it was, and the cleanup after it removes all three of its devices.

docs.title: OEM Name Override
docs.text:
HMOemNameOverride overrides the label joy.cpl and DirectInput consumers show for a given USB VID:PID. Use it when you want a HIDMaestro virtual (or any device sharing that VID:PID) to display a specific name in joy.cpl and DirectInput, overriding any Windows-shipped pre-populated label.

The implementation is more involved than "write one registry value" because Windows pre-populates clone PIDs in registry locations the obvious-looking write doesn't reach. The API exists because there is no simpler reliable way to override the label.

docs.title: The three label sources
docs.text:
The DirectInput / joy.cpl label is sourced from three registry locations. Windows pre-populates at least one of them for many common clone PIDs (e.g. VID_0079&PID_0006 ships with the label "PC TWIN SHOCK Gamepad"). To reliably override, all three must be written:

Location Value name Reader HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\MediaProperties\PrivateProperties\DirectInput\VID_####&PID_####\OEM\ "OEM Name" (with space) DirectInput consumers HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\MediaProperties\PrivateProperties\Joystick\OEM\VID_####&PID_####\ "OEMName" (no space) MME joy.cpl HKCU\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\MediaProperties\PrivateProperties\Joystick\OEM\VID_####&PID_####\ "OEMName" (no space) per-user joy.cpl (preloaded by Windows for clone PIDs)

Per-user (HKCU) takes precedence over HKLM Joystick and is the first place Windows checks for many clone PIDs. Writing only the HKLM DirectInput path leaves the HKCU clone label intact, and joy.cpl continues showing the wrong name.

HMOemNameOverride.Set writes all three under a global mutex, capturing the prior value of each before any are mutated.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
public static class HMOemNameOverride
{
    public static void Set(ushort vid, ushort pid, string label);
    public static void Clear(ushort vid, ushort pid);
    public static int  RecoverOrphans();
    public static IReadOnlyList<HMOemNameOverrideEntry> ListActive();
}

public sealed class HMOemNameOverrideEntry
{
    public string  VidPid { get; }
    public string? OriginalOemName { get; }
    public bool    OriginalKeyExisted { get; }
}

Set, Clear and RecoverOrphans require admin (HKLM write access) and throw UnauthorizedAccessException if the calling process isn't elevated. ListActive is a read-only HKLM read and works unelevated.

docs.title: Set(vid, pid, label)
docs.text:
HMOemNameOverride.Set(0x0079, 0x0006, "My Custom Gamepad");

Writes all three registry locations with the new label, in a single transaction under a global mutex. Captures the prior value of each target to a HIDMaestro-owned pending record at HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOemOverrides\VID_xxxx&PID_xxxx before any target is mutated.

If a prior Set for this VID:PID is already active, this replaces the label but keeps the originally-captured value for restore purposes. Re-calling Set is safe and cumulative.

Throws ArgumentNullException if label is null.

docs.title: Clear(vid, pid)
docs.text:
HMOemNameOverride.Clear(0x0079, 0x0006);

Restores the pre-Set DirectInput OEM-name label for (vid, pid). Replays the pending record to restore all three target locations independently. If no prior Set is tracked for this VID:PID, this is a no-op.

For each target, the restore matches what Set captured:

  • If the target key existed with a value, the value is reset to the original.
  • If the target key existed without the named value, the named value is deleted (key remains).
  • If the target key did not exist, the entire subkey is deleted.

After all three restores succeed, the pending record at HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOemOverrides\VID_xxxx&PID_xxxx is deleted.

docs.title: RecoverOrphans()
docs.text:
int restored = HMOemNameOverride.RecoverOrphans();

Scans the pending hive at HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOemOverrides and restores every prior override left behind by a crashed, force-killed, or otherwise uncleanly-exited consumer. Returns the count restored.

Safe to call on every consumer startup. No-op if no orphan records exist.

docs.title: ListActive()
docs.text:
foreach (var entry in HMOemNameOverride.ListActive())
{
    Console.WriteLine($"  {entry.VidPid} (was: {entry.OriginalOemName ?? "<no original value>"})");
}

Enumerates every override currently tracked by the pending hive. Useful for diagnostics or for showing the user which virtuals are currently overriding their joy.cpl label.

HMOemNameOverrideEntry:

Property Meaning VidPid Canonical registry form, e.g. "VID_0079&PID_0006". OriginalOemName The label captured before Set ran. Null if the OEM key existed without the named value. OriginalKeyExisted True if the DirectInput OEM subkey existed when Set first ran. False means the subkey will be deleted on restore.

docs.title: Crash safety
docs.text:
The pending hive at HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOemOverrides is written before any registry mutation. The state machine looks like this:

  1. Consumer calls Set(vid, pid, "label"). Acquires global mutex.
  2. Pending record written capturing all three targets' prior values.
  3. All three targets written with the new label.
  4. Mutex released.
  5. ...consumer runs, virtual is live, joy.cpl shows "label"...
  6. Consumer calls Clear(vid, pid) (or process ends).
  7. Acquires global mutex.
  8. Reads pending record.
  9. Replays each target: reset value, delete value, or delete subkey per OriginalKeyExisted.
  10. Pending record deleted.
  11. Mutex released.

If the process dies between steps 4 and 6, meaning the override is in place but Clear never ran, the pending hive still has the record. The next RecoverOrphans() call replays the record and restores the original.

Steps 2 and 3 happen under the same mutex, so a crash mid-sequence leaves the system in a recoverable state: either step 2 didn't complete (no override in effect, no orphan record: nothing to recover) or step 3 partially completed (RecoverOrphans restores what step 3 mutated even if only some of the three writes landed).

The captured per-target state lets Clear and RecoverOrphans restore each target independently, which matters when only one of the three keys existed pre-Set.

docs.title: Usage pattern
docs.text:
The canonical pattern in a consumer with multiple virtuals is:

// Once at consumer startup, before creating any virtuals:
int restored = HMOemNameOverride.RecoverOrphans();
if (restored > 0)
    Logger.Info($"Recovered {restored} orphan OEM-name override(s) from prior session");

// For each virtual where you want a custom joy.cpl label:
HMOemNameOverride.Set(profile.VendorId, profile.ProductId, "PadForge Slot 0");
using var ctrl = ctx.CreateController(profile);

// At virtual teardown:
ctrl.Dispose();
HMOemNameOverride.Clear(profile.VendorId, profile.ProductId);

For consumers that lock to single-instance execution (PadForge does), RecoverOrphans at startup plus a paired Set/Clear per virtual covers the full lifecycle.

For consumers that may run multiple instances simultaneously, the global mutex serializes write attempts. The pending record is per-VID:PID, so two consumers overriding two different VID:PIDs don't conflict; two consumers fighting over the same VID:PID will have whichever Set call ran last win, and the other consumer's Clear will restore the original (skipping the intermediate label).

docs.title: System-wide visibility
docs.text:
The HKLM DirectInput and HKLM Joystick targets are system-wide per VID:PID. If a real device with that VID:PID is connected while your override is active, DirectInput consumers see the override label for it too.

For VID:PIDs where you have a virtual but no real device connected (e.g. an Xbox 360 controller spoofed when no physical 360 is attached), this is exactly what you want. For VID:PIDs that might collide with a connected real device, choose your label accordingly.

docs.title: Per-user vs per-machine
docs.text: The HKCU Joystick target is per-calling-user. On a single-user workstation that matches the DirectInput scope visually; on a multi-user machine, only the user who called Set sees the joy.cpl label change: the HKLM paths still carry the override for DirectInput consumers regardless of user.

docs.title: Cache lifetime in DirectInput / joy.cpl
docs.text: Both DirectInput and joy.cpl cache OEM names per-process on first enumeration. A joy.cpl window that was already open when the override changes keeps showing the stale label until it is closed and re-opened. Games that were already running behave the same way. Set before opening joy.cpl or launching games.

docs.title: Admin requirement
docs.text: Set, Clear and RecoverOrphans require admin, because all three write HKLM. ListActive reads the pending hive read-only and works without elevation, so a non-elevated diagnostic can list overrides it would need elevation to clear.

docs.title: Why not just write HKLM\...\DirectInput\...
docs.text:
The naive approach, writing HKLM\...\DirectInput\VID_xxxx&PID_xxxx\OEM\"OEM Name" and calling it done, works for VID:PIDs Windows hasn't preloaded. Most clones come with a preloaded HKCU label that wins the precedence battle, and the user sees no change.

Writing only HKLM DirectInput was the v1.x.0 implementation. Real-world bug reports came in for clone-PID controllers showing pre-populated names like "PC TWIN SHOCK Gamepad" even after Set was called. The fix is the three-target write under a global mutex, captured before mutation. Issue #7.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text: The full sequence lives in OemNameOverrideStore.cs (~325 lines). The API surface is HMOemNameOverride.cs (~150 lines). Three named registry-key constants, three target descriptors, a global mutex, and the pending-hive layout. Read those files for the byte-level details.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• SDK Reference: the raw HMOemNameOverride API surface in context.
  • Quickstart: usage in the example/SdkDemo walkthrough (Step 0 + Step 3a).
  • docs/oem-name-override.md: the long-form rationale doc shipped in the repo.

docs.title: Output Passthrough
docs.text:
How rumble, haptics, force feedback, adaptive trigger config, LED color, and any other host-to-device data reaches the consumer. The driver captures the bytes; the SDK surfaces them via HMController.OutputReceived events; the consumer decodes per the active profile.

The SDK does not classify packets as "rumble" vs "haptic" vs "FFB": that distinction is semantic and lives in the consumer. All three end up in the same payload at different byte offsets per profile.

This page covers the wire format, the ring buffer mechanics, and consumer decoding patterns. For the driver-side IOCTL handling, see UMDF2 Driver Internals and XUSB Companion. For the canonical PID FFB packet flow, see Force Feedback.

docs.title: The output channel
docs.text:
public event Action<HMController, HMOutputPacket>? OutputReceived;

public readonly struct HMOutputPacket
{
    public readonly HMOutputSource Source;
    public readonly byte ReportId;
    public readonly ReadOnlyMemory<byte> Data;
    public readonly uint SeqNo;
}

public enum HMOutputSource : byte
{
    HidOutput  = 0,    // HidD_SetOutputReport / dinput8 PID effects / HIDAPI write
    HidFeature = 1,    // HidD_SetFeature
    XInput     = 2,    // XInputSetState (XUSB-wire 5-byte vibration)
}

Subscribe at any time after HMContext.CreateController returns. Unsubscribe before disposing the controller, or just rely on dispose to break the event-source link. Multiple subscribers work; each gets a copy of the invocation.

docs.title: OutputDecoded (v1.3.5+)
docs.text:
For profiles whose JSON declares an extendedOutputReport block (Sony BT family in v1.3.5; future profiles via JSON only), the SDK additionally raises a parsed-field event whenever an inbound output report matches the declared report ID:

public event EventHandler<HMOutputDecodedEventArgs>? OutputDecoded;

public sealed class HMOutputDecodedEventArgs : EventArgs
{
    public byte ReportId { get; init; }
    public IReadOnlyDictionary<string, object> Fields { get; init; } = null!;
    public ReadOnlyMemory<byte> RawBytes { get; init; }
    public bool CrcValid { get; init; } = true;
}

Fields is keyed by the profile JSON's semantic names. Field-type → runtime-type mapping:

JSON type Fields[semantic] runtime type uint8, uint8-rolling byte uint8-axis float (mapped from byte via the declared center) uint8-trigger float (mapped from byte / 255) rgb24 byte[3] (R, G, B) bytes-passthrough byte[] (length per the declared range) button-mask List<string> of pressed-button names

Both OutputReceived (raw) and OutputDecoded (parsed) fire on every matching report: choose whichever the consumer needs. Pure raw consumers can ignore OutputDecoded; consumers wanting named field access can ignore OutputReceived. CrcValid reports the result of any crc32-le field declared in the spec; consumers decide whether to act on a mismatch.

controller.OutputDecoded += (sender, e) =>
{
    if (e.Fields.TryGetValue("leftMotor", out var lm)
        && e.Fields.TryGetValue("rightMotor", out var rm))
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[rumble] L={lm} R={rm}");
    }
    if (e.Fields.TryGetValue("lightbar", out var rgb) && rgb is byte[] c)
    {
        Console.WriteLine($"[lightbar] #{c[0]:X2}{c[1]:X2}{c[2]:X2}");
    }
};

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: HMOutputSource tells the consumer which API the host used to send the packet. The bytes have different wire formats per source even on the same controller.

docs.title: HidOutput (0)
docs.text:
Host wrote via HidD_SetOutputReport / IOCTL_HID_WRITE_REPORT. Bytes are the raw HID output report payload. ReportId carries the HID Report ID byte (0 if the descriptor uses no Report IDs); Data is everything after the Report ID.

Use case: every HID-aware FFB / rumble path.

  • DirectInput PID FFB: every Output report 0x11 / 0x14 / 0x15 / 0x16 / 0x17 / 0x18 / 0x1A / 0x1B / 0x1C / 0x1D / 0x1E lands here. See Force Feedback.
  • DualSense rumble + adaptive triggers + lightbar: a single 47-byte (USB) or 78-byte (BT) Output report 0x02 carries motor magnitudes, trigger profiles, LED color, mute LED state.
  • Switch Pro vendor protocol: 0x10 / 0x80 prefix bytes, vendor commands.

docs.title: HidFeature (1)
docs.text:
Host wrote via HidD_SetFeature. Used by some controllers (DualSense, DualShock 4) for configuration writes; used by pid.dll for PID FFB Create New Effect (Report ID 0x11).

For a HIDMaestro virtual with AddPidFfbBlock-built descriptor, every OutputReceived(HidFeature, 0x11) is a Create New Effect notification: the driver has just allocated an EBI in shared memory. Read it via HMController.GetCurrentPidBlockLoad.

docs.title: XInput (2)
docs.text:
Host called XInputSetState. Bytes are the XUSB-wire-format vibration packet, typically 5 bytes:

Offset Field 0 Command (0x00) 1 Size byte 2 Low-frequency motor (left, 0..255) 3 High-frequency motor (right, 0..255) 4 Reserved

Only fires for profiles with the XUSB companion (non-xinputhid Xbox profiles like Xbox 360 Wired). xinputhid profiles route XInput rumble through the kernel filter, which translates it back into a HID Output report; those surface as HidOutput.

Browser put_Vibration from Chromium dispatches IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE to the XUSB companion via the xinputhid UpperFilter tripwire (see Cross-API Coverage). The companion captures the bytes and writes them into the output ring as HMOutputSource.XInput.

docs.title: The 64-slot ring buffer (v1.1.40+)
docs.text:
The output channel is a 64-slot ring on a per-controller pagefile-backed shared section. Wire format is HIDMAESTRO_SHARED_OUTPUT:

#define HIDMAESTRO_OUTPUT_RING_SLOTS     64u
#define HIDMAESTRO_OUTPUT_SLOT_DATA_CAP  256u

typedef struct {
    volatile ULONG  SeqNo;
    UCHAR           Source;
    UCHAR           ReportId;
    USHORT          DataSize;
    UCHAR           Data[HIDMAESTRO_OUTPUT_SLOT_DATA_CAP];
} HIDMAESTRO_OUTPUT_SLOT;

typedef struct {
    volatile ULONG          Head;
    ULONG                   _Reserved;
    HIDMAESTRO_OUTPUT_SLOT  Slots[64];
} HIDMAESTRO_SHARED_OUTPUT;

Total size: ~16.5 KB per controller. Pagefile-backed; never touches disk.

docs.title: Writer (driver) protocol
docs.text:
Single producer. Inside the relevant IOCTL handler (IOCTL_UMDF_HID_SET_OUTPUT_REPORT, IOCTL_UMDF_HID_SET_FEATURE, or IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE on the companion):

  1. Take OutputLock (per-device lock that serializes IOCTL handler races).
  2. Increment Head to get the new SeqNo (the value that will identify the slot).
  3. Compute slot index (Head - 1) % 64.
  4. Write Source / ReportId / DataSize / Data into that slot.
  5. Write SeqNo last (memory-barrier; readers detect torn writes by re-reading SeqNo).
  6. Release OutputLock.

SeqNo = 0 is reserved for "never written"; first write is SeqNo = 1.

docs.title: Reader (SDK) protocol
docs.text:
Single consumer (the per-controller HMOutputReader_<index> background thread):

// Initialize lastSeen to current Head so pre-existing ring contents
// (stale or legitimate) never fire a spurious OutputReceived.
uint lastSeen = (uint)Marshal.ReadInt32(_outputView, 0);

while (!ct.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    // Drain every slot the driver wrote since last poll, in monotonic SeqNo order.
    while (SharedMemoryIO.TryReadOutputFrame(_outputView, ref lastSeen,
            out byte source, out byte reportId, out int dataSize, buf))
    {
        var data = new ReadOnlyMemory<byte>(buf, 0, dataSize);
        var pkt = new HMOutputPacket((HMOutputSource)source, reportId, data, lastSeen);
        OutputReceived?.Invoke(this, pkt);
    }
    WaitHandle.WaitAny(new[] { ct.WaitHandle, doorbell }, 500);  // event-driven (issue #34)
}

Each TryReadOutputFrame call reads Head, computes slots from lastSeen + 1 to Head, and returns one slot at a time. The reader uses per-slot SeqNo for torn-write detection: if SeqNo before-read ≠ SeqNo after-read, the slot was being rewritten: skip it.

docs.title: Why the ring depth is 64
docs.text:
pid.dll writes Set Effect → Set Constant Force → Effect Operation Start within 1-3 ms. Pre-1.1.40 the channel was a single slot: the magnitude packet (Set Constant Force, in the middle) got coalesced and dropped. With 64 slots the reader has 512 ms of headroom (handler-stall bound) before the oldest slot would be overwritten, which is plenty for any realistic FFB burst pattern.

The 256-byte payload covers DualSense BT report 0x31 (78 bytes) and any current PID FFB Output (largest is Set Effect at 22 bytes). Profile descriptors with larger output reports than 256 bytes would need the section widened.

docs.title: Reader-stall threshold
docs.text: If the consumer's handler stalls for >512 ms while the driver is writing at burst rate, the oldest packets get overwritten. The consumer would see a SeqNo jump (e.g. from 17 to 80) that signals a drop. Keep handlers cheap: no synchronous I/O, no long locks, no UI marshaling on the SDK poll thread (use Dispatcher.BeginInvoke to fire-and-forget the marshal).

docs.title: Cadence
docs.text:
The SDK reader is event-driven (issue #34): the driver signals Global\HIDMaestroOutputEvent<N> after each published packet, so the reader wakes at dispatch cost instead of poll quantization. Against a pre-#34 driver that never created the event, the reader falls back to the historical ~125 Hz (8 ms) poll. Multiple invocations of OutputReceived per wake are normal: the loop drains every new slot before waiting again, so three-packet PID FFB bursts arrive together.

Dispose latency: cancel-token-driven. The output thread waits on the cancel handle alongside the doorbell, so cancellation returns within ~1 ms.

docs.title: Pattern: parsed-field subscription (v1.3.5+)
docs.text:
For profiles with extendedOutputReport, the simplest path is to subscribe to OutputDecoded and read named values directly. No byte-offset knowledge in the consumer:

ctrl.OutputDecoded += (_, e) =>
{
    if (e.Fields.TryGetValue("rightMotor", out var rm))   ApplyHighFreqMotor((byte)rm);
    if (e.Fields.TryGetValue("leftMotor",  out var lm))   ApplyLowFreqMotor((byte)lm);
    if (e.Fields.TryGetValue("lightbar",   out var rgb)
        && rgb is byte[] c)                                ApplyLightbar(c[0], c[1], c[2]);
    if (e.Fields.TryGetValue("rightTriggerEffect", out var rte)
        && rte is byte[] rteBytes)                         ApplyAdaptiveTriggerR(rteBytes);
};

Pair with HMOutputEncoder.Encode to drive a real device from synthesized state without reimplementing byte layouts:

var fields = new Dictionary<string, object>
{
    { "btTag",       (byte)0x02 },
    { "validFlag0",  (byte)0xFF },
    { "validFlag1",  (byte)0xF7 },
    { "rightMotor",  (byte)200 },
    { "leftMotor",   (byte)64 },
    { "lightbar",    new byte[] { 0xFF, 0x00, 0x80 } },
};
byte[] wireBytes = HMOutputEncoder.Encode(profile, fields);
// Hand wireBytes to a raw-HID write into the real device.

docs.title: Pattern: dispatch by (Source, ReportId)
docs.text:
ctrl.OutputReceived += (_, packet) =>
{
    var bytes = packet.Data.Span;
    var key = (packet.Source, packet.ReportId);

    switch (key)
    {
        case (HMOutputSource.XInput, 0):
            // 5-byte XINPUT_VIBRATION-style payload, motor bytes at [2] and [3]
            byte left = bytes[2], right = bytes[3];
            HandleXInputRumble(left, right);
            break;

        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x02):
            // DualSense Report 0x02: full motor + adaptive trigger + LED bytes
            HandleDualSenseOutput(bytes);
            break;

        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x11):
        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x14):
        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x15):
        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x1A):
        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x1B):
        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x1C):
        case (HMOutputSource.HidOutput, 0x1D):
            // PID FFB output reports: see Force Feedback page
            HandlePidFfbOutput(packet.ReportId, bytes);
            break;

        case (HMOutputSource.HidFeature, 0x11):
            // PID FFB Create New Effect: driver allocated an EBI
            var bl = ctrl.GetCurrentPidBlockLoad();
            WireEbi(bl);
            break;
    }
};

docs.title: Pattern: ring-buffer-aware drop detection
docs.text:
uint lastSeenSeqNo = 0;

ctrl.OutputReceived += (_, packet) =>
{
    if (lastSeenSeqNo > 0 && packet.SeqNo > lastSeenSeqNo + 1)
    {
        // Driver wrote (packet.SeqNo - lastSeenSeqNo - 1) packets we missed.
        // Probably handler stalled. Log and continue.
        long dropped = packet.SeqNo - lastSeenSeqNo - 1;
        Telemetry.RumbleDropsTotal.Add(dropped);
    }
    lastSeenSeqNo = packet.SeqNo;
    DispatchPacket(packet);
};

docs.title: Pattern: marshal off the poll thread
docs.text:
ctrl.OutputReceived += (sender, packet) =>
{
    // Don't decode on the poll thread: push to a queue, decode on UI thread
    _decoderQueue.Enqueue(packet);
    _decoderSignal.Set();
};

PadForge uses this pattern for FFB-to-audio conversion (the audio mix happens on the audio thread, not the SDK poll thread).

docs.title: Pattern: copy the data
docs.text:
packet.Data is a ReadOnlyMemory<byte> over the SDK's reusable buffer. It's only valid for the duration of the handler call. If you need the bytes past the handler return:

ctrl.OutputReceived += (_, packet) =>
{
    byte[] copy = packet.Data.ToArray();    // explicit copy
    Task.Run(() => ProcessAsync(copy));     // safe to use later
};

The buffer is reused on the next slot read. Don't store the ReadOnlyMemory reference past the handler.

docs.title: XInput rumble (XUSB companion path)
docs.text:
For non-xinputhid Xbox profiles (Xbox 360 Wired), the XUSB companion (HMXInput.dll) handles IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE. Inside its handler it reads the IRP's input buffer (5 bytes, XINPUT_VIBRATION-style), takes the per-controller OutputLock against the main HID device's shared section, writes a slot with Source = XInput, ReportId = 0, Data = 5 bytes. The companion signals the same output event after publishing, so the SDK reader picks it up at dispatch cost (8 ms poll against pre-#34 drivers).

For xinputhid profiles (Xbox Series BT), xinputhid.sys handles IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE itself and converts to a HID Output report against the HID child: so rumble surfaces as HMOutputSource.HidOutput with whatever Report ID xinputhid writes (typically 0).

docs.title: Browser vibration
docs.text:
Chromium's Gamepad.Vibration::put_Vibration dispatches through WGI. The path depends on the architecture group:

  • Xbox 360 Wired: WGI dispatches IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE to the XUSB companion via the xinputhid UpperFilter tripwire. Surfaces as HMOutputSource.XInput.
  • Xbox Series BT: WGI dispatches via the HID path (xinputhid.sys is the kernel filter). Surfaces as HMOutputSource.HidOutput.
  • Plain HID profiles (DualSense, etc.): WGI dispatches a HID Output report via the standard HID path. Surfaces as HMOutputSource.HidOutput.

In all three cases the consumer's OutputReceived handler fires; only the wire format differs.

docs.title: DirectInput PID FFB
docs.text: See Force Feedback for the full mechanism. Briefly: every Output report pid.dll writes (Set Effect 0x11, Set Constant Force 0x15, Effect Operation 0x1A, etc.) surfaces as HMOutputSource.HidOutput. Create New Effect (Feature 0x11) surfaces as HMOutputSource.HidFeature.

docs.title: Vendor-specific output
docs.text: Vendor-specific output reports (Logitech rotation calibration, DualSense lightbar color, Thrustmaster TARGET binding writes) surface as HMOutputSource.HidOutput with the Report ID the vendor declared. Decoding is profile-specific; HIDMaestro doesn't ship pre-built decoders for vendor protocols.

docs.title: What HIDMaestro does not do
docs.text:
• Auto-routing to physical hardware. The driver accepts the bytes and the SDK surfaces them. Forwarding to a physical FFB device, mixing into XInput rumble, or rendering as audio is the consumer's job. PadForge is the reference example of a consumer that does all three.
  • Effect mixing or condition synthesis. The SDK delivers raw decoded packets. Multi-effect mixing, gain application, and condition-effect dispatch (Spring / Damper / Friction / Inertia) are consumer-side.
  • XInput rumble synthesis from PID FFB. A DirectInput-only game writing PID FFB to an Xbox 360 Wired profile won't get XInput rumble unless the consumer maps the FFB output back to motor magnitudes and writes them via a separate path.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Force Feedback: HID PID 1.0 architecture, the canonical packet flow, EBI auto-allocation.
  • Shared Memory Protocol: HIDMAESTRO_SHARED_OUTPUT wire format and seqlock invariants.
  • XUSB Companion: how IOCTL_XUSB_SET_STATE becomes an HMOutputSource.XInput packet.
  • UMDF2 Driver Internals: how IOCTL_UMDF_HID_SET_OUTPUT_REPORT becomes an HMOutputSource.HidOutput packet.
  • Cross-API Coverage: per-API browser vibration / WGI dispatch path.

docs.title: Programs Side by Side
docs.text:
As of v2.0.0, two or more programs that embed HIDMaestro run on one machine. Between programs on v2.0.0 or later, none removes, replaces or writes to another's controllers, driver or files, except through the remove-everything cleanup described under Sweeps. A program built on HIDMaestro 1.x still can, as Programs built on 1.x describes, and programs built on 1.x must move to 2.0.0. Through v1.12.0 two programs that each created a first controller both got index 0 and wrote each other's shared sections.

Source: the design note, docs/design/coexistence.md, which records each mechanism with its sources, and test/probes/coexist_check, which runs programs side by side.

docs.title: What a program can rely on
docs.text:
Each of these holds between programs on v2.0.0 or later.

  • Its controllers stay its own. No other program removes, replaces or writes to them while it runs, unless that program calls RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, ...), which removes every HIDMaestro controller on the machine. A controller the calling program still holds is then left with no device until it disposes it: DriverVersion is null, DeliversEveryReport and ReleasesOnConsumerExit are false, and its submits reach nothing. Another program's controllers lose their devices without that change and still read the removed driver's state.
  • Creates do not collide. Each controller claims a machine-wide transport index, which names its shared sections, events, owner pipe and registry key. A program running alone gets its slot numbers, as before, unless an index's names were taken by another program or a keyed create reclaims a dead program's device on another index. Two programs that each create a first controller get indices 0 and 1, unless a program built on v1.12.0 runs, as described under Transport index.
  • An identity belongs to one controller. Asking for an identity key another live controller holds, in any program, throws HMResourceInUseException. When the holder runs v2.0.0 or later, the exception names its process, image and SDK version. A v1.12.0 holder is named only as a running program built on HIDMaestro 1.12.0. The refused create does no PnP work, so the holder's devices stay as they were.
  • Sweeps remove only what exited programs left. InstallDriver, the cleanup a program runs on its first create, and RemoveAllVirtualControllers() remove a device only when its program is gone.
  • One driver deploy at a time, and never a downgrade. An older installed driver is upgraded whatever runs on it, and a newer one is kept. A program's running controllers keep the driver their host loaded until their device restarts.
  • No program registers a device while another removes one. Every devnode registration and removal holds one machine-wide lock, as described under Registrations and removals.
  • Nothing runs elevated from a folder users can write. What the SDK runs elevated or hands to pnputil is staged under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging, and every file staged from the SDK's embedded payload is checked against its SHA-256 before it runs. A WinUSB package's INF is generated from the profile, not embedded.

docs.title: Claims
docs.text:
A program takes an ownership claim before its first machine-wide write and holds it until it exits. Each controller claims its transport index and its identity the same way. A claim is a named pipe created with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE and one instance. Creating it is the check: the second claimant learns it lost from the same call that would have won. Windows deletes the pipe when the process ends, however it ends, so a killed program's claims go with it. Probing a claim opens no handle, so a sweep cannot keep a dead program's claim alive.

The claims live under the pipe prefix ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\, where only a process whose token has Administrators enabled can create a pipe, so a program that is not elevated cannot take a claim first and pass for a running owner. A program that is not elevated takes no claim at all. In such a program, RemoveAllVirtualControllers() and RemoveAllVirtualControllers(bool) return without doing anything, InstallDriver returns AlreadyCurrent when this build's driver is installed, and a create, a deploy or anything else that takes a claim or a machine-wide lock throws UnauthorizedAccessException.

Claim Pipe Held for Owner \\.\pipe\ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\HIDMaestro.Owner.<owner id> the program, from its first machine-wide write Transport index \\.\pipe\ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\HIDMaestro.Index.<N> the controller's life Identity \\.\pipe\ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\HIDMaestro.Identity.<token> the controller's life

Beside its owner claim, each program writes a record under HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOwners\<owner id>: its process id, image path, start time and SDK version, the staging directory it uses, its USB/IP server port once it has one, and one entry per live controller with its identity, transport index, backend and profile, and later its devnode instance id or vhci port. A controller's entry is written before any PnP work and removed once its devices are gone. A record whose owner claim no longer exists describes a program that has exited.

docs.title: Transport index
docs.text:
HMController.TransportIndex is the slot number when no other program uses that index, and otherwise the lowest free one. A keyless controller's default identity derives from its transport index, so when other programs are running, a keyless controller can land on another index and another identity than last time. Pass an identity key for device paths that must stay put, as the identity key contract has said since v1.8.0.

While a program built on v1.12.0 runs, a create's search starts at index 64 instead: slot 0 on 64, slot 1 on 65. A running v1.12.0 program's next create takes the lowest index free among its own controllers, whatever else runs, and replaces a device of that index's default identity as its own prior life, so a lower index would put this program's device in its path. The SDK knows such a program runs from a present device whose owner pipe the driver watches, from a USB/IP import no record names whose index's owner pipe is held, or, while a present device's index cannot be read, from the registry ledger, as described under Sweeps. Everything derived from the index moves with it:

  • a keyless controller's identity token, such as HM_0064, and with it its instance path, ParentIdPrefix, container id and HID interface path
  • every controller's HID serial (HM-CTL-0064 and up), the DualSense pairing MAC byte and the Switch Pro MAC's last byte
  • a byte of the XUSB capabilities
  • the USB/IP bus id, 1-<index+1>, and a keyless composite's USB serial and USB instance id

A keyed controller keeps its paths, container id and composite USB serial, and its HID serial and MAC bytes follow the index. A program restarted after a crash gets its old index back only when that index is 64 or more. A key of the form index:N names index N's default identity, the one a v1.12.0 program gives its own controller on that index. While such a program runs, a create with index:N and N below 64 takes that identity as asked, on an index from 64, and the v1.12.0 program's next create on index N replaces a devnode of that name.

Native writers that open the shared sections themselves read the names from HMController.SectionNames, or compute them from TransportIndex. See Shared Memory Protocol.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
The identity claim is taken before any PnP work. A create that asks for an identity key a live controller holds, in any program or in another context of the same program, is refused with HMResourceInUseException. Another program's sweep holds an identity's claim while it removes the device a dead program left under it, and no record lists the identity then. So while no live record lists the identity, a keyed create waits for the claim, up to 120 seconds, and then takes its census again. A keyless create waits the same way for the identity of its transport index, and keeps that index.

A context dropped without Dispose keeps its controllers, their transport indices and their identity keys until the process exits. A create of one of those keys in that process is refused until then, and the exception's message says so.

A v1.12.0 program takes no identity claim. When a present device carries the identity and that device's v1.12.0 program runs, the create is refused the same way.

docs.title: Sweeps
docs.text:
A sweep removes a present device only on proof that its program is gone. A census of the owner records and the present HIDMaestro devices decides:

Present device Its program Action In a record whose owner claim is gone exited removed, with everything the record lists, unless a running program holds the device's index or identity In a live record running left alone, the caller's own included In no live record, its index or identity claim held a running program on v2.0.0 or later left alone In no record, its HIDMaestroOwner<N> pipe held by a running v1.12.0 program, as below a running v1.12.0 program left alone In no record, no owner pipe, Global\HIDMaestroInputAck<N> present a v1.12.0 program that has exited removed In no record, no owner pipe, no InputAck section a program older than v1.12.0, state unknown left alone

A device with an identity token belongs to the record that lists its token. Only a device older than identity tokens is matched to a record by its index, since a running v1.12.0 program takes indices without looking at other programs. A program on v2.0.0 or later takes its claims before it writes its record entry, so a device whose index or identity claim is held is a running program's, with or without a record.

The census reads a device's index from its Device Parameters\ControllerIndex, and logs why when it reads none: no value, no key, or a key it may not read. A keyless device's token, HM_<index>, names its index, so the census takes the index from there and the allocator skips that one index. A keyed device with no readable index is tied to no owner pipe. With no record naming it, it counts as the device of a program whose state is unknown, and a sweep leaves it. A dead record that names it still makes it removable.

While such a device is present, the census looks for a running v1.12.0 program in the registry ledger. A v1.12.0 create writes a holder <pid>-<start>-<index> under HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroRegistryLedger\JoystickOem\<VID&PID>\Holders before its devnode exists, for every controller but a keyboard or mouse, and removes it at teardown. A v2.0.0 program writes the same holders only after its owner record, and its exit deletes the record only once its holders are gone. So a holder on an index below 64 whose process runs and that no live record names belongs to a v1.12.0 program, and it raises the floor to 64. The census reads the holders, then the records, then the holders again, and counts a holder both reads have. It also counts an index that no live record and no present device accounts for when its owner pipe is held beside its input section and an acknowledgement section without the ended marker. One case stays unseen: a v1.12.0 program of only keyboards and mice, or one whose ledger write failed, whose device's index cannot be read, on an index a running v2.0.0 program holds. A device a closed program left raises no floor.

A v1.12.0 program creates its owner pipe unprotected, so any program can create one under the same name, and a held pipe alone does not keep a device. The driver is that pipe's client. When its owner watch connects, it records the pipe's server process and owner, and that the watch is connected, in the device's Device Parameters\HIDMaestro registry key. When the watch ends, it records that it is no longer connected and marks the end of the watch in the device's InputAck section. Where those records exist, the pipe stops counting once they show the watched program gone: the watch has ended, or the server it named no longer runs. Where they do not, as on a driver older than v2.0.0, the pipe counts only while Global\HIDMaestroInput<N> and Global\HIDMaestroInputAck<N> exist and the acknowledgement section does not mark the watch ended. A program that is not elevated can create neither section.

A device from a program older than v1.12.0 leaves no sign of whether its program still runs, so it is never removed on a guess. RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, preserveInstall) removes it, along with every other HIDMaestro device on the machine, a running program's included. That is what an uninstaller, a test harness or a support tool calls.

A sweep takes each dead group's index and identity claims before it acts on the group, and keeps them until every group it removes, and every orphaned HID child it removes after them, is out of the device tree, waiting up to 10 seconds for each orphan. A create on v2.0.0 or later takes both claims before it writes its configuration or makes a device, so none lands on a group a sweep holds, and a sweep skips a group whose claims another program holds. A v1.12.0 program takes no claim, so its owner pipe is checked again right before each removal. A group the sweep cannot confirm gone keeps its configuration and its dead record, so the next sweep still sees a dead owner's device.

USB/IP imports are matched to their program by the server port its record names. An import whose server no longer listens is detached.

The default cleanup, RemoveAllVirtualControllers() and (bool), also removes the GameInput tables HIDMaestro wrote through v1.11.0, as v1.12.0's cleanup did, where no running program uses them. A table stays while a present device or any Controller<N> configuration carries its VID and PID, and every table stays while an input section exists that nothing explains, which is a v1.11.0 create still in flight.

docs.title: Exit and the phantom cleanup
docs.text:
A program that exits normally without disposing its controllers has their devices removed by the SDK's own ProcessExit handler. The handler waits at most 10 seconds, in all, for the phantom cleanup below and for a create in flight, then removes the devices to the end, as Dispose does. Its removals take the PnP lock within what is left of those 10 seconds, counting only the time another program holds it. The devices stay present, in the program's record, until a program on v2.0.0 or later next sweeps, when:

  • a create of the program still holds on at the 10 seconds, on another thread, waiting for another program's sweep or behind a transport install
  • one phantom uninstall of the cleanup outlasts the 10 seconds
  • a device does not leave
  • another program holds the PnP lock past what is left of the 10 seconds
  • under .NET, a thread inside a create calls Environment.Exit

The exit deletes the program's record only once its GameInput and joy.cpl holds are released, and a hold of its own that still stands keeps the record until the process ends. A killed program runs no exit handler, and its devices go with the next sweep of any program on the machine.

A Dispose or cleanup the program calls from its own ProcessExit handler waits for another program's hold of the PnP lock within one 10-second budget the whole process shares. A controller it cuts short keeps its devices and its record entry. The runtime runs ProcessExit handlers in the order they were added, and the SDK adds its own at the program's first create, InstallDriver or cleanup. When the program's handler came first, the SDK's handler runs next and removes such a controller within its own 10 seconds. Otherwise the next sweep removes it.

The records Windows keeps of removed devices, the phantoms, go with a cleanup that runs once per process on a background thread, started by the first of InstallDriver, the first create and RemoveAllVirtualControllers(). The call that starts it does not wait for it, and a later call removes no phantom. A create in the program, and the Everything cleanup, wait while it runs: one pass over the phantoms and their uninstalls, and two passes over interface registrations, with at most 5 seconds of waiting in all, for the PnP lock and for Windows to let each phantom go. Each uninstall runs under the identity claim of the phantom's controller, and a phantom whose claim another program holds is skipped.

When the program's first such call comes inside a ProcessExit handler of its own, the call runs the cleanup on the calling thread before it returns. The SDK learns that exit has begun from AssemblyLoadContext.Default.Unloading, which the runtime raises before ProcessExit. Under .NET it cannot learn it when no code that refers to the SDK ran or was compiled before exit began, such as in a program that uses the SDK only inside that handler, and the cleanup then ends with the process. The next process's first cleanup removes what is left.

docs.title: Driver deploys
docs.text:
Deploys take the machine-wide deploy lock, HIDMaestro.Admin\Deploy (see Machine-wide locks). Of two programs calling InstallDriver at once, one deploys and the other finds the result current. The installed version is the newest DriverVer among the hidmaestro.inf packages in the driver store.

Installed driver What InstallDriver does LastDriverInstall none installs its own Installed its own, with both packages present nothing AlreadyCurrent its own, with a package missing adds the missing package and installs nothing else Installed newer keeps it, and runs on it KeptNewer older, from 1.x or an older 2.0.0 build, nothing on it a full deploy that removes the old packages Upgraded older, devices or a create of another program on it adds this build's packages beside the old ones and updates no present device Upgraded

The 2.0.0 driver takes precedence over every older one, and nothing is refused because another program's devices hold an older driver. The add beside it updates no present device, so those controllers keep the driver their host loaded until their device restarts, while every device a 2.0.0 program creates binds the newest package.

A create installs the driver on its own devnode only, with DiInstallDevice. Through v1.12.0 it used UpdateDriverForPlugAndPlayDevices with the profile's hardware ID, which installs on every present device of that ID.

docs.title: Machine-wide locks
docs.text:
The locks are mutexes in a private object namespace whose boundary holds the Administrators SID and whose DACL admits SYSTEM and Administrators. A program that is not elevated can neither create nor open it, so no such program can take a lock first and hold every HIDMaestro program behind it. Each name below is the namespace alias, HIDMaestro.Admin, and the lock's own name.

Lock Held for HIDMaestro.Admin\Deploy a driver deploy past its fast path, the deploy gate of a UMDF2 create, the driver package removal, the add of a WinUSB package, the test certificate's creation, and the public DriverBuilder steps SignDrivers, GenerateCatalogs and RemoveOldDriverPackages. Waits 10 minutes, then throws InvalidOperationException HIDMaestro.Admin\Transport the usbip-win2 install, the repair of a host controller that stopped answering, and the move off an older host controller, each on a thread of its own, so a UMDF2 create never waits for them HIDMaestro.Admin\WinUsb the devnode work of a WinUSB binding: a bind's claim and install, a restore, and the cleanup HIDMaestro.Admin\WinUsbFollowUp.<entry> one per WinUSB entry, held by the program that watches that entry's devnode until it is gone HIDMaestro.Admin\Ledger every registry ledger and OEM name override operation, on the registry keys a virtual shares with real devices. Most calls wait without a bound. WinUSB claims, restores and package note reads give up after 30 s, scaled by HIDMAESTRO_TIMEOUT_SCALE, with TimeoutException HIDMaestro.Admin\Staging a program's note of the staging directory it uses, and a deploy's prune of the directories no running program names HIDMaestro.Admin\Pnp each devnode registration and each removal, and the other devnode work listed under Registrations and removals. Waits 10 minutes, then throws InvalidOperationException. Once the process is exiting, it waits only what is left of the exit's 10 seconds

The ledger's lock also takes v1.12.0's Global\HIDMaestro-OEM-Recovery after its own, because v1.12.0 programs write the same GameInput and joy.cpl keys under that name, and any program can create that name first. When SYSTEM or Administrators owns it, the lock waits for it as v1.12.0 does. When anyone else owns it, or its owner cannot be read, the lock waits five seconds and goes on without it. Once a wait has run its full five seconds, later acquisitions in that process wait 500 ms, until one takes the mutex or finds it owned by SYSTEM or Administrators again. Both bounds are scaled by HIDMAESTRO_TIMEOUT_SCALE. A caller's own bound, the 30 seconds of the WinUSB claims and restores, covers both mutexes, and a wait it cuts short throws TimeoutException whoever owns the legacy mutex. OEM name override calls wait without a bound.

A program takes them in one order, deploy, then WinUSB, then the ledger, and never the other way around. The transport lock is taken on a thread that holds no other machine-wide lock. The PnP lock comes after the deploy lock and before the staging lock, and is never held with the WinUSB, follow-up, ledger or transport locks. The staging lock is taken last, with nothing else taken under it.

docs.title: Registrations and removals
docs.text:
Every devnode registration and removal a program on v2.0.0 or later makes holds the machine-wide lock HIDMaestro.Admin\Pnp, so no such program registers a device while another removes one. One hold covers one registration or one removal, never both. The lock is held for:

  • each devnode registration, from the registration gate's last checks through DIF_REGISTERDEVICE, or SwDeviceCreate for the two software companions
  • each removal and uninstall, from its call through its removal test: a device with its children, its fallbacks and the SWD helper's close, each orphaned HID child, and each phantom record
  • a full deploy's pnputil /add-driver /install, which reinstalls every present devnode the package matches, other programs' controllers included
  • each create's bus type stamp on the parent it made
  • the ghost XUSB interface sweep and the interface-class cleanup, each per devnode

These change devnodes without the lock: the surprise removal a Dispose asks of a ROOT device's driver when a program refuses its removal query (v2.0.0), a USB/IP import's attach and detach, the host controller's driver update on a transport swap, a WinUSB bind's DiInstallDevice, a registration's DiInstallDevice once its hold has ended, and every program built before v2.0.0. So do, on a controller's own devnodes or on residue, the naming writes after a registration, RestartDevice, the package removal's pnputil /delete-driver, the usbip-win2 host controller's repair and installer, and a WinUSB restore's reinstall flag on a devnode that has left. S77 lists each of these calls and fails on a devnode change made anywhere else outside the lock. Its source check does not see the surprise removal, which the SDK starts by signaling an event.

Another program waits up to ten minutes for the lock, then throws InvalidOperationException. Threads of one process queue on an in-process gate first, so the bound counts only other programs' holds. The longest hold is one removal, whose budgets add up to about 150 seconds for a devnode with a few children.

docs.title: The registration gate
docs.text:
Everything that takes time happens before the lock. Rivals for the device's ParentIdPrefix are removed. hidclass names a child after its parent's enumerator segment and ParentIdPrefix, so as of v2.0.0 a rival is a parent under the create's enumerator, in ROOT or SWD, on a prefix the create's child can arrive under, or the same token under another HIDMaestro ROOT enumerator. A prior life of its id that is still in the tree or, for a ROOT id, still on record is removed too, each removal in a hold of its own. The gate then waits up to 30 seconds for Windows' pending device installs with CMP_WaitNoPendingInstallEvents. Last, it takes the lock and looks once more, removing and waiting for nothing. When a rival or a prior life has come back, or an install is pending while the 30 seconds have time left, it lets the lock go and goes round again, up to three times for what came back. An install still pending when the 30 seconds end does not stop the registration, since it can belong to any device on the machine, and is logged. A failed wait refuses the registration, and so does a prior life whose removal ends NotGone.

Learn says not to call CMP_WaitNoPendingInstallEvents "while processing any events inside of a system-initiated callback function that is expected to return within a short amount of time", which includes a service's ServiceMain and its control handler (CM_WaitNoPendingInstallEvents). A service should not call CreateController from either.

A software companion's create that runs past its 15 seconds is retried after 1.5 seconds and then 3 seconds, on the same id and inside the same hold, with a removal test on the id after each attempt that timed out. A device still in the tree ends the attempts.

docs.title: The removal test
docs.text:
Every removal ends on a test with one of three outcomes. The devnode must be out of the tree, so a CM_LOCATE_DEVNODE_NORMAL locate fails. An uninstall, a ROOT or HID id removed with SetupDiRemoveDevice or CM_Uninstall_DevNode, also needs its record gone, so a CM_LOCATE_DEVNODE_PHANTOM locate fails. A devnode that was in the tree when the wait began must then deliver CM_NOTIFY_ACTION_DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED within 2 seconds more. A HID child removed with its parent counts on the parent's notification.

Outcome When What follows Removed the notification arrived nothing GoneWithoutRemoved the devnode and its record are gone, and the notification is not logged and counted, never refused NotGone the devnode, or the record an uninstall should have deleted, is still there when the budget ends the next registration of that id is refused

Through v1.12.0 a failed NORMAL locate ended the wait. No locate passes CM_LOCATE_DEVNODE_CANCELREMOVE, which cancels a removal in progress.

Each removal gets the budget it needs. A parent removed with SetupDiRemoveDevice or SwDeviceClose, which can wait on open handles, gets its caller's: 120 seconds for a create's prior life. A removal whose call finishes its work before it returns gets 2 seconds: a child, a fast removal, an orphan, a phantom, and the pnputil and devcon fallbacks. A software device's record is never waited for. The Everything cleanup now waits up to 2 seconds per removal, where it waited for none, and a teardown's surviving HID child waits 2 seconds, where it waited its caller's 120.

The HID orphan sweep looks for an orphan's parent again under the lock, and leaves a child whose parent came back while it waited.

docs.title: Creates that now fail
docs.text:
A create throws InvalidOperationException:

  • when another program holds the PnP lock for ten minutes
  • when its ROOT devnode's prior life, or that devnode's record, is still there after its removal
  • when another program still holds its previous device open and Windows has that device marked for removal, within about 2 s, and the message says so
  • when a software companion's prior life is still in the tree after its removal
  • when the wait for pending installs fails
  • when what the gate removed comes back three times
  • when a gamepad or XUSB companion is not made, for any reason, and the message names it. Through v1.12.0 the create succeeded without it: an xinputhid controller had no other device, and an Xbox 360 controller got no XInput.

A failed create's cleanup removes what it made, its parent by the instance ID the registration gave it, so a plain HID parent under ROOT\HIDClass, which no sweep by index reaches, goes too. A create no longer restarts a leftover ROOT\XNACOMPOSITE\0000. Since v1.8.0 that devnode belongs to a program built before v1.8.0 or is residue, so the restart could take another program's devnode down.

docs.title: The cost
docs.text: Removals run one at a time, in a program and across programs, so a dispose of several controllers takes about the sum of their removals, where it took about the longest one, and another program's create or removal waits that long too. Each removal also waits for its notification, up to 2 seconds more when it is late. No dispose time for v2.0.0 has been measured, and every dispose figure elsewhere on this site was measured before v2.0.0.

docs.title: Programs built on 1.x
docs.text:
Programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0. Moving from 1.x lists every change a 1.x program meets.

A v2.0.0 program takes precedence over a 1.x program. It installs its driver over any older one, whatever runs on it, and refuses nothing because a 1.x program is in the way. Its sweeps still never remove the controllers of a running v1.12.0 program, which they recognize by its owner pipes and by what the driver records about them. A 1.x program's running controllers keep the driver they loaded until their device restarts. On the 2.0.0 driver a 1.x controller keeps its input and output and gets no feature answers, which the driver serves only for a 2.0.0 SDK's controller, so a Sony profile created by a 1.x program loses its calibration, pairing and firmware replies, and a Bluetooth DualSense or DualShock 4 its extended report.

A 1.x program makes no such promise:

  • A running v1.12.0 program's InstallDriver and its first create in a session each remove every HIDMaestro device on the machine, v2.0.0 controllers included, and its InstallDriver replaces the installed driver with its own whenever the payload differs. Every older program does the same.
  • With no controller present at the moment of the v2.0.0 program's create, it leaves no sign, so that create does not start at 64, and the v1.12.0 program's next create can take the v2.0.0 program's low index.
  • Its CreateControllerAt(index) takes whatever index it is given.
  • It reaches index 64 with 65 controllers alive at once.

  • A v1.12.0 program whose device's index cannot be read is found by the registry ledger holder each of its creates writes, except one that runs only keyboards and mice.

  • v1.8.0 and v1.8.1 must not run on a machine that runs a later release. They run no ParentIdPrefix rival scan, and a v1.8.x create of index:N beside a later release's HM_000N parent on the same enumerator makes the machine stop at every boot.

Moving every program on the machine to 2.0.0 is the fix.

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
• S71 runs programs side by side as separate processes. Keyless creates land on their own indices, and each device carries only its own program's input. An identity a live program holds is refused with the holder named. A second program's install and create leave the first program's devices, XInput slot, WGI and Raw Input entries alone, and the first program's frame gaps stay within its one-program p99, with a small allowance for the spread between two baseline runs. A killed program's devices go with the next sweep while a live program's stay. Peers built on v1.12.0 and v1.11.0 run beside this release through each branch of the install policy. Sections E6 and E7 reach the policy through a create alone: beside a running v1.12.0 program's controller, a generic pad's input arrives, a dualsense-bt answers SDL's calibration read and an xbox-360-wired gets its XUSB interface on this release's companion while the older controller keeps its device and driver, and once that program has gone the same creates upgrade the driver in full. Two programs deploy at once on a machine without the driver, two USB/IP composites keep each other's imports, and a killed program's claims go even while a child it started still runs. Further sections pit a thread acting as a program that is not elevated against the SDK's and the driver's machine-wide names, the deploy and ledger locks and the claims included, and cover the driver's owner watch, the transport and WinUSB locks, a WinUSB binding that follows a dropped adapter, and pnputil run from System32. Section W runs sweeps beside running programs: a killed program's device whose claims another program holds is left, a sweep holding a dead group's claims while the restarted program creates the same identity, creates beside a running v1.12.0 program landing clear of its indices, and an index:N below 64 created as asked, the exit handler beside a create in flight and a handler of the program's own, and v1.11.0 GameInput tables kept while their device or a v1.11.0 create in flight needs them.
  • S77 feeds the removal test and the registration gate recorded sequences, with no device, and fails when either answers before the DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED notification and the PHANTOM record's removal, or a locate cancels a removal. It checks the PnP lock's bounds during the exit and fails on a devnode change made outside the lock other than the ones listed above. Its live part disposes a DualShock 4, an Xbox 360 wired and an Xbox Series over Bluetooth and fails on a removal that ended with its devnode still there, on a devnode that left without DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED, and on a refused registration.
  • S72 checks the staging. Every directory on the path is writable only by Administrators and SYSTEM, and hmswd.exe is no longer staged in %TEMP%. A staged tool overwritten with other bytes of the same length is restored from the embedded copy, a staging directory replaced by a link is moved aside rather than followed, and a deploy prunes the staging of versions no running program uses. Its offline part also runs the census over registry keys, with no device: a device whose transport index cannot be read, the ledger holders that raise the floor of 64, and the exit that keeps its record while a hold of its own stands.

docs.title: SDK Reference
docs.text:
The full public surface of HIDMaestro.Core.dll. Five primary types: HMContext (process-wide entry point), HMController (live virtual device), HMProfile (immutable profile handle), HMProfileBuilder (custom-profile builder), and HMGamepadState (abstract input frame). Plus HidDescriptorBuilder, HMDeviceExtractor, HMOemNameOverride, the PID FFB output types, the port types of devices that carry several controllers, HMBuildInfo, and the SDK's exceptions.

This page documents every method's contract, thread safety, throw conditions, and the underlying mechanics that affect when you'd call which.

The deep-dive subjects each get their own page:

  • HID Descriptor Builder: HidDescriptorBuilder API.
  • Force Feedback: PublishPidPool / PublishPidBlockLoad / PublishPidState / GetCurrentPidBlockLoad.
  • Output Passthrough: OutputReceived event, HMOutputPacket, HMOutputSource.
  • OEM Name Override: HMOemNameOverride.Set / Clear / RecoverOrphans / ListActive.
  • Wii U GameCube Adapter: HMController.Ports, DeviceProtocol and BindWinUsb on a four-port adapter.
  • Programs Side by Side: what programs that embed HIDMaestro on one machine can expect of each other.
  • Custom Profiles: the HMProfileBuilder patterns.
  • Profile Extractor: HMDeviceExtractor API used by the GUI tool.

docs.title: HMContext
docs.text:
The SDK's process-wide entry point. One per consuming application. Owns the loaded profile catalog, the per-controller index allocator, and the lifecycle of every HMController it creates.

public sealed class HMContext : IDisposable
{
    public HMContext();
}

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
• Construct one at app startup. Disposing the context disposes every controller it owns.
  • The constructor is non-blocking. It kicks off three background prewarm tasks (staging the driver payload when a deploy is coming, profile catalog parse, GameInput service warm-up) so the first InstallDriver / LoadDefaultProfiles / CreateController call hides 200-500 ms of cold-start cost in the consumer's think-time budget. Failures are silently swallowed, and the foreground call retries.
  • Multiple contexts in one process work. Each numbers its own slots, and transport indices and identities are claimed machine-wide, so two contexts never collide. There is no good reason to create more than one.

docs.title: Driver lifecycle
docs.text:
public bool IsDriverInstalled { get; }
public void InstallDriver();
public HMDriverInstallOutcome? LastDriverInstall { get; }

public static void RemoveAllVirtualControllers();
public static void RemoveAllVirtualControllers(bool preserveInstall);
public static void RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope scope, bool preserveInstall);

IsDriverInstalled is true when both HIDMaestro driver packages, hidmaestro.inf and hidmaestro_xusb.inf, are in the driver store, whatever their version. Does not require admin. When the driver store cannot be read, as when the pnputil listing fails, it answers false, logs why and lets InstallDriver report the failure. It throws only ObjectDisposedException. The internal DriverBuilder.IsDriverInstalled() throws InvalidOperationException on a failed listing, where it returned false.

InstallDriver first removes the controllers of programs that exited without removing theirs, then deploys. It stages the embedded driver files under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging, in a directory only Administrators and SYSTEM can write, checks each against its embedded SHA-256, installs the self-signed code-signing certificate, signs the binaries and registers them with pnputil. When the installed driver is this build's, it returns after the sweep without deploying. The first of InstallDriver, the first create and RemoveAllVirtualControllers() in a process also starts the once-per-process phantom cleanup on a background thread, which the call does not wait for (see Programs Side by Side). Requires admin (UnauthorizedAccessException if not elevated), except that a process that is not elevated and finds this build's driver installed gets AlreadyCurrent, with no sweep. Throws InvalidOperationException if a signing or pnputil step fails, and HMPayloadMissingException in a build that carries no driver for the machine's architecture. See Driver Install and Signing for the full sequence.

As of v2.0.0 several programs that embed HIDMaestro can share one machine, so a deploy decides which driver the machine runs. Deploys take the machine-wide deploy lock, HIDMaestro.Admin\Deploy, a mutex in a namespace only elevated programs can open, so of two programs calling InstallDriver at once, one deploys and the other finds the result current. LastDriverInstall reports what the last call on this context did:

HMDriverInstallOutcome Meaning AlreadyCurrent The installed driver is this SDK's. Nothing changed. Installed No driver was installed and this SDK installed its own, or this SDK's driver was installed with one of its two packages missing and the missing one was added. Upgraded An older driver was installed, from 1.x or an older 2.0.0 build. With nothing on it, this SDK deployed in full and removed the old packages. With devices or a create of another program on it, this SDK added its packages beside the old ones and updated no present device. KeptNewer A newer driver is installed. A driver is never downgraded, and this SDK runs on the newer one.

The 2.0.0 driver takes precedence over every older one, and nothing is refused because another program's devices hold an older driver. Programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0: see Moving from 1.x.

RemoveAllVirtualControllers is static and instance-free, and requires admin. Without a scope, which is HMCleanupScope.Orphaned, it removes the controllers of programs that exited without removing theirs. With preserveInstall false it then removes the driver packages, the WinUSB packages no devnode uses and HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro, but only when no HIDMaestro device is present, no other program that embeds HIDMaestro runs, and the caller has no controller. A running program with no controllers still keeps the packages. In a process that is not elevated both overloads return without doing anything. A running program's controllers, the caller's own included, are never touched. Dispose a controller to remove it. Both overloads also remove the GameInput tables HIDMaestro wrote through v1.11.0 where no running program uses them: a table stays while a present device or any Controller<N> configuration carries its VID and PID, and every table stays while an input section that nothing explains shows a v1.11.0 create in flight. They no longer remove phantom records on every call. The first of them, unless InstallDriver or a create came first, starts the once-per-process phantom cleanup, and a later call removes no phantom. With preserveInstall true the driver packages and HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro stay, which keeps the next InstallDriver on its fast path. Use that from a program's own launch or exit sweep.

HMCleanupScope.Everything removes every HIDMaestro controller and USB/IP import on the machine, whoever made it and whether or not that program still runs. That is the remove-everything cleanup every release before v2.0.0 did, and what an uninstall, a test harness or a support tool wants. HIDMaestroTest cleanup calls it with preserveInstall: false. With that, it then removes the driver packages and HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro with no check for other programs or the caller's controllers. A controller the calling program still holds is left with no device: its submits and PID calls return and reach nothing, its output events stop, DriverVersion is null, DeliversEveryReport and ReleasesOnConsumerExit are false, and a keyboard or mouse submit no longer waits for delivery. It keeps its transport index and sections until disposed, so dispose it after the sweep. Another running program's controllers lose their devices too, but keep reading the removed driver's state: their DriverVersion names it, DeliversEveryReport and ReleasesOnConsumerExit stay true, their keyboard and mouse submits wait up to 200 ms on each of the next three frames, and a protocol controller's next send waits up to 200 ms for the reply the device never delivered.

A program that exits normally without disposing its controllers has their devices removed as it exits. The SDK's exit handler waits at most 10 seconds for the phantom cleanup and a create in flight, then removes the devices to the end, as Dispose does. When that wait runs out, or a device does not leave, the devices stay until the next sweep of any program on v2.0.0 or later, as a killed program's do. See Programs Side by Side.

A context dropped without Dispose keeps its controllers, their transport indices and their identity keys until the process exits. A create of one of those keys in that process throws HMResourceInUseException until then, and the message says so.

docs.title: Profile catalog
docs.text:
public IReadOnlyList<HMProfile> AllProfiles { get; }
public HMProfile? GetProfile(string id);
public int LoadDefaultProfiles();
public int LoadProfilesFromDirectory(string profilesDir);
public IReadOnlyList<HMProfileLoadIssue> ProfileLoadIssues { get; }   // v2.0.0

AllProfiles returns every profile loaded into this context, sorted by stable ID. Empty until you call one of the LoadProfiles* methods.

GetProfile(id) looks up by stable ID slug (e.g. "xbox-360-wired", "dualsense", "thrustmaster-t300rs"). Returns null if no such profile is loaded. Case-insensitive.

LoadDefaultProfiles loads the embedded catalog (337 entries shipping inside HIDMaestro.Core.dll) and returns the count added. An id already loaded refuses the later file.

LoadProfilesFromDirectory(path) loads *.json from a directory matching the Profile System schema. Useful for shipping a curated subset, or for hot-loading runtime-modified profiles. Schema validation files (schema.json) are skipped, and so is a models folder at the directory's top, which holds named device models and identity defaults for the directory's profiles (see Device models). Files load recursively, in ordinal path order. Does not auto-load the embedded catalog: call both if you want catalog + custom.

As of v2.0.0 profiles load strictly, and no load throws for a file's content. A file that does not parse, a key the schema lacks, a key written twice, a value a check refuses, a removed spelling or an id already loaded refuses the file, and ProfileLoadIssues lists it:

public sealed class HMProfileLoadIssue
{
    public string File { get; }
