A consumer that already filters its own virtual pads by testing hardware IDs for HIDMAESTRO needs only to walk far enough up the device tree: from the persona's HID interface, that node is four parents away, so a depth limit of five or more finds it. Filtering on the transport's usbip2_ude service instead would also catch an unrelated usbip install, and would break outright if the backend is ever replaced.

The same absence of a marker changes how a persona is cleaned up. The device sweep behind RemoveAllVirtualControllers walks the ROOT and SWD enumerators looking for exactly that HIDMAESTRO token, so it can never see a composite, and before v1.4.5 a consumer that created one and exited left a USB DualSense enumerated on the machine with nothing left running to feed it. The sweep now detaches personas from the emulated host controller before it walks the enumerators. As of v2.0.0 it detaches only the personas of programs that have exited, matched by the server port in each program's owner record, along with any import on the SDK's port ranges whose server no longer listens, and RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, preserveInstall) detaches every one. See Programs Side by Side.

The order matters and is not an implementation detail a consumer can ignore. A persona's input pump maps the shared input section directly and reads it in a loop, taking no part in the stop-event drain the UMDF2 controllers use, so the pump has to be joined before the sweep destroys those sections. Detaching without stopping it first is not a leak, it is an access violation on a background thread that takes the process down. If you build your own teardown path over the internals rather than calling the SDK's, stop the pumps first.

One fidelity note worth knowing: Windows persists per-endpoint enable/disable state by device identity. Because the composite presents the real pad's exact identity, it inherits whatever state the machine last had for the real controller's endpoints. If the real pad's speaker endpoint was ever disabled in the Sound control panel, the virtual one arrives disabled too. Re-enable it there once.

docs.title: Profile schema
docs.text:
Composite personas add these fields to the profile JSON:

  • "backend": "usbip" selects the create path. It is a property of the device, never a mode toggle on an existing profile: a profile that presented four interfaces on some machines and one on others would name a device plus a machine state.
  • "usbConfiguration" carries the full USB identity: the structured interface/endpoint model the backend routes with, plus the verbatim wire blobs (deviceDescriptor, configurationDescriptor, otherSpeedConfigurationDescriptor), the busSpeed ("low", "full" or "high", the default), and audioControls with the pad's real UAC volume ranges. The blobs are served byte-for-byte and cross-checked against the structured model at create time.
  • An interface's alt setting may carry its own "reportDescriptor", for a persona presenting more than one HID interface. The primary interface (the one whose function is "hid") serves the profile's own descriptor as always; the others serve theirs from here.
  • An interface whose function is "vendor" may declare "bulk" endpoints. The backend serves them for a persona with a responder behind them, the Switch 2 Pro Controller, and stalls them for any other.
  • "microsoftOs" carries the Microsoft OS 1.0 descriptors a device answers Windows with, as hex: string, the 18 bytes Windows reads at string index 0xEE, and extendedCompatId and extendedProperties, the feature descriptors a vendor request with wIndex 4 and 5 reads. With them Windows binds WinUSB to the interface they name, with no driver install. A profile without the block stalls all three.
  • "winUsb" and "sharedSerial" (v2.0.0) inside usbConfiguration describe a WinUSB binding on request and a serial every unit shares. A device's command protocol is "protocol" at the profile's top level, and usbConfiguration.protocol is refused at load. See Devices with ports and protocols.
  • "featureStubs" declares the answers the persona gives to GET_REPORT(Feature), for a device whose claiming software interrogates it before it will use it. messageByte says where the message id sits in a write's payload, and a report may declare the param it answers for, when one message carries several. A report may also carry a patch that writes a value from one of the profile's valueSources into its bytes. steam-controller-2 patches the four bytes at offset 19 with the firmware build TRITON_FW_TS names in Steam's hardwareupdater.cfg, little-endian, through a keyedHexFile source, and keeps the captured build without Steam. steamFirmwareStamp, the older spelling, is refused at load with its replacement named.

See Profile System for the rest of the schema.

docs.title: A second kind of persona: the Valve devices
docs.text: The audio personas above exist because UMDF2 can present exactly one HID interface and a DualSense has four. The three Valve personas use the same backend for a different reason: what a device is to Steam.

docs.title: The Steam Deck
docs.text:
The plain steam-deck profile carries Valve's real ids over a standard gamepad descriptor. Steam files it under Generic DirectInput, and none of Steam Input's Valve-device treatment applies: no gyro lane, no trackpads, no HD haptics, no Valve button prompts. The ids alone are not what earns that treatment; the device behind them is.

So the persona presents the device, reproduced from a real unit's lsusb dump rather than assembled, because the identity Steam inspects is the whole configuration and not just the controller interface: bcdDevice 3.00, product string Steam Controller, a serial string at index 3, bmAttributes 0x80, wTotalLength 150 and five interfaces. Mouse on 0 (endpoint 0x81), keyboard on 1 (0x82, boot protocol), the vendor-page controller on 2 (06 FF FF, 0x83, 64-byte input and feature reports), then an Interface Association Descriptor and the CDC ACM pair on 3 and 4. An earlier revision of this page described a three-interface device with bcdDevice 2.00 and the product string Steam Deck Controller, taken from a different unit's dump with the CDC pair dropped. Steam claimed that device, read its attributes and named it, and then decoded every input as zero.

docs.title: The interrogation
docs.text:
Steam does not simply read input from a Deck. It asks the device what it is, over the feature-report channel, and the Deck's protocol declares no report ids at all: the host writes a message with SET_REPORT(Feature) and reads its answer with GET_REPORT(Feature). ID_GET_ATTRIBUTES_VALUES (0x83) returns a block of (tag, u32) records: the product id, the firmware build time, the board revision, and the connection interval Steam uses to pace its own reads.

That is what featureStubs answers, keyed match: "lastMessage" so a lookup follows the message the preceding write carried. The shipped values come from a capture of a real Deck answering a real Steam client, with the connection interval matching the persona's own 4 ms endpoint rather than being copied blindly.

docs.title: Driving it
docs.text:
The persona's input report is the 64-byte Neptune frame (ID_CONTROLLER_DECK_STATE, type 0x09), and extendedReport packs it from SteamDeckStatePacket_t, so an ordinary SubmitState call drives it. That matters more than it sounds: a profile whose descriptor is an opaque vendor blob declares no axes, and every layer that keys off declared axes will quietly emit nothing rather than fail. The profile must also set alwaysArmed, or the encoder is built and never armed and SubmitState falls through to the descriptor-driven builder, which has nothing to fill. Consumers can still submit the frame whole through SubmitRawReport. Steam's rumble (0xEB), haptic (0xEA) and pulse (0x8F) writes arrive as HID feature output on OutputReceived.

The real device also exposes a CDC ACM debug serial pair, which the persona omits: it carries no controller data and nothing in the input stack reads it.

docs.title: The 2015 Steam Controller
docs.text:
steam-controller-composite is the wired D0G at 28DE:1102, and it presents three interfaces for a blunter reason than the Deck's: SDL's driver refuses the pad on any interface but number 2. A single-interface profile carrying the same descriptor and the same ids is skipped outright. So the persona reproduces the real unit's whole configuration from its lsusb dump, wTotalLength 0x54 and all: keyboard on interface 0 (endpoint 0x81, 8 bytes, bInterval 10), mouse on interface 1 (0x82, 4 bytes, interval 6), and the controller on interface 2 (0x83, 64 bytes, interval 6), which is where the driver looks.

Every descriptor is verbatim from a real unit: the device and configuration blobs, the 63-byte keyboard and 56-byte mouse report descriptors its lizard mode drives, and the 33-byte vendor-page controller descriptor. Its input frame is ValveControllerStatePacket_t. The pad has one stick and the wire carries no separate stick field: with STEAM_LEFTPAD_FINGERDOWN clear, SDL's FormatStatePacketUntilGyro reads sLeftPadX/Y as the joystick, so that is where the stick is written. Its analog triggers come from the 8-bit values inside the ButtonTriggerData union, which SDL remaps against 26000 rather than full scale, not from the redundant 16-bit copy further down the packet.

Its featureStubs answer the same 0x83 interrogation the Deck's do, since both speak the same Valve protocol with no report ids, keyed off the message the preceding SET_REPORT carried. The attribute block carries three records in the order two real Valve captures use: the product id, a zero capabilities word (zero on both of those real devices too), and the 9000 µs connection interval, which is SDL's documented fallback for this family and what it turns into the gyro and accelerometer sample rate.

Three records, not six. A real block also carries a firmware build timestamp, a bootloader build timestamp and a board revision, and no public capture of a 2015 unit's exists. Those are absent rather than invented: SDL ignores all three, and a wrong firmware timestamp is what makes Steam re-ask forever.

docs.title: The 2026 Steam Controller
docs.text:
steam-controller-2 is the wired unit at 28DE:1302, the one SDL calls Triton. It is built differently from both of the above: one HID interface carries everything, addressed by report id rather than split across interfaces. The mouse (0x40) and keyboard (0x41) reports its lizard mode drives live in the same descriptor as the 53-byte controller state (0x42), the BLE state (0x45), battery (0x43), wireless status (0x79), the 0x80–0x89 haptic and rumble output reports, and a 63-byte command channel on feature reports 1 and 2. The command channel is why this persona's featureStubs set "messageByte": 1: the message id sits after the feature report id rather than at byte 0.

The 372-byte descriptor is verbatim from OpenPuck's ReversePuckFirmware, an emulation of this controller that a live Steam client already accepts, and every report id in it matches SDL's own ID_TRITON_* constants.

The feature answers are grounded on two independent reads of real hardware that agree record for record: OpenPuck's identity.cpp, and sc2-research, which logs the same five attribute tags in the same order off a live controller and matches Steam's own firmware-update JSON on two of the values. The 0x83 block is those 25 bytes: product id 0x1302, a zero capabilities word, the bootloader and firmware build timestamps, and the board revision. Steam validates them byte for byte, so none of them is a guess.

The firmware build is the one value that moves. Steam's updater, bin\hardwareupdater\hardwareupdater.exe in its install, offers an update to any unit whose build differs from the one it ships, so a fixed capture goes stale with Valve's next firmware release. With Steam installed, the persona answers with the build TRITON_FW_TS names in the updater's hardwareupdater.cfg, which is what a real unit reports once it takes that update. The file is read on each request, so a Steam update that ships new firmware is followed without recreating the controller. Without Steam, the captured build stands. Battery scenario S62 runs Steam's updater against the persona and requires it to find no update.

0xAE reads a string by index, and the persona declares one answer per index the real device provisions: the board serial, the unit serial, and the constant at index 3 that Steam checks. Every other index reads back 0xFF where the index would be, which is how a real unit says a string is not provisioned, and the byte Steam's own updater tests.

Its input frame is the 54-byte TritonMTUFull_t on report 0x42, packed by extendedReport so an ordinary SubmitState drives it. Consumers can still submit it whole through SubmitRawReport. As of v2.0.0 the frame's timestamp counts elapsed microseconds, clock: "accumulate" with divisor 3 over the SDK's 1/3 microsecond ticks, and holds still while the IMU is off, as a real Triton's does: the field's holdWhile names the imuMode register the profile's protocol sets from the host's settings write. A port reset keeps the IMU setting, and an attach and LOAD_DEFAULT_SETTINGS clear it. Through v1.12.0 it added 4000 per report whatever the time. Steam's haptic writes arrive on OutputReceived as output reports 0x80 and up.

SDL binds Triton on any interface of a wired unit, so nothing here depends on interface numbering the way the 2015 controller does.

All three report on their own clock, as the hardware does: every 4 ms for the Deck and the 2026 controller and every 8 ms for the 2015 one, whether or not the consumer has anything new to send. While the consumer is quiet, the persona repeats the consumer's last frame, raw bytes included. SDL's Deck driver reads once with a 16 ms timeout before it accepts a Deck, so a persona that fell silent would be passed over.

docs.title: Using them without Steam
docs.text:
These pads speak only Valve's vendor protocol. Nothing generic reads it: not DirectInput, not XInput, not joy.cpl. That is equally true of real hardware, which is what lizard mode exists to cover. What makes a real Steam Controller work with Steam closed is SDL, which implements the protocol directly and turns lizard mode off itself.

The personas never emit keyboard or mouse reports at all, so they sit permanently in the gamepad state and nothing needs disabling. An SDL application reads them with Steam not running.

Battery scenario S52 proves this without a client: it creates each persona, drives it through SubmitState, reads the frame back off the real HID stack, and decodes it with SDL's own per-device arithmetic, asserting both stick extremes and a trigger pulled and released. It also measures each persona's clock and feeds it raw frames, asserting that only the consumer's frames reach the wire. ValveWireCheck.exe --monitor <persona> runs the same path interactively and prints what an SDL application would read.

docs.title: A third kind of persona: the Switch 2 Pro Controller
docs.text: switch2-pro-controller-composite uses the backend for a third reason: the host has to talk to the pad before it sends anything. A Switch 2 Pro Controller has HID on interface 0 and a vendor bulk pair on interface 1, and Steam and SDL start it with commands on the second one. The persona answers those commands, and Windows binds WinUSB to interface 1 from the persona's own Microsoft OS 1.0 descriptors. See Switch 2 Pro with Motion.

docs.title: VR Controllers
docs.text:
HMVRController instantiates a pair of virtual VR motion controllers inside SteamVR (HIDMaestro issue #32). This page covers the mental model, the API, the dependency story, and precisely what is and is not verified.

Source: driver/openvr/ (the native OpenVR driver), HMVRController.cs, HMVR.cs.

docs.title: Why this is not an HMController
docs.text:
A VR controller is not an OS device. It exists only inside a VR runtime's session: games never enumerate it, they ask the runtime "where is the left hand, and what is its trigger doing." So HIDMaestro's VR support is an OpenVR driver DLL that SteamVR's vrserver loads, embedded in HIDMaestro.Core.dll and registered in SteamVR's OpenVR path registry on first use. Nothing UMDF2, nothing PnP, no descriptor.

OpenVR's driver API is the one public door on Windows. It is not in competition with OpenXR: OpenXR standardizes the game-to-runtime boundary, deliberately left the runtime-to-device boundary to each vendor (the planned device plugin layer never shipped after 1.0), and SteamVR is itself an OpenXR runtime. One OpenVR driver therefore serves native OpenVR games AND OpenXR games running on SteamVR, which is the default PCVR configuration. Out of reach: Oculus-native titles and OpenXR sessions pinned to Meta's runtime, both closed to third-party devices.

docs.title: The dependency, stated plainly
docs.text:
SteamVR is required, free, and almost always already present on a machine that plays PCVR (for lighthouse headsets it IS the headset driver). HIDMaestro never installs it, never launches a user's copy, and machines without it are untouched: HMVR.IsSteamVRInstalled reports false and everything else works as before.

For a machine without the Steam client there is a verified Steam-free install path using Valve's own command-line tool, no account needed:

curl -L -o steamcmd.zip https://steamcdn-a.akamaihd.net/client/installer/steamcmd.zip
steamcmd +force_install_dir "C:\SteamVR" +login anonymous +app_update 250820 validate +quit

Discovery handles both shapes: Steam-client installs are found through the registry, steamcmd installs through HMVR.SetSteamVRPathHint or the conventional C:\SteamVR.

docs.title: API
docs.text:
public static class HMVR
{
    public static bool IsSteamVRInstalled { get; }
    public static bool IsSteamVRRunning { get; }
    public static string? SteamVRPath { get; }
    public static void SetSteamVRPathHint(string steamVrDir);   // admin
    public static bool EnsureDriverRegistered();                // admin
    public static void UnregisterDriver();                      // admin
}

public sealed class HMVRController : IDisposable
{
    public HMVRController();                       // creates + claims the IPC channel
    public bool DriverConnected { get; }           // driver attached inside vrserver
    public bool ControllersLive { get; }           // both hands registered
    public void SubmitState(in HMVRState state);   // both hands, once per frame
    public event EventHandler<HMVRHapticEventArgs> HapticReceived;
    public HMVRHmdPose GetHmdPose();               // real headset pose, for head-as-input
}

HMVRState carries per hand: an HMVRButton mask (System, A, B with touch variants, trigger/grip/stick clicks), trigger and grip [0..1], stick X/Y [-1..+1], and an optional pose override (meters + unit quaternion, SteamVR standing universe). With no override the driver anchors the hands ahead of the headset, so pointing works by looking. With an override the consumer owns hand placement, which is how stick-driven or gyro-driven virtual hands are built.

GetHmdPose is the reverse direction: the driver publishes the real headset pose every server frame, so a consumer can map head lean onto any flat-game input (the PadForge #49 request) without FreePIE-class tooling.

EnsureDriverRegistered extracts the embedded driver to %ProgramData%\HIDMaestro\openvr\hidmaestro (a stable path, because the path registry stores absolute paths), registers it, and is content-hash idempotent. As of v2.0.0 the SDK writes the registry file itself, the one VR_PATHREG_OVERRIDE names when it is set and %LOCALAPPDATA%\openvr\openvrpaths.vrpath otherwise, the way vrpathreg adddriver and removedriver edit it, and runs nothing from the SteamVR folder. Through v1.12.0 it ran vrpathreg.exe elevated from that folder, which Steam lets users write. The registry written is the one in the profile of the account the process runs as: the signed-in user for a program elevated through UAC, the administrator's own account when an administrator's credentials were typed at a standard user's prompt, and SYSTEM's profile for a service. From the elevated half of a split token the write runs with the user's own rights. SteamVR reads the registry of the user it runs as when it starts, so a driver registered while SteamVR runs loads at its next start, and SteamVR shows no new-driver warning for it. A registration is refused when the account has no local application data folder.

EnsureDriverRegistered and UnregisterDriver throw InvalidOperationException when the registry cannot be updated, such as while SteamVR holds the file open for reading. A failure that came from another exception carries it as the inner exception. The refusal for a missing local application data folder carries none. A UnregisterDriver that throws keeps the idempotence gate set and the entry in place. Controllers appear only while a consumer holds the channel: no consumer, no phantom devices, and a dead consumer flips them to disconnected within seconds.

The driver stays under %ProgramData%\HIDMaestro\openvr\hidmaestro because SteamVR loads the driver name hidmaestro from one registered path, and a v1.12.0 program registers that path again. %ProgramData%\HIDMaestro and the OpenVR folders are written so only Administrators and SYSTEM can change them, with read and execute for Users, since SteamVR reads them as the user. Each is reset in place when SYSTEM or Administrators own it and nobody else may change or delete it. Any other is moved aside, and refused when it cannot be moved. One case remains: a program that is not elevated and creates one of those folders first, then holds a file under it, or any program that holds one of the folders open while the extraction renames a file into it, makes EnsureDriverRegistered throw InvalidOperationException naming the folder. None of this can make the staging under %ProgramFiles% refuse.

docs.title: Hand roles
docs.text:
SteamVR distinguishes a device from a hand. Haptics and the "Waiting" window address devices. /user/hand/left, /user/hand/right, and SteamVR's own Test Controller page address roles, and the runtime decides which device holds each role. Prop_ControllerRoleHint_Int32 only hints. The property that actually influences the decision is Prop_ControllerHandSelectionPriority_Int32, which the driver sets on both hands at activation (HIDMaestro issue #51).

The default is 1000, matching VRCHOTAS's mapped-controller value. Left unset the property reads back 0, the same value SteamVR's own Index profile ends up with, which leaves the winner to an unstated runtime tiebreak on a machine that has both. A positive value states the answer.

That default means the virtual hands take the roles from real controllers while a consumer is live. On a machine where the real hardware should keep them, set the priority negative in steamvr.vrsettings, the same register Valve's own Oculus Touch profile uses with hand_priority: -1:

"driver_hidmaestro": {
   "hand_selection_priority": -1000
}

The driver logs the value it used and whether it came from settings or its built-in fallback, so vrserver.txt answers "which number is live" directly.

docs.title: The legacy input lane (GetControllerState)
docs.text:
Two client APIs read controller input from SteamVR. Games on the modern SteamVR Input system read actions through their action manifest. Background tools and older titles read the legacy API, IVRSystem::GetControllerState, and that lane only carries data vrserver generates through the controller profile's legacy_binding. The driver ships one (legacy_bindings_hidmaestro.json, HIDMaestro issue #55), mapped by the convention every Valve-shipped binding uses:

Legacy slot Virtual control axis0 joystick position (+ k_EButton_Axis0 on stick click) axis1 trigger pull (+ k_EButton_Axis1 on trigger click) axis2 grip pull (+ k_EButton_Axis2 and k_EButton_Grip on grip click) k_EButton_A / k_EButton_ApplicationMenu A / B, with touch k_EButton_System system

The driver also declares Prop_Axis0Type_Int32 through Prop_Axis2Type_Int32 (joystick, trigger, trigger), because vrserver does not synthesize those for IVRDriverInput drivers and legacy consumers classify axes by them.

Two behaviors of this lane worth knowing before debugging an "empty state" report, both measured:

  • Legacy state follows SteamVR's input focus. A client that reads all-zero state with unPacketNum frozen at 0 while poses stream fine should check IVRSystem::IsInputAvailable(). On a headless rig with no scene application, nothing holds input focus and background clients read zeros indefinitely, while the same read from a scene application (one that pumps WaitGetPoses) streams within milliseconds. On a normal rig with a game running, background readers see the state whenever input is not captured.
  • The binding routes by /user/hand/left|right, so a hand without an assigned role reads empty even with the binding present. Check roles first (see Hand roles above).

docs.title: Lifecycle and ordering
docs.text: Any start order works. The driver (loaded whenever SteamVR runs) polls for the consumer's shared-memory channel, and the consumer's properties (DriverConnected, ControllersLive) report progress. Dispose releases the channel claim.

docs.title: Verification status (v1.6.2)
docs.text:
Machine-verified end-to-end on two headless rigs (real SteamVR, null HMD, no headset, no Steam client), by test/probes/vr_controller_smoke (battery scenario S50): payload extraction, vrpathreg registration, vrserver loading the driver, deferred device registration, both controllers enumerating as connected TrackedDeviceClass_Controller with HIDMaestro serials through Valve's own openvr_api, hand roles held by both hands, the legacy axis-type declarations, a haptic pulse round-tripping client → vrserver → driver → HapticReceived with correct hand attribution, the consumer-restart cycle, and the legacy lane: a spawned scene-app reader observes GetControllerState packets advancing at 90 Hz with every axis tracking the submitted state and every mapped button landing on its legacy bit. The IPC protocol is additionally pinned byte-for-byte between the C# and C++ mirrors, both by S50's driver-role phase and by static_asserts compiled into the driver.

Not verified without a headset, and stated here rather than implied: input values read back through the SteamVR Input action-binding system under a real game's action manifest, in-game interaction feel, and the elevated-consumer/medium-integrity-vrserver ACL case (the rig runs vrserver elevated, while the SDDL grants Interactive explicitly for the real case). Real-hardware reports belong in HIDMaestro #32.

docs.title: The generic controller identity
docs.text: The controllers present as hidmaestro_controller (manufacturer HIDMaestro, serials HMVR-LEFT-0001 / HMVR-RIGHT-0001) with a full input profile: system, A, B, trigger, grip, joystick, haptics. Games that use SteamVR Input rebinding work with it directly. Games that only ship bindings for specific controller types (Index, Vive, Touch) may need a community binding or SteamVR's controller rebinding UI. Impersonating an Index controller identity is deliberately not done in this release: partial impersonation (without skeletal input) risks breaking the games it aims to help, and the honest generic identity is rebindable everywhere.

docs.title: Start
docs.text:
Everything between an empty project and a live virtual controller.

  • Installation: reference HIDMaestro.Core.dll from a release ZIP or build from source. The driver install is self-bootstrapping: no EV certificate, no test-signing mode, no manual signing. Windows 10/11 x64 and Windows 11 ARM64, .NET 10, admin required for CreateController.
  • Quickstart: the example/SdkDemo walkthrough. Load the embedded profile catalog, install the driver, create a DualSense and an Xbox 360 Wired side by side, push input, capture rumble.
  • Glossary: XUSB, WinExInput, SWD, ContainerID, &IG_, mshidumdf, GIP. The terms that show up everywhere else in these docs.
  • Moving from 1.x: programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0. Every profile key 2.0.0 refuses, every changed exception, and what changes on the wire, at create, at cleanup and on the driver.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms that show up across this wiki. Most are Windows-internal or HID-spec lingo with HIDMaestro-specific meaning attached.

docs.title: Driver framework / kernel
docs.text: Term Meaning UMDF2 User-Mode Driver Framework version 2.15. Microsoft's official user-mode driver framework (search Microsoft Learn for "User-Mode Driver Framework version 2"). UMDF2 drivers compile as DLLs and are hosted by WUDFHost.exe; a bug crashes the host process, not the kernel. WUDFRd The kernel-mode reflector that proxies IRPs from the kernel HID stack into the user-mode WUDFHost instance hosting the UMDF2 driver DLL. Listed in every HIDMaestro INF as a LowerFilters service. WUDFHost The user-mode host process that loads UMDF2 driver DLLs. With UmdfHostProcessSharing = ProcessSharingDisabled (HIDMaestro's INFs both set this), each device instance gets its own WUDFHost.exe (~8 MB RSS, ~10 threads) instead of pooling into a shared host. mshidumdf mshidumdf.sys: Microsoft's kernel-mode HID minidriver proxy. Acts as the function driver. The HID class stack (HidClass.sys) sees a real HID device; HIDMaestro.dll attaches as a UMDF2 lower filter under it. KMDF Kernel-Mode Driver Framework. Not what HIDMaestro uses. UMDF2's user-mode constraint is what eliminates the EV-cert + reboot requirement; that's the entire point of the project. VHF Microsoft's Virtual HID Framework. Kernel-only. Mentioned for context: another approach HIDMaestro deliberately did not take. WDF Windows Driver Frameworks. Umbrella term for KMDF + UMDF.

docs.title: HID stack
docs.text: Term Meaning HID Human Interface Device. The USB device class that gamepads, keyboards, mice, and joysticks use. The HID protocol is bus-agnostic: the same descriptor format works over USB, Bluetooth, BLE, and virtual buses. HID descriptor The byte string a HID device returns from the GET_DESCRIPTOR(HID Report) request. Defines every input/output/feature report's field layout. HIDMaestro profiles ship these as a hex string in descriptor; HidDescriptorBuilder constructs them programmatically. Report ID A 1-byte prefix that can disambiguate multiple report types on the same HID interface. Profiles where the descriptor declares Report ID (0x85, n) carry it as the first byte of every input/output/feature report. Not all profiles use one (Xbox Series BT does not; Xbox 360 Wired uses 0x01 for the input). Input report Device-to-host data. Buttons, axes, hat, etc. Polled or read async by IOCTL_HID_READ_REPORT. Output report Host-to-device data. Rumble, LED color, adaptive trigger config. Sent via HidD_SetOutputReport / IOCTL_HID_WRITE_REPORT. Captured by HIDMaestro and surfaced as HMOutputSource.HidOutput. Feature report Bidirectional configuration data. Sent via HidD_SetFeature (host → device) and HidD_GetFeature (device → host). HID PID 1.0 force-feedback uses Feature reports for Pool / Block Load / State; some controllers (DualSense, DualShock 4) use them for vendor-specific config. Preparsed data The opaque blob HidD_GetPreparsedData returns to user mode. Internally it's Microsoft's compressed representation of the HID descriptor's report layout. HidP_GetCaps and HidP_GetButtonCaps parse fields out of it. HMDeviceExtractor reconstructs the original descriptor from this blob using a C# port of the libusb/hidapi algorithm. HID PID 1.0 HID Physical Interface Device specification, version 1.0 (USB-IF; download from usb.org/document-library). The standard for HID-class force feedback. Defines Report IDs 0x11 (Create New Effect), 0x12 (Block Load), 0x13 (Pool), 0x14 (PID State), 0x1A (Effect Operation), 0x1B (Block Free), 0x1C (Device Control), 0x1D (Device Gain), and the Set Effect / Set Constant Force / Set Periodic / etc. output reports.

docs.title: Cross-API plumbing
docs.text: Term Meaning DirectInput The legacy Win32 game controller API. Reads HID descriptors directly (preparsed data). Sees axes by HID usage code. Does not understand Vx/Vy velocity usages, which is what lets HIDMaestro carry separate trigger values for WGI / browser without exposing them as DI axes: every Xbox profile presents in DI as 5 axes with combined Z, matching real xusb22.sys. XInput The simplified Xbox-controller API. Discovers controllers via the XUSB device interface GUID ({EC87F1E3-...}), not by HID class. Hard-caps at 4 slots regardless of physical controllers. xinput1_4.dll is the active version on Win10/11. XUSB Xbox USB protocol. The wire format Xbox controllers use over USB and the device interface class ({EC87F1E3-...}) xinput1_4.dll walks to find them. HIDMaestro's XUSB companion (HMXInput.dll) registers this interface for non-xinputhid Xbox profiles. WinExInput Windows Extended Input. A device interface GUID ({6C53D5FD-...}) that historical HIDMaestro versions registered on HID parents. Ghidra decomp of Windows.Gaming.Input.dll on Win11 26200 found zero references; it is not WGI's actual GamepadAdded source. The interface registration is no longer used by the XUSB companion INF. WGI Windows.Gaming.Input. The WinRT API surface that powers Gamepad.Vibration, RawGameController, IGameController, etc. Used by Chromium for browser Gamepad and by UWP / WinUI games. Admits devices via a HIDClass pass-list in ProviderManagerWorker::OnPnpDeviceAdded, falling back to an IsDeviceOrAncestorFilteredBy(L"xinputhid") check. Microsoft GameInput Microsoft's newer game controller API (GameInput.dll). Distinct from the older Windows.Gaming.Input (WGI) WinRT surface, but both run through the same kernel-side dispatch on current Windows builds. Reads device-to-Gamepad mapping from HKLM\...\GameInput\Devices\{VID}{PID}\.... SDL3 Simple DirectMedia Layer version 3. Cross-platform game-input library. Detects gamepads through XInput (SDL_HINT_JOYSTICK_XINPUT), HIDAPI, and a RawInput fallback. HIDMaestro is validated against it; SDL3 is not a dependency. HIDAPI The libusb-maintained cross-platform HID library. Skips devices whose path contains &IG_ (XInput-handled, by design). Detects Bluetooth via the parent's compatible IDs: a Bluetooth profile carries the BTHENUM or BTHLEDevice IDs of a real device of its transport, so HIDAPI reports bus_type = BT. STANDARD GAMEPAD Chromium's "this is a real gamepad with two sticks, four face buttons, four shoulders, two triggers, dpad, start, select" mapping bucket. The browser Gamepad API exposes such devices with .mapping = "standard". HIDMaestro Xbox profiles all hit this bucket because of the Vx/Vy + GameInput-mapping trigger trick.

docs.title: HIDMaestro-specific
docs.text: Term Meaning XUSB Companion A separate UMDF2 device (HMXInput.dll, INF: hidmaestro_xusb.inf) created alongside non-xinputhid Xbox profiles like Xbox 360 Wired. Lives at SWD\HIDMAESTRO\<token>. Registers the XUSB device interface and serves XInput IOCTLs. Needed because mshidumdf suppresses XUSB IOCTLs on HID devices. See XUSB Companion. xinputhid xinputhid.sys: Microsoft's inbox kernel filter for Xbox controllers using the GIP (Gaming Input Protocol) descriptor over HID. Binds as an upper filter on HID children matching [GIP_Hid] hardware IDs in xinputhid.inf. Provides XInput delivery and the 16-button HID descriptor synthesis natively. Used by Xbox Series / Xbox One / Xbox Elite v2 BT profiles. xinputhid UpperFilter tripwire A registry string "xinputhid" written to a device's DEVPKEY_Device_UpperFilters (via INF HKR AddReg or per-instance SetupAPI) that satisfies WGI's IsDeviceOrAncestorFilteredBy wcsncmp check without loading xinputhid.sys. The filter only attaches to HID-class devices, so a System-class XUSB companion gets the WGI admission it needs without descriptor mutation. See XUSB Companion and Cross-API Coverage. driverMode Profile-level field. "xinputhid" = the profile binds Microsoft's xinputhid kernel filter for native XInput + 16-button synthesis (Xbox Series BT, Xbox One BT, Xbox Elite v2 BT). null (default) = plain HID via mshidumdf. As of v2.0.0 it is the alias of the xinput block's "via": "xinputhid", and the xinput block, or the presentation the profile takes from a model, selects which of the three architecture groups the profile lands in. Profile A JSON file in profiles/<vendor>/<slug>.json describing one real-world controller's identity (VID, PID, product string, manufacturer string) and HID characteristics (descriptor, input report size, trigger mode, connection). 337 ship in the embedded catalog. Every controller HIDMaestro creates is parameterized by exactly one profile. HMContext The SDK's process-wide entry point. Owns the loaded profile catalog, the slots of its controllers, and the lifecycle of every HMController it creates. One per consuming process. Transport index The machine-wide number a controller's shared sections, events, owner pipe and registry key are named with, and the ControllerIndex the driver reads. The slot number when no other program uses it, and from 64 while a program built on v1.12.0 runs (v2.0.0). See HMController.TransportIndex. Ownership claim A named pipe created with FILE_FLAG_FIRST_PIPE_INSTANCE under the prefix ProtectedPrefix\Administrators\, where only an elevated program can create one, that a program holds while it runs: one for the program, and one for each controller's transport index and identity. Windows deletes it when the program ends, however it ends, which is how a sweep knows the program is gone (v2.0.0). HMController A live virtual controller. Created by HMContext.CreateController(profile). Two channels: input (consumer pushes HMGamepadState via SubmitState) and output (SDK raises OutputReceived for rumble/haptics/FFB). Dispose to remove the device. HMProfile An immutable handle to a profile (catalog or runtime-built). Carries identity, descriptor bytes, parsed layout (axis count, button count, hat presence). Can be cloned via HMProfileBuilder.FromProfile. HMGamepadState The abstract input frame: every analog input in one Dictionary<HMAxis, float> Axes keyed by HID usage, values [0.0, 1.0] with 0.5 centered for sticks and 0.0 released for triggers, buttons bitmask, hat enum (or higher-resolution HatDegrees / HatHundredths / HatRaw). The SDK encodes into the active profile's HID descriptor. HMOutputPacket One captured output report from a host application targeting a virtual. Carries Source (HidOutput / HidFeature / XInput), ReportId, Data, and a monotonic SeqNo. Decoded per-profile by the consumer. HMOemNameOverride The static API for overriding the joy.cpl / DirectInput OEM-name label for a given VID:PID. Crash-safe via HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOemOverrides. HMDeviceExtractor The static API for reading HID descriptors back out of currently-connected physical devices. Used by HIDMaestroProfileExtractor.exe and consumers that want a "scan for devices" UI. No admin needed.

docs.title: PnP / device-tree
docs.text: Term Meaning PnP Plug and Play. Windows' device-tree subsystem. Every devnode has an InstanceId, ContainerID, hardware IDs, compatible IDs, and a stack of upper/lower filter drivers. Devnode One entry in the PnP tree. Identified by <EnumeratorPrefix>\<Suffix>, e.g. ROOT\VID_045E&PID_028E&IG_00\0000 or SWD\HIDMAESTRO\A7B4_0002. DriverStore C:\Windows\System32\DriverStore\FileRepository\. Where pnputil caches every installed driver package. Survives uninstall: budget for ~40 MB per HIDMaestro version churn on dev machines. ContainerID A devnode property (DEVPKEY_Device_ContainerId) grouping multiple devnodes that belong to the same physical device. Two devnodes sharing a ContainerID dedupe in WGI / Settings / xinput1_4.dll. HIDMaestro's main HID device and its XUSB companion share {48494430-4D41-4553-5452-4F00...<idx>} so they appear as one logical controller. Null-sentinel ContainerID {00000000-0000-0000-FFFF-FFFFFFFFFFFF}. Windows assigns this to ROOT-enumerated devnodes when the creator doesn't provide one. Triggers the bit-2 path in xinput1_4!FUN_18000de2c that skips XInput slot 0: the bug behind the historical "slot 1 is empty" symptom. The SWD migration assigns explicit non-sentinel ContainerIDs to bypass this branch. See SwDevice and PnP. SWD "Software Device". The PnP enumerator name for devices created via the modern SwDeviceCreate API in cfgmgr32.dll. Devices appear at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\SWD\<enumerator>\<suffix>. SwDevice lets the creator specify an explicit pContainerId, which is the linchpin of the slot-1-skip fix. SWDeviceLifetimeParentPresent The SwDevice lifetime flag that keeps the device alive as long as its PnP parent is present (i.e. across process exit). HIDMaestro uses this so a virtual outlives the creating SDK process and can be cleanly removed via DIF_REMOVE later. The only documented teardown path is to re-SwDeviceCreate with identical args (returns a fresh handle), downgrade lifetime to Handle, then SwDeviceClose. DIF_REMOVE The SetupAPI device-installation function code that removes a devnode. Used by HIDMaestro for non-SwD devices and as a fallback for survivors after SwD parent close. CM_NOTIFY_ACTION_DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED The PnP notification kind fired when a devnode is fully gone (not just handle-closed). HIDMaestro blocks on this in v1.3.1's removal ordering so the caller knows the kernel has propagated the cascade, not just that SwDeviceClose returned. Phantom devnode A registry entry under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\SWD\<...> with no live devnode. Cosmetic registry residue from SWDeviceLifetimeParentPresent cleanup; ignored by every consumer-visible API including XInput slot allocation. The regression battery treats them as PASS. Identity key The string a consumer passes to CreateController(profile, identityKey). Every device path, the ContainerId and a USB/IP persona's serial derive from it, so the controller comes back at the same paths on every life. A missing key means the controller index. See SwDevice and PnP. Identity token The instance-name segment every devnode of one controller carries: HM_0000 for the default key of index 0, HM_ plus sixteen hex digits for a consumer key. ParentIdPrefix The level&hash&n value in a parent's instance key that PnP prepends to the instance id of every child that reports a non-unique id (HID children do). HIDMaestro writes the identity's value so the HID child keeps its path across lives. Sticky reuse-fast-path The empty devnode shell a SwDeviceCreate produced in releases before v1.1.31 when its (enumerator + instanceId + ContainerId) tuple matched a device that a DIF_REMOVE had left half-removed in the kernel. The handle-lifetime teardown removed the cause; since v1.8.0 every life reuses one fixed tuple on purpose. See SwDevice and PnP. &IG_ "Interface Group" marker substring in Xbox device paths (e.g. VID_045E&PID_028E&IG_00). Chromium's RawInput backend skips devices with &IG_ in the path; HIDAPI skips them too (XInput handles them). SDL3 falls through to its RawInput backend for these and maps by VID/PID anyway. One substring controls three different detection paths. BTHENUM / BTHLEDevice The enumerators Windows gives classic and Low Energy Bluetooth devices, which appear in their hardware and compatible IDs. HIDAPI and SDL3 check the compatible IDs to set bus_type = BT. A Bluetooth profile's bluetoothTransport picks which IDs its parent carries, set from user mode without Bluetooth hardware.

docs.title: Build / signing
docs.text: Term Meaning Inf2Cat Microsoft tool that generates a .cat catalog file containing hashes of every file the INF references. Required for INF + binary signature validation. Shipped in the SDK's embedded payload from the WDK (%WindowsSDKDir%\bin\<sdk-ver>\x64\Inf2Cat.exe). signtool Microsoft Authenticode signing tool. Signs the catalog and binaries with the per-machine self-signed certificate. Shipped in the SDK's embedded payload. TrustedPublisher The Windows certificate store that lets a self-signed driver install without prompting "Windows can't verify the publisher". HIDMaestro adds its self-signed cert here on first install. EV certificate An "Extended Validation" code-signing certificate. Required by Windows for drivers signed for kernel mode. Costs $300+/year; project-fatal for hobbyists. Not required for HIDMaestro: UMDF2 + self-signed + TrustedPublisher trust path is sufficient. WHQL Windows Hardware Quality Labs. Microsoft's driver certification process. Not required for HIDMaestro. UMDF2 + self-signed lets the consumer's machine trust the cert without crossing the WHQL boundary. bcdedit /set testsigning The Windows boot flag that disables driver signature enforcement. Not required for HIDMaestro: the trusted self-signed cert is enough. Mentioned because every other "no EV cert" project on Windows requires it; HIDMaestro is the exception.

docs.title: Other
docs.text: Term Meaning GIP Gaming Input Protocol. Microsoft's modern Xbox controller protocol. The 14-byte GIP-format buffer the SDK writes into shared memory carries Xbox 360-compatible state for the XUSB companion to translate into IOCTL_XUSB_GET_STATE responses. Vx / Vy HID velocity usages (Generic Desktop Page 0x01, Usages 0x40 and 0x41 per HID Usage Tables 1.5 §4: usb.org/document-library). Used by HIDMaestro to carry separate trigger values without DirectInput recognizing them as axes. DirectInput sees 5 axes; Microsoft GameInput / WGI enumerate Vx/Vy as additional axes via the GameInput\Devices registry mapping and read separate triggers from them. EBI Effect Block Index. HID PID 1.0 §5.5: the 1-byte handle the device assigns to a Create New Effect request. The SDK's PID State shared section carries an EbiAllocBitmap (32-bit; 32 simultaneous effects) and the driver atomically allocates from it inside the SetFeature(0x11) IOCTL handler so DirectInput's follow-up GetFeature(0x12 Block Load) reads consistent state. Mirrors vJoy's Ffb_GetNextFreeEffect. Seqlock A reader-writer synchronization protocol. Writer increments a sequence number, writes data, increments sequence number again. Reader samples seqno before and after; mismatch = retry. HIDMaestro uses this for the input shared-memory channel and the PID state mirror. Writer is single-threaded; reader is single-threaded; no kernel synchronization primitive in the hot path. MultiPadTester Nefarius's recommended XInput / WGI multi-slot tester. Canonical tool for HIDMaestro multi-controller validation. Updated upstream (per nefarius/MultiPadTester#15) to remove the historical 4-slot WGI cap; if a user reports only 4 slots, ask them to update first.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Architecture Overview: how all of the above pieces fit together.
  • Cross-API Coverage: which terms apply at which downstream consumer.
  • Profile System: how driverMode, connection, and VID determine the runtime path.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Applications reference HIDMaestro.Core.dll and call HMContext.InstallDriver(). The SDK carries its driver payloads and installation tools.

v2.0.0 ships for x64 and ARM64. See platform support for what was measured on each.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirement Details Operating system Windows 10 or 11 on x64, or Windows 11 on ARM64 Consumer process 64-bit .NET 10 process Privileges Administrator for installation and virtual device creation Source build Visual Studio C++ tools for x64 and ARM64, Windows SDK/WDK 10.0.26100.0, .NET 10 SDK

The SDK assembly is AnyCPU and contains both native architectures. A 32-bit consumer is not supported. Read-only catalog operations do not require elevation.

docs.title: Reference the SDK
docs.text:
<PropertyGroup>
  <TargetFramework>net10.0-windows10.0.26100.0</TargetFramework>
  <RuntimeIdentifier>win-arm64</RuntimeIdentifier>
</PropertyGroup>
<ItemGroup>
  <Reference Include="HIDMaestro.Core">
    <HintPath>path\to\HIDMaestro.Core.dll</HintPath>
  </Reference>
</ItemGroup>

Use win-x64 for an x64 application. The same SDK DLL serves both targets. Native drivers follow the OS architecture.

The SDK also works in NativeAOT apps and in trimmed, self-contained, single-file apps (v2.0.0). Publish them as any app. Profiles load through source-generated JSON, so the catalog loads in both. See platform support.

docs.title: Create a controller
docs.text:
using HIDMaestro;

using var ctx = new HMContext();
ctx.LoadDefaultProfiles();
ctx.InstallDriver();
using var controller = ctx.CreateController(ctx.GetProfile("xbox-360-wired")!);
controller.SubmitState(new HMGamepadState { Buttons = HMButton.A });

Dispose the controller to remove it. Dispose the context to release its controllers. See Quickstart for output capture and additional inputs.

docs.title: Several programs on one machine
docs.text: As of v2.0.0, two or more programs that embed HIDMaestro can run on one machine. Each program calls InstallDriver() itself. Only one deploys at a time, the driver is never downgraded, and the 2.0.0 driver is installed over any older one, whatever runs on it. HMContext.LastDriverInstall reports which of these happened. No program of this release registers a device while another removes one, so disposing several controllers takes about the sum of their removals. Everything the SDK runs elevated is staged under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging, in directories only Administrators and SYSTEM can write. A running program built on v1.12.0 or older still removes every HIDMaestro device on the machine at its InstallDriver and at its first create, so programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0. See Programs Side by Side and Moving from 1.x.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
scripts\build_all.cmd

The native build creates both payloads before compiling the SDK. Missing native files stop the SDK build. The driver, the companion and the OpenVR driver compile at /W4 and hmswd at /W3, with the UMDF headers and Valve's openvr_driver.h marked external so their warnings stay off. Warnings print and do not stop the build. See Build and Release.

As of v2.0.0 the build takes settings from environment variables or -p: properties. HMSkipArm64=true leaves out the ARM64 payload, HMSkipUsbip=true leaves out the USB/IP transport, and HM_SDK_ROOT, HM_WDK_ROOT and the rest point at the Windows SDK and WDK when they are not in their default places, as with the NuGet WDK. The defaults also read the variables an EWDK prompt sets. A build without the ARM64 payload or the transport refuses a controller that needs it with HMPayloadMissingException, before it changes anything on the machine, and HMBuildInfo says what the build carries. Official releases carry everything. See Build and Release.

For one ARM64 application:

dotnet build test\HIDMaestroTest.csproj -c Release -p:HMTargetArchitecture=arm64

See Build and release for output directories and validation.

docs.title: Composite profiles and upgrades
docs.text:
Composite profiles install the bundled USB/IP transport, usbip-win2 0.9.8.1, the first time one is created on a machine that has none. No separate download is required on the consumer's machine. The build checks the pinned hashes, and the SDK checks the installer again before running it. As of v2.0.0 the installer runs with the smallest set it allows (/COMPONENTS=main,client /TASKS=vcredist /NOICONS), so no GUI, SDK headers, debug symbols, desktop icon or Start menu folder are added, and a machine that holds the installer's uninstall record and its uninstaller file, without its driver package, gets a refusal, not the installer.

A machine that HIDMaestro put on an older usbip-win2, 0.9.7.7 through v1.8.1 or 0.9.7.5 in v1.9.0 and v1.9.1, is moved to 0.9.8.1 automatically. The SDK carries the host controller's own signed driver files and puts them on the existing controller with one Windows driver update. It never runs the vendor installer for this, and it leaves the root-hub filter alone, so no USB device drops and no window appears. It happens only in a Windows session where nothing has used the controller yet, because a used controller does not release its driver. Until then the older transport keeps working. Any other usbip-win2 version was installed by another program and is left as it is. HIDMAESTRO_KEEP_TRANSPORT=1 turns the move off. There is nothing for a user to do. USB devices blink once during a first-time install on a machine with no transport, while Windows re-enumerates the root hubs.

See platform support for the architecture matrix and measured results. ARM64 hardware has not run the battery.

docs.title: Moving from HIDMaestro 1.x to 2.0.0
docs.text:
Programs built on HIDMaestro 1.x must move to 2.0.0. A 2.0.0 program installs its driver over any older one, whatever runs on it, and refuses nothing because a 1.x program is in the way. A running 1.x program still removes every HIDMaestro device on the machine at its InstallDriver and its first create, 2.0.0 controllers included, so a machine works only once every program on it is on 2.0.0.

This page lists what a program built on v1.12.0 meets when it moves. The design notes give the reasons: programs side by side and every device as data. Programs Side by Side and the Profile System describe the same changes on this site.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• HIDMaestroProfileCheck, in the release ZIP beside the profile extractor, loads a profile file or directory as 2.0.0 does and prints every refusal with its JSON path. Run it over your own profiles first.
  • HMLayoutJsonOptions.Default is the source-generated context's options, so it is read-only and reads and writes the SDK's own types only. Code that changed a setting on it, to add a converter or change the naming policy, throws InvalidOperationException. Copy it with new JsonSerializerOptions(HMLayoutJsonOptions.Default) to change a copy.
  • The SDK publishes as NativeAOT and as a trimmed single-file app. A 1.x app published that way loaded none of the 336 profiles.
  • Creates, deploys and the machine-wide locks need an elevated process and throw UnauthorizedAccessException without one. Two calls return instead: RemoveAllVirtualControllers() and RemoveAllVirtualControllers(bool) do nothing, and InstallDriver returns AlreadyCurrent when its fast path finds this build's driver recorded and both packages in the store.

docs.title: Profile JSON
docs.text:
Profiles load strictly. A key the schema lacks, a key written twice, a value a check refuses, a removed spelling and an id already loaded each refuse the file, where 1.x dropped an unknown key without a word, let the second of two keys win and skipped a file that did not parse. A load never throws for a file's content: HMContext.ProfileLoadIssues lists every refused file, and every profile that loaded with a model problem, with the file, the JSON path and the reason. Files load in ordinal path order, and a repeated id refuses the later file and names the earlier one, where 1.x skipped it without a word, so a user's edited copy of a catalog profile needs an id of its own. Check ProfileLoadIssues after a load to see why a profile is missing.

A profile written for 1.x that left out a key and got a behavior from code now states it, so no such profile changes its bytes unseen. Each refusal below is an InvalidOperationException at create, before anything machine-wide, that names the profile, the field's JSON path and the value that keeps 1.x's bytes.

  • A uint16-trigger or uint16-pressure field needs max. 1.x wrote a full pull or press as 32767: add "max": 32767 for that, or "max": 65535 for the full width.
  • An int16-axis, int16-pad or int16-pad-or-stick field of a Y semantic needs invert. 1.x negated every int16 Y: add "invert": true for that, or "invert": false for a wire that grows downward.
  • The ds3-battery type is gone. Write it as uint8-level-map with levels [1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5], chargingValue 238 and fullValue 239.
  • An output field refuses min, max and dpad, invert on any type but uint8-axis, and center on int16-le, since its decoder ignores them.
  • A parameter on a type that ignores it is refused: min and max on a type with no normalized value, invert on a type with no axis, scale on anything but an int16-le field of a calibrated source, and min equal to max.
  • The device model is checked when a file loads and again at create: the top-level report fields, the ports, the protocol, the report programs and the WinUSB block. A profile built or changed in code is refused at create with HMProfileException, derived from InvalidOperationException, which carries ProfileId, File, JsonPath and Reason. It replaces the ArgumentException a profile with no descriptor threw and the HMLayoutValidationException a layout that did not fit its descriptor threw, which the create no longer throws. HMProfileBuilder.Build throws it for its own errors. A button name the SDK cannot express fails the create, where it failed the first submit. Every catalog profile compiles.
  • usbConfiguration.protocol moved to protocol at the profile's top level and is refused at its old place, with the path that says where it went. steamFirmwareStamp is refused, with its replacement named: a patch with a keyedHexFile value source. nativeDescriptor, and a comment inside extendedReport, are mapped keys now, so a copy of a catalog profile that carries them loads.
  • A profile with no feature answers, protocol or presentation of its own takes them from the model it names with deviceModelFrom, or from the identity defaults, the gates 1.x kept in code turned into data: the Switch Pro (057E:2009) over USB and over Bluetooth, sixaxisCompatible, Sony's VID 054C by product and connection, and VID 045E with "xbox" in the id, name or product string, which keeps an XUSB companion. A profile's xinput block, or driverMode as its alias, states the presentation itself. "deviceModel": "none" takes no model. HMProfile.HasDeviceModel, DeviceModelSource and DeviceModelProblem report what a profile got, and HMDeviceExtractor.Extract writes the deviceModelFrom its identity gives.
  • A descriptor hex string with a character that is not a hex digit, or an odd number of digits, refuses the file at load, and a profile built in code at create with HMProfileException. HMProfile.GetDescriptorBytes and HMProfile's layout properties throw FormatException naming the profile and its descriptor field. An odd count used to load a descriptor a byte short.
  • inputReportSize is the input report's whole length, its ID byte included. dataReportId names the input report a profile's data frames fill when the SDK's choice is not the one the device sends.
  • A custom USB/IP profile 1.x accepted can be refused for descriptor checks 1.x did not make: one transfer type per endpoint across alternate settings, an isochronous endpoint in one setting only, a structured endpoint matching within its own interface and setting, and the low-speed limits. busSpeed "low" is now a low-speed device, with Windows' low-speed poll table and packet limits, where 1.x treated it as high speed.

New keys: min, max, invert, center on int16-le, scale with negate and repeat, dpad: "resolved", "#n" in buttons, the uint8-level-map type, clock: "accumulate" with divisor and holdWhile, the packed-uint output type, and at the top level axisCenters, deviceModelFrom, deviceModel, per-entry featureStubs tables, valueSources, protocol, stateBlock, inputReports, liveFeatureReports, stream, xinput, bluetoothTransport and bluetoothVendorIdSource. The Profile System page describes each.

docs.title: Bytes on the wire
docs.text:
• Every normalized value goes to the wire as min + RoundHalfEven(v' x (max - min)) in double, where 1.x truncated or multiplied in float. A value can arrive one count higher than under 1.x. An unsigned axis of 2^n - 1 counts rests one count higher (0..255 at 128, 0..65535 at 32768). XInput thumbs rest at 0 and 0, and every XInput trigger byte arrives as passed, where 252 of 256 arrived one lower.
  • A stick the program leaves out of Axes rests at its center. 1.x rested a 0..255 or 0..65535 stick at its minimum, full left or up. Other axes keep their old rest.
  • A NaN in Axes writes the axis's resting value on every path and never reads the key a slot falls back to. 1.x wrote whatever each encoding gave a NaN: XInput X full left and Y full up, the codec's and the Switch 2 Pro's sticks at a corner.
  • amazon-luna-usb centers its sticks at 0x7F and amazon-luna-ble at 0x7FFF, where SDL reads zero.
  • steam-controller-2's report 0x42 timestamp counts elapsed microseconds, where it added 4000 per report whatever the time, and holds still while the host has its IMU off.
  • 21 catalog profiles repeat their last frame at rest at their device's period, 18 of which sent nothing at rest under 1.x: the DualSense family at 1, 1.25 or 4 ms, the DualShock 4 USB family and steam-deck at 4 ms, openffboard at 101 ms and five Thrustmaster wheels at 250 ms. A consumer that counts frames sees them.
  • ps-move presents the descriptor a real Move serves over USB: a Game Pad with three top-level collections, so Windows creates three HID children where it made one, and its HID child's usage hardware ID becomes UP:0001_U:0005. Its input report is the Move's own. Cross is HMButton.A, Circle B, Square X, Triangle Y, Select Back, Start Start, PS Guide and Move Misc1, and the T trigger is the left trigger. Motion goes in AccelGX/GY/GZ and GyroDpsX/Y/Z, and the raw Accel* and Gyro* shorts are not read. Its battery byte is 0xEE, or 0xEF with BatteryFull. Its manufacturer string is "Sony Computer Entertainment". Its descriptor declares no feature report 0x02, which drew a DualShock 4's calibration from the driver under 1.x.
  • xbox-360-flight-stick presents the 127-byte joystick descriptor its notes cite: 8-bit Z and Rz ahead of its 16-bit axes, a 12-byte report. Its HID child's usage hardware ID becomes UP:0001_U:0004.
  • A program that stored the HID child path of ps-move or xbox-360-flight-stick sees a new device once.
  • The nine Microsoft profiles that are no XInput device, the SideWinder Force Feedback 2 and eight keyboards and mice, move their parent from ROOT\VID_045E&PID_xxxx&IG_00 to ROOT\HIDClass with root\VID_045E&PID_xxxx and no XUSB compatible IDs, and SDL now lists them. xbox-360-wireless presents its HID child as 045E:02A1 and reports itself wireless in XInput, with PID 0 in its 36-byte capability reply, and its parent moves to VID_045E&PID_02A1&IG_00. A program that stored one of these ten profiles' HID child path sees a new device once.
  • xbox-360-wheel-v1 and -v2 report XInput subtype 2, the wheel, where they reported 1.
  • A Bluetooth profile carries the hardware and compatible IDs of a real device of its transport, BTHENUM for classic and BTHLEDevice for LE (bluetoothTransport), and no USB bus type. A create stamps the bus type only on the parent it made, where 1.x stamped GUID_BUS_TYPE_USB on every HIDMaestro devnode on the machine and its first child.
  • switch-pro sends its 0x30 reports on a 15 ms grid on the device clock, where the driver slept 15 ms between frames, about 15.6 ms at the default timer resolution. It sends 0x3F when its bytes change, before the handshake and after a host selects simple mode, where it streamed 0x3F every 15 ms before the handshake and sent nothing in mode 0x3F. A new profile, switch-pro-usb, is the pad on its USB descriptor, and a profile outside the catalog of 057E:2009 over USB takes its protocol.
  • dualshock-3-full's battery byte reads 0xEE, charging, at every level and 0xEF with BatteryFull, as a DualShock 3 on USB reports, where an unset state read as a dying pad.
  • The nine Xbox 360 profiles whose manufacturer string was mangled read U+00A9 "Microsoft Corporation" in HMProfile.ManufacturerString. Nothing on the wire changes.
  • Sixteen catalog profiles send their data-only frames as a different input report or at a different length on a UMDF2 controller: logitech-wingman-formula-gp, gamecube-adapter-hid, joypad-gc-adapter, microsoft-designer-keyboard, genesis-nso, n64-nso, snes-nso, joycon-l, joycon-charging-grip, switch2-pro-controller, joypad-steam-input, ps3-remote, circuitpython-gamepad, pxn-vd6, thrustmaster-t16000m and vader-4-pro. HMProfile.InputReportSize is 7 for circuitpython-gamepad, 63 for pxn-vd6, 9 for thrustmaster-t16000m and 9 for vader-4-pro. ps3-remote, saitek-x52, thrustmaster-t80 and joypad-steam-input present corrected report descriptors.
  • ps3-remote's corrected descriptor is 69 bytes. tinyusb-generic-gamepad and nacon-bigben-ps4 carried descriptors Windows' HID parser refuses, so their devices failed to start. tinyusb-generic-gamepad serves TinyUSB's gamepad descriptor: input report 2 of 12 bytes with six 8-bit axes, an 8-bit hat and 32 buttons, and no output or feature report. nacon-bigben-ps4 serves the descriptor the pad serves: a 27-byte input report with X, Y, Z and Rz, L2 and R2 as buttons 7 and 8, and 8-byte vendor output and feature reports. It is now named "BigBen Game Pad for PS3", with "Bigben Interactive" and "Bigben Game Pad" as its USB strings, since 146B:0902 is that pad. Its id is unchanged.
  • An int16-le field with a center clamps its word to 0 to 65535.
  • HMButton bits 23 and 24 gain names, LeftTriggerClick and RightTriggerClick. A descriptor-built report maps them to buttons 24 and 25, as it mapped those bits before.
  • An output button mask wider than one byte reports its bits 8 and up on OutputDecoded.
  • SubmitMouse on a profile whose relative field excludes zero, such as corsair-k70-rgb-mk2-low-profile, no longer splits a movement the field cannot carry without end.
  • HidReportBuilder.InputFields: an element past a field's last usage carries that last usage, not 0, and a field's page is its usage's page. A stick added after HidDescriptorBuilder.AddRaw bytes that push, change the page and pop is on the Generic Desktop page, where it landed on the Button page.

docs.title: Creates
docs.text:
• CreateController and CreateControllerAt throw HMResourceInUseException, derived from InvalidOperationException, when another live controller on the machine holds the identity key, where 1.x checked only its own context. The same exception refuses a create when no transport index is free, when a v1.12.0 program starts on the index during the create, when another program made one of the index's events, and when the device of a running program, or of one whose owner cannot be known, holds the same ParentIdPrefix. 1.x removed that rival device.
  • A keyless controller can land on a transport index other than its slot when another program uses that index, so its default identity and device paths can differ between runs. Pass an identity key for stable paths. The slot of CreateControllerAt(n) is n, and its transport index can differ from n. HMController.TransportIndex and SectionNames give the numbers and names.
  • While a v1.12.0 program runs, a create's transport index starts at 64. A keyless controller's paths, container id, HID serial and MAC bytes, and a keyless composite's USB serial and instance id, move with it. A keyed controller keeps its paths and container id, and its HID serial and MAC bytes move. A create with the key index:N, N below 64, takes index N's default identity as asked, and that program's next create on index N replaces a devnode of that name.
  • A keyed create whose identity another program's sweep is removing waits for that sweep, up to 120 seconds, instead of failing. A keyless create waits the same way for its index's identity.
  • A create waits while another program of this release registers or removes a devnode, and throws InvalidOperationException after ten minutes. It waits up to 30 seconds for Windows' pending device installs through CMP_WaitNoPendingInstallEvents, which Microsoft says not to call "while processing any events inside of a system-initiated callback function that is expected to return within a short amount of time", a service's ServiceMain or control handler among them, so a service should not create controllers there.
  • A create throws InvalidOperationException when a prior life of its ROOT devnode, or that devnode's record, is still there after its removal, and when a software companion's prior life is still in the tree after its removal, where it reconnected to it. A gamepad or XUSB companion that is not made fails the create, where it succeeded without it: an xinputhid controller had no other device, and an Xbox 360 controller got no XInput. The failed create's cleanup removes what it made.
  • A create no longer restarts a leftover ROOT\XNACOMPOSITE\0000.
  • A create throws HMPayloadMissingException, derived from InvalidOperationException, when the build lacks the payload it needs, before any machine-wide step. InstallDriver, InstallUsbipBackend and HMVR.EnsureDriverRegistered throw it too, and IsUsbipBackendAvailable is false in a build without the USB/IP transport.
  • A context dropped without Dispose keeps its controllers, their transport indices and their identity keys until the process exits, and a create of one of those keys in that process throws HMResourceInUseException until then.

docs.title: Cleanup, exit and the driver
docs.text:
• RemoveAllVirtualControllers() and RemoveAllVirtualControllers(bool) no longer remove the controllers of running programs, the caller's own included. With preserveInstall: false they keep the driver packages while a device is present, another program runs or the caller has a controller. They remove packages under the deploy lock and throw InvalidOperationException after waiting ten minutes for another program's deploy. A tool that wants every controller gone, such as an uninstaller or a test harness, calls RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, preserveInstall).
  • After RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, ...), a controller the program still holds has no device. Its submits return and reach nothing, its output events stop, DriverVersion is null, DeliversEveryReport and ReleasesOnConsumerExit are false, and it keeps its transport index until disposed. Dispose it after the sweep.
  • Both also remove the GameInput tables v1.11.0 left, except a table whose VID and PID a present device or any controller configuration carries, and none while an input section exists that nothing explains. They no longer remove phantom records on every call: the first of InstallDriver, the first create and RemoveAllVirtualControllers() starts the once-per-process cleanup on a background thread and returns without waiting, and a create and the Everything cleanup wait behind it.
  • A program that exits normally without disposing its controllers has their devices removed as it exits, within one 10-second wait for a create in flight and the phantom cleanup. When that wait runs out, or a device does not leave, the devices stay present until the next sweep of any program, as a killed program's do. The exit keeps the program's record while a GameInput or joy.cpl hold of its own stands.
  • A Dispose or cleanup a program calls from its own ProcessExit handler waits for another program's hold of the PnP lock within one 10-second budget the process shares. A controller it cuts short keeps its devices and its record entry, for the SDK's own exit handler when it runs after the program's, or the next sweep.
  • A dispose of several controllers takes about the sum of their removals, since every devnode removal holds the machine-wide PnP lock, where it took about the longest one. Each removal waits for its DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED notification, up to 2 s more when it is late, and a HID child removed with its parent counts on the parent's. RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, …) waits up to 2 s per removal, where it waited for none.
  • InstallDriver no longer removes devices of running programs before deploying and never downgrades the driver. It installs the 2.0.0 driver over any older one and returns Upgraded: a full deploy when nothing runs on the old driver, and this build's packages added beside the old ones when another program's devices or create hold it, which updates no present device. HMDriverInstallOutcome has no KeptInUse, and nothing is refused for a holder. HMContext.LastDriverInstall says what it did. It can throw HMPayloadMissingException, InvalidOperationException after waiting ten minutes for another program's deploy, and InvalidOperationException after waiting two minutes for another program's staging prune.
  • A UMDF2 CreateController checks the installed driver set under the deploy lock and runs the install policy when either INF is missing or older than this build's, so a program whose packages another program uninstalled or replaced with older ones gets its own back at its next create, and a create can wait for another program's deploy. A create whose started driver does not serve protocol 4, or could not read a value the create wrote, removes its device and throws HMDriverVersionException, whose Problem says which (ProtocolNotServed, ValueNotRead). A start the driver fails fails the create within one poll and names the device and its problem code. While Windows has a device installation pending, a failed start waits for it, since a device Windows flagged for reinstall fails its start until the queued install restarts it, and a wait that runs out fails the create on any problem the device shows. A USB/IP composite create takes the transport lock for the usbip-win2 install instead.
  • A plain HID or non-xinputhid create installs the driver on its own devnode only, so a newer SDK no longer moves another program's controller of the same profile onto its package.
  • InstallUsbipBackend and a process's first composite create throw InvalidOperationException after waiting ten minutes for the transport lock, when a usbip-win2 installer still runs after five minutes, and when usbip-win2's uninstall entry exists without its driver package.
  • Staging moved from %TEMP% to %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging. InstallDriver, a UMDF2 create whose device needs the SWD helper, InstallUsbipBackend, a first composite create, BindWinUsb and the public DriverBuilder steps throw InvalidOperationException when %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro belongs to another program, when a staging directory that cannot be moved aside is hostile, when another program creates one while HIDMaestro creates it, when a staged file does not match its SHA-256 or changed between its repair and its use, and, in an elevated process, when the protected TEMP for pnputil or devcon cannot be made.
  • HMContext.IsDriverInstalled answers false when the driver store cannot be read, logs why, and throws only ObjectDisposedException. DriverBuilder.IsDriverInstalled() throws InvalidOperationException when the pnputil listing fails, where it returned false.
  • %TEMP%\HIDMaestro\hmswd_<enumerator>_<suffix>.log is no longer written, and hmswd.exe writes no hmswd_self.log. hmswd's exit code and output go into teardown_diag.log under HIDMAESTRO_DIAG=1, and the diagnostic logs are written as the user.
  • The driver changed, so the first InstallDriver() after updating reinstalls it once.

docs.title: Controllers and events
docs.text:
• An exception a handler throws on one of the SDK's threads no longer reaches the program. The SDK drops it and the next handler runs. A throwing audio handler no longer unplugs a composite controller, and a throwing FramesReceived, StreamingChanged or HapticReceived handler no longer ends the process. The InstallUsbipBackend progress callback is isolated the same way and runs on the calling thread with no machine-wide lock held. Set HIDMAESTRO_DIAG=1 to see each dropped exception in the diagnostic log.
  • Dispose waits for a submit in progress, and a submit that races it throws ObjectDisposedException. OnSubmitLatencyMicros runs after the submit lock is released, so two submitting threads can run it at the same time.
  • A handler can dispose its own controller, or call HMContext.Dispose or DisposeControllersInParallel, without a wait on its own thread. The reader raises the rest of that packet's events on the disposed controller.
  • HMContext.DisposeControllersInParallel disposes every controller of the set when perControllerCallback throws, runs the batch orphan sweep, and then throws one AggregateException holding each exception. In a set of two or more, controllers not yet started were left undisposed once a callback threw. With one controller the callback's exception came out bare.
  • On a composite, HMUsbAudio.ControlChanged and both StreamingChanged events run on an audio event thread of their own, in the host's order, and can come after Dispose returns. A newer write to a control replaces one still waiting. IsStreaming reads the device's stream state, so it can change before StreamingChanged is raised. Dispose waits up to 500 ms for a running audio handler. A USB/IP Dispose no longer waits up to 500 ms for its input thread.
  • A USB/IP persona without a protocol answers GET_REPORT(Input) with the requested report's latest bytes, or its ID and zeros before one is sent, and stalls an ID its descriptor does not declare. The Switch 2 Pro persona answers report ID 0 with its selected report, and the GameCube adapter answers the requested ID alone. 1.x answered with the last report sent whatever the ID.
  • A device that builds its own reports (HMProfile.BuildsItsOwnReports: switch-pro, switch-pro-usb, dualshock-3-full and the Switch 2 Pro composite) takes a raw submit as its state block, verbatim and of the state block's size, and throws ArgumentException for another length. 1.x's driver read whatever bytes landed at fixed offsets of a Switch Pro raw submit, and the composite threw NotSupportedException. HMDeviceProtocol.HostPollInterval's setter throws InvalidOperationException on such a device and on one whose protocol names no input endpoint, where it took the value and did nothing. HMDeviceProtocol gains GetRegister, CounterNames and GetCounter.
  • The USB/IP server answers an import from anything but the host controller with ST_NA. A program that drove the SDK's server with its own user-mode USB/IP client, which was never supported, no longer can.

docs.title: Other APIs
docs.text:
• HMVR.EnsureDriverRegistered writes the OpenVR path registry itself and runs no vrpathreg, so a driver registered while SteamVR runs loads at its next start. Each failure to update the path registry is an InvalidOperationException with the cause inside. HMVR.UnregisterDriver throws InvalidOperationException when the registry cannot be updated, where it returned. HMVR.EnsureDriverRegistered throws InvalidOperationException naming the folder when an OpenVR folder another program owns cannot be moved aside, or when a program holds a folder or file there open while the extraction writes it, where it threw IOException.
  • HMOemNameOverride.Set needs an elevated process. Clear and RecoverOrphans need one only when a record is pending, and return without one when nothing is.
  • HMController.BindWinUsb throws TimeoutException when the registry ledger's lock, or v1.12.0's mutex beside it, stays held for 30 s, scaled, InvalidOperationException when the WinUSB lock stays held for two minutes, and ObjectDisposedException when the controller is disposed during the bind. An uninstall-grade cleanup that keeps a WinUSB package notes it in HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroPackagesLeft, and a later program's sweep removes the key with the last noted package.
