  • DeviceManager.WaitForDeviceRemoval(id, timeout), public in HIDMaestro.Internal, waits for the DEVICEINSTANCEREMOVED notification of a devnode present at the call, up to 2 s past the devnode's leaving, where it returned once a locate failed. DeviceManager.RemoveDevice and RemoveOrphanHidChildren take the PnP lock, so they need an elevated process to touch a present devnode, and RemoveDevice can throw InvalidOperationException when another program holds the lock for ten minutes, with nothing removed. RemoveDevice can also throw the SWD helper's staging refusal before any wait, and leaves the device in place.
  • DriverBuilder.SignDrivers() and GenerateCatalogs() hold the deploy lock, up to ten minutes, then throw InvalidOperationException. InstallDrivers() runs the install policy and returns true only when it installed or upgraded, where it always returned true. RemoveOldDriverPackages() throws InvalidOperationException stating what holds the packages instead of removing them under running devices. FullDeploy() runs the install policy and never downgrades. EnsureExtracted() and BuildDir stage under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging, check every staged file on each call and need an elevated process. They throw HMPayloadMissingException when the build lacks the driver for the machine's architecture, and InvalidOperationException after waiting two minutes for another program's staging prune. EnsureTestCertificate() creates the certificate under the deploy lock.
  • HMProfile.XInput and HMProfileBuilder.XInput read and set the xinput block, and the builder gains BluetoothTransport and BluetoothVendorIdSource.
  • HMDeviceExtractor.Extract reads the bus from the parent devnode's compatible IDs, as hidapi and SDL do, where it read the device path. A Bluetooth device, a HIDMaestro one included, extracts as bluetooth with its bluetoothTransport and, for a Bluetooth SIG vendor ID, bluetoothVendorIdSource, and ToJson writes both.
  • HMProfileBuilder.FromProfile copies the whole profile, its model keys and deviceModelFrom included, where it dropped the feature table, driverPid, the extended reports and the protocol. Vid and Pid on a copy of a USB/IP persona write into its USB device descriptor too. A builder given no VID or PID throws HMProfileException, a copy keeps its source's, and an explicit Vid(0) or Pid(0) builds. DescriptorHex(null) clears the descriptor and the keys it governed. The builder gains ClearDeviceModel, DeviceModel, DeviceModelFrom, DriverPid and FeatureAnswers.
  • A copy whose descriptor is replaced, FromProfile then FromDescriptorBuilder or a descriptor setter with other bytes, drops buttonMap, triggerButtons, axisMap and triggerMode with the other keys the old descriptor's report format governs. A program that customizes a copy that way sets them again after the descriptor. 1.x kept them, describing fields the new descriptor may not have.
  • A layout's kind is read in any case. An axisMap usage named twice, or a name no slot takes, is refused. HMLayoutValidationException's message names camelCase keys with indexes.
  • New in the HIDMaestro namespace: HMController.TransportIndex, SectionNames and DriverVersion, HMContext.LastDriverInstall and ProfileLoadIssues, HMProfileLoadIssue and HMProfileLoadIssueKind, HMProfileException, HMProfile.HasDeviceModel, DeviceModelSource, DeviceModelProblem and BuildsItsOwnReports, HMDeviceExtractor.ResolveDeviceModel, HMCleanupScope and the RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope, bool) overload, HMResourceInUseException, HMDriverInstallOutcome, HMDriverVersionException with Problem and HMDriverVersionProblem, HMBuildInfo, HMPayload and HMPayloadMissingException, and for devices described as data HMController.Ports, DeviceProtocol and BindWinUsb, HMPortSet, HMPort, HMPortFlags, HMPortOutputEventArgs, HMDeviceProtocol and HMWinUsbBinding.
  • The types in HIDMaestro.Internal are the profile JSON's object model and the SDK's plumbing, public so a program can read and build profiles. They follow the JSON schema, so a key the schema adds, renames or removes changes them. 2.0.0 removes SteamFirmwareStampSpec, FeatureStubReport.SteamFirmwareStamp, and ControllerProfile's IsXboxBranded, UsesXusb22, UsesUpperFilter, UpperFilterName, CompanionOnly and SixaxisCompatible (the companionOnly key goes with them, and sixaxisCompatible still loads and picks the DualShock 3 model), and changes FeatureStubReport.Param from int? to AnswerParamSpec (a bare number still loads), FeatureStubReport.Notify to bool? and FeatureStubSpec.Match's default to null. It adds the spec classes of the ports, the WinUSB block, the answer tables (AnswerCrcSpec, AnswerMessageSpec, AnswerParamSpec, AnswerPatchSpec, ValueRootSpec, ValueSourceSpec) and the protocol, state block, report programs and stream (ProtocolSpec and its parts, StateBlockSpec, InputReportSpec, LiveFeatureReportSpec, StreamSpec, HIDMaestro.Internal.Programs), ScaleSpec, PackedPartSpec and PackedPieceSpec, the field members Min, Max, Scale, Negate, Repeat, Dpad, Levels, ChargingValue, Parts, Clock and HoldWhile, ControllerProfile's AxisCenters, XInput, BluetoothTransport, BluetoothVendorIdSource, ValueSources, DeviceModel, DeviceModelFrom, NativeDescriptor, Protocol, StateBlock, InputReports, LiveFeatureReports, Stream and BuildsItsOwnReports, ExtendedReportSpec.Ports and Comment, UsbConfigurationSpec.SharedSerial and WinUsb, and HidReportBuilder.InputReports. DeviceManager.WaitForHidChild gains a three-argument form and WaitForDeviceInterface a four-argument form beside the old ones.

docs.title: Native writers
docs.text:
• Each index's configuration gains InputReportId (REG_BINARY), which the driver checks against InputReportByteLength and the descriptor before it uses it, and loses DeviceInstanceId, which no driver read. A create writes VendorId and ProductId first.
  • When several programs run, a native writer reads a controller's section names from HMController.SectionNames of the program it feeds, or computes them from HMController.TransportIndex, since the transport index can differ from the slot.
  • Global\HIDMaestroVersion<N> is a new 64-byte per-controller section the SDK and the driver both write, at protocol 4: the SDK's protocol range and version, the identity tag of the controller's token, and the driver's protocol range, version, capabilities and error word. The SDK also writes the controller's index under HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestro\Identity\<token> before any PnP work, and the driver reads it before its first start. No existing section's layout changed.
  • A 2.0.0 controller's configuration gains FeatureAnswers, the compiled answer table, and the cached input report IDs. The driver reads them only under the version contract, so a native writer that wants feature answers writes the section and the identity entry as the SDK does.
  • InputAck's capability word can carry bit 31, the driver's ended marker. Test bits 0 and 1 one at a time, never the whole word.
  • The driver's Global\HIDMaestroStopEvent<N> and Global\HIDMaestroOutputEvent<N> carry a DACL that admits SYSTEM, Administrators and LocalService only, so a process that is not elevated opens neither.
  • The driver lets go of the index's sections, events and owner pipe when its device is surprise removed, where it held them until the removal.
  • A devnode with no index, neither an identity entry nor a ControllerIndex, or with no Controller<index> key holding a descriptor, fails its start with STATUS_DEVICE_CONFIGURATION_ERROR. Both drivers started such a devnode as an Xbox 360 pad on Controller0 in 1.x. HidAttrPid is no longer read.
  • A 2.0.0 XUSB companion reads its answers from XusbAnswers under the version contract and registers its XUSB interface only when it holds them. Its INF adds no interface, as xusb22.inf adds none, so the interface exists only once the driver has started.

docs.title: A 1.x program on a machine with 2.0.0
docs.text:
• Its create installs its own driver package with UpdateDriverForPlugAndPlayDevices, which Windows applies to every present device of the hardware ID. Its controllers that are running when a 2.0.0 program installs its driver keep the driver their host loaded until their device restarts.
  • A 1.x controller that runs on the 2.0.0 driver keeps its input and output and loses the device behavior 1.x kept in its driver, which 2.0.0 serves only for a 2.0.0 SDK's controller: a Sony profile's calibration, pairing and firmware replies, and a Bluetooth DualSense or DualShock 4's extended report, which the 1.x SDK arms on the feature read, the Switch Pro's replies and stream, the DualShock 3's sixaxis form, and XInput through the XUSB companion, which registers no interface for it.

  • v1.8.0 and v1.8.1 must not run on a machine that runs a later release: they run no ParentIdPrefix rival scan, and a v1.8.x create of index:N beside a later release's HM_000N parent on the same enumerator makes the machine stop at every boot (bugcheck 0xCA). Programs on those releases must move.

  • Its InstallDriver removes every HIDMaestro device on the machine, 2.0.0 controllers included, and installs its own driver whenever the payload differs. Its first create in a session runs a cleanup that removes every device too.

  • While it has a controller present, 2.0.0 sweeps never remove its controllers, and 2.0.0 creates take transport indices from 64, above every index it reaches with fewer than 65 controllers alive. A 2.0.0 program sees it through its owner pipes, what the 2.0.0 driver records about them, its USB/IP imports, and, while its device's index cannot be read, the registry ledger entry its create writes. A 1.x program of only keyboards and mice whose device's index cannot be read, on an index a 2.0.0 program holds, goes unseen.
  • With no controller present it leaves no sign, so its next create can take a 2.0.0 program's low index and share its sections. Its CreateControllerAt(index) takes whatever index it is given.
  • A program older than v1.12.0 leaves no sign of whether it still runs, so its devices are never removed on a guess. Only RemoveAllVirtualControllers(HMCleanupScope.Everything, preserveInstall) and a create of that device's own identity key remove them.

docs.title: Platform support
docs.text:
HIDMaestro runs on x64 and ARM64 Windows. Use v1.9.1 or later on ARM64. One HIDMaestro.Core.dll serves both. It carries a native driver and helper payload for each architecture and picks the set matching the operating system, so an x64 consumer running under emulation on ARM64 Windows still gets ARM64 drivers.

Component x64 Windows ARM64 Windows Managed SDK AnyCPU assembly Same assembly HID and XInput drivers Native x64 Native ARM64 Device helper and signing tool Native x64 Native ARM64 USB/IP transport Microsoft-signed x64 package Microsoft-signed ARM64 package Test app, example, ProfileExtractor win-x64 win-arm64 OpenVR driver x64 SteamVR plugin Same x64 plugin for an x64 SteamVR host NativeAOT and trimmed single-file apps (v2.0.0) win-x64 win-arm64

Virtual device creation requires a 64-bit process and administrator privileges. The x64 target supports Windows 10 and 11. The ARM64 target is Windows 11. The OpenVR plugin follows the SteamVR host's architecture, independently of the SDK process.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
Install the .NET 10 SDK, Windows SDK/WDK 10.0.26100.0, and Visual Studio C++ build tools for both x64 and ARM64. The ARM64 compiler and C runtime libraries are a separate Visual Studio component.

scripts\build_all.cmd

build_all.cmd builds both native payloads and the x64 OpenVR plugin, then the SDK. The native scripts compile the driver, the companion and the OpenVR driver at /W4, and hmswd at /W3. The UMDF headers and Valve's openvr_driver.h are passed with /external:I and /external:W0, which turn warnings off in those headers and the headers they include, while every warning in HIDMaestro's own sources still prints. No /WX is set, so a new warning prints and does not stop the build. A full build_all.cmd printed 70 compiler warnings at commit c5c0f05 and none at a6fbbe8, development measurements. Native x64 files are under build/, and ARM64 files are under build/arm64/. A missing native payload fails the SDK build with a message naming the script.

A source build can leave the ARM64 payload out with HMSkipArm64=true, the USB/IP transport out with HMSkipUsbip=true, and can take its Windows SDK and WDK from an installed kit, the NuGet WDK or an EWDK prompt. See Build and Release. HMBuildInfo.DriverArchitectures and UsbipArchitectures report what a built HIDMaestro.Core.dll carries.

To build a single application for ARM64:

dotnet build test\HIDMaestroTest.csproj -c Release -p:HMTargetArchitecture=arm64
dotnet build tools\HIDMaestroProfileExtractor\HIDMaestroProfileExtractor.csproj -c Release -p:HMTargetArchitecture=arm64

docs.title: NativeAOT, trimmed and single-file apps
docs.text:
As of v2.0.0 HIDMaestro.Core.dll works in NativeAOT apps and in trimmed, self-contained, single-file apps, for x64 and ARM64. Profiles load through source-generated JSON, every Win32 call goes through LibraryImport, and hmswd.exe always comes from the embedded resource, since Assembly.Location is empty in a single-file app. At v1.12.0 both kinds of app loaded 0 of the 336 catalog profiles, because reflection-based JSON is switched off in them. The aot_smoke probe publishes one source four ways, NativeAOT and trimmed single-file for each architecture. Each app loads the catalog, installs the driver, creates a dualshock-4-v2 on the UMDF2 driver and a dualsense-composite on USB/IP, submits input, reads it back, writes an output report, waits for OutputReceived and disposes. Battery scenarios S74 and S75 run the two apps for the machine's architecture, so the ARM64 apps are built and published and have not run on ARM64 hardware. See Build and Release.

InstallDriver() builds a catalog for each driver INF with Inf2Cat before it signs the package and adds it to the driver store. Inf2Cat's ARM64 values name a Windows release, from 10_RS3_ARM64 on, and it has no bare 10_ARM64. v1.9.0 asked for 10_ARM64, which Inf2Cat rejects, so on ARM64 InstallDriver() failed before any driver reached the store. v1.9.1 asks for 10_RS3_ARM64, version 1709, the first Windows 10 release on ARM64. x64 keeps 10_X64.

One Inf2Cat serves both architectures. It is an x64 .NET program, which Windows 11 on ARM64 runs under its x64 emulation.

Battery scenario S61 extracts each architecture's payload with the embedded Inf2Cat, runs Inf2Cat with the value the SDK picks for that architecture, and requires one catalog per INF. Inf2Cat only parses the INFs and hashes the files, so the check runs on x64 for both architectures.

docs.title: USB/IP 0.9.8.1
docs.text:
Composite personas use the bundled usbip-win2 0.9.8.1. It is the first release with the fix for the attach work item that blocked driver unload in 0.9.8.0 (usbip-win2#188). The release page carries the x64 installer only. The ARM64 installer is the same tag's build that the project's signing service posted in usbip-win2#13. Both installers ship the 0.9.8.1 tag's own headers, and neither carries the development branch's later changes.

Both installers are inside the SDK DLL. The build checks each against its pinned SHA-256, and the SDK checks the extracted copy again before running it. Both drivers are signed by Microsoft: the x64 one after hardware certification testing, the ARM64 one by attestation.

The driver's request layout changed in 0.9.8.0 and again in 0.9.8.1. The SDK speaks 0.9.7.x, 0.9.8.0 and 0.9.8.1 and asks the driver which one it has.

Where no usbip-win2 exists, the SDK runs the bundled installer silently, with no window and no prompt. As of v2.0.0 it passes /COMPONENTS=main,client /TASKS=vcredist /NOICONS, so the installer leaves out the GUI, the SDK headers, the debug symbols, the desktop icon and the Start menu folder. A machine that holds the installer's uninstall record and its uninstaller file, without its driver package, gets a refusal, because the installer would run that record's uninstaller first. See Driver Install and Signing. Windows re-enumerates the USB root hubs once during that install, so USB devices blink for a moment. If usbip-win2 is installed and its host controller is not answering, the SDK restarts that device and does not reinstall.

A machine that HIDMaestro put on an older usbip-win2, 0.9.7.7 through v1.8.1 or 0.9.7.5 in v1.9.0 and v1.9.1, is moved to 0.9.8.1 automatically. The SDK carries the host controller's own signed driver files and puts them on the existing controller with one Windows driver update. It never runs the vendor installer for this, and it leaves the root-hub filter alone, so no USB device drops and no window appears. It happens only in a Windows session where nothing has used the controller yet, because a used controller does not release its driver. Until then the older transport keeps working. Any other usbip-win2 version was installed by another program and is left as it is. HIDMAESTRO_KEEP_TRANSPORT=1 turns the move off.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
[D3-PLACEHOLDER: v2.0.0 battery result]

The v1.12.0 release gate ran on x64: the full 70-scenario battery passed all 70 scenarios on the release binaries on Windows 11 26200. The gate machine's host controller runs 0.9.8.1, put there by the v1.9.2 move, so every composite scenario ran through the client's 0.9.8.1 request format against the live driver. The DualSense composite passed 26/26 end to end, and the Switch 2 Pro composite 255/255, with Windows binding WinUSB to its vendor interface from the persona's own descriptors. Its root-hub filter is still the older one the move leaves alone, so SET_INTERFACE never reaches a composite there, and audio stream state comes from the traffic instead (USB audio composite).

The 0.9.8.0 request format was checked by compiling that version's own header with MSVC for x64 and ARM64, and the client sends its exact sizes and offsets. It has not run against a live driver. The move from 0.9.7.5 to 0.9.8.1 uses the same Windows driver update that moved machines from 0.9.7.7 to 0.9.7.5 in v1.9.0, which took 878 ms on 26200.

0.9.8.1 rounds a full-speed device's interrupt polling interval up where 0.9.7.5 rounded it down. Windows does not pace interrupt reads by that interval. Measured on 26200 by giving the DualShock 4 composite an interval that 0.9.7.5 converts to the same 8 ms period, the composite delivered 146 to 158 reports per second either way.

Both native payloads and the ARM64 applications compile, link and stamp as ARM64, and both bundled transport drivers are verified as the right architecture with valid Microsoft signatures.

ARM64 hardware has not run the battery. On ARM64, the steps after the catalog, signing it and adding the package to the driver store, have not run. The Atom fixture was not reachable for this release.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
The shortest possible path from "I just cloned this repo" to "I have a virtual Xbox 360 controller and a virtual DualSense both visible in joy.cpl, both responding to input, and rumble events being captured".

The walkthrough mirrors example/SdkDemo/Program.cs: a minimal SDK consumer that exercises every public surface.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• HIDMaestro built (scripts\build_all.cmd: see Installation).
  • An elevated terminal. CreateController and InstallDriver require admin.
dotnet run --project example\SdkDemo

That's it. Five seconds later you have two virtual controllers, the demo pulses inputs through them for a few seconds, captures any rumble the OS sends back, and disposes everything cleanly. Open joy.cpl while the demo runs to see them.

The rest of this page walks through what just happened.

docs.title: Step 0: orphan recovery
docs.text:
int recovered = HMOemNameOverride.RecoverOrphans();

If the previous run of any HIDMaestro consumer crashed mid-execution and had set OEM-name overrides for joy.cpl labels, those would persist as registry entries pointing at labels for VID:PIDs that no longer have a virtual. RecoverOrphans reads the pending-override hive at HKLM\SOFTWARE\HIDMaestroOemOverrides and restores every captured pre-override value.

Safe to call on every startup. Returns the number restored. See OEM Name Override for the crash-safe write protocol.

docs.title: Step 1: context + profiles
docs.text:
using var ctx = new HMContext();
int loaded = ctx.LoadDefaultProfiles();   // returns 337

HMContext is the SDK's process-wide entry point. The constructor is cheap: it kicks off three background prewarm tasks (staging the driver payload when a deploy is coming, profile catalog parse, GameInput service warm-up) but doesn't block.

LoadDefaultProfiles reads the embedded JSON catalog out of HIDMaestro.Core.dll. Consumers don't need to ship profile files alongside their app. To load profiles from disk instead (custom directory, modded profiles), use LoadProfilesFromDirectory(path).

After this call, ctx.AllProfiles is populated and ctx.GetProfile("xbox-360-wired") resolves.

docs.title: Step 2: install the driver
docs.text:
ctx.InstallDriver();

Idempotent. On a fresh machine this:

  1. Removes the controllers of programs that exited without removing theirs. A running program's controllers stay.
  2. Takes the machine-wide deploy lock, so two programs never deploy at once.
  3. Generates a per-machine self-signed certificate if needed.
  4. Stages the embedded driver payload under %ProgramFiles%\HIDMaestro\Staging, writable only by Administrators and SYSTEM, and checks each file's SHA-256.
  5. Signs HIDMaestro.dll, HMXInput.dll, and the catalog files.
  6. Calls pnputil /add-driver for both INFs.

Total: ~1.7s on a clean machine, ~50 ms on a machine where the same hash is already installed. A newer installed driver, or an older one that controllers run on, is kept, and ctx.LastDriverInstall says which. See Programs Side by Side.

Throws UnauthorizedAccessException if the calling process isn't elevated and has a deploy to do. A process that is not elevated and finds this build's driver installed gets AlreadyCurrent. Throws InvalidOperationException if any signing or pnputil step fails.

docs.title: Step 3: create two virtual controllers
docs.text:
var ds = ctx.GetProfile("dualsense") ?? throw new InvalidOperationException();
var x360 = ctx.GetProfile("xbox-360-wired") ?? throw new InvalidOperationException();

using var ctrl0 = ctx.CreateController(ds);
using var ctrl1 = ctx.CreateController(x360);

CreateController takes the lowest free slot in the context (linear scan from 0) and a machine-wide transport index, runs the per-archetype SetupController orchestration, and returns once the device's HID child has reached DN_STARTED and any required XInput slot has been claimed (capped at 500ms post-v1.3.2).

Measured before v2.0.0: ~200 ms warm for a single controller, ~1 s for two mixed. Since v2.0.0 each create waits for Windows' pending device installs, the previous create's included, before it registers its devnode, and no live run has timed that.

ctrl0 is the DualSense at slot 0. ctrl1 is the Xbox 360 Wired at slot 1. In a program running alone their transport indices are 0 and 1 as well. A running program built on HIDMaestro 1.12.0 moves them to 64 and 65. The XInput slot allocator hands the Xbox 360 user-index 0 (DualSense doesn't claim an XInput slot: it's a non-Xbox-VID profile).

using var matters: Dispose removes the device and frees the kernel slot. Forgetting it leaks the virtual until HMContext.Dispose() runs.

docs.title: Step 3a: override the joy.cpl label
docs.text:
HMOemNameOverride.Set(x360.VendorId, x360.ProductId, "My Custom 360");

joy.cpl and DirectInput consumers will now show "My Custom 360" instead of "Controller (XBOX 360 For Windows)" for any VID_045E:PID_028E device until you Clear. The label sources from three registry locations and Windows pre-populates at least one for many clone PIDs: Set writes all three in a single transaction under a global mutex, capturing the prior values to the pending hive first so a crash doesn't leave the override stuck. See OEM Name Override for the full mechanism.

docs.title: Step 4: subscribe to output events
docs.text:
ctrl0.OutputReceived += (sender, packet) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine($"DS rumble  src={packet.Source}  rid=0x{packet.ReportId:X2}  bytes={packet.Data.Length}");
};

ctrl1.OutputReceived += (sender, packet) =>
{
    if (packet.Source == HMOutputSource.XInput)
    {
        // 5-byte XInput rumble: cmd, size, lo, hi, reserved
        var bytes = packet.Data.Span;
        if (bytes.Length >= 4)
            Console.WriteLine($"X360 rumble  lo={bytes[2]:X2}  hi={bytes[3]:X2}");
    }
};

The output channel is a 64-slot ring drained on every SDK poll (~125 Hz). Multiple OutputReceived invocations per poll iteration are normal: DirectInput PID FFB writes Set Effect → Set Constant Force → Effect Operation Start within 1-3 ms and all three surface here. See Output Passthrough for the wire format and decoding.

Handlers run on the SDK's poll thread, not your UI thread. Marshal back if needed. Keep handlers cheap: the ring will overwrite the oldest packets if a reader stalls past ~512 ms.

docs.title: Step 5: submit input
docs.text:
var sw = System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch.StartNew();
while (sw.Elapsed < TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5))
{
    float t = (float)(sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds % 2.0 / 2.0);
    float angle = t * 2 * MathF.PI;

    ctrl0.SubmitState(new HMGamepadState
    {
        Axes = HMGamepadStateHelpers.StandardAxes(ctrl0.Profile,
            leftStickX: (MathF.Cos(angle) + 1) / 2,    // [0..1] uniform; 0.5 = center
            leftStickY: (MathF.Sin(angle) + 1) / 2),
        Buttons = HMButton.Cross,                       // Sony alias for HMButton.A
        Hat = HMHat.North,
    });

    ctrl1.SubmitState(new HMGamepadState
    {
        Axes = HMGamepadStateHelpers.StandardAxes(ctrl1.Profile,
            leftTrigger: t,
            rightTrigger: 1 - t),
        Buttons = HMButton.A | HMButton.Start,
    });

    Thread.Sleep(8);   // 125 Hz; consumers typically run at the rate of their input source
}

HMGamepadState is the abstract input frame. Analog inputs live in a single Dictionary<HMAxis, float> Axes keyed by HID usage; values normalize to [0..1] (0.5 = centered for signed axes, 0.0 = released for unsigned). Buttons stay as a flags bitmask, hat as a cardinal/diagonal enum. The SDK encodes into the active profile's HID descriptor: you don't need to know whether the target is a DualSense, Xbox 360, or arcade stick.

For the common 4-stick + 2-trigger gamepad shape, HMGamepadStateHelpers.StandardAxes(profile, ...) resolves the canonical (LX, LY, RX, RY, LT, RT) slots into the right axis keys per profile (Sony's Z=right-stick, Rx=left-trigger axis map is honored). For HOTAS / wheel / pedal devices, drive any descriptor-declared usage directly: state.Axes[HMAxis.Slider] = 0.7f.

The struct also carries the Sony touchpad, motion, battery and DualShock 3 button pressure. For data it doesn't model, such as vendor extensions, use SubmitRawReport with bytes you assembled yourself.

There is no SDK-managed pump thread. The consumer drives the cadence. PadForge runs at 1000 Hz; the demo runs at 125 Hz; a profile-switch utility might submit zero frames. The driver's worker thread reads from shared memory event-driven, so submit rate and idle CPU cost are independent.

docs.title: Step 6: cleanup
docs.text:
HMOemNameOverride.Clear(x360.VendorId, x360.ProductId);
// `using` disposes ctrl0, ctrl1, and ctx as the scope ends.

Each HMController.Dispose() removes its device via DIF_REMOVE and (for SwD-enumerated profiles) closes the HSWDEVICE handle so the kernel cascade fires. HMContext.Dispose() disposes any controllers it still owns plus the prewarm threads.

For batch teardown of N controllers without N orphan-sweeps, use DisposeControllersInParallel:

ctx.DisposeControllersInParallel(
    new[] { ctrl0, ctrl1 },
    perControllerCallback: (c, ms) => Console.WriteLine($"  {c.Profile.Id} disposed in {ms} ms"));

The system-wide HID orphan sweep runs once at the end instead of per-controller. The removals themselves run one at a time, so the batch takes about the sum of the controllers' removals.

docs.title: Verifying it worked
docs.text:
While the demo is running, in another terminal:

:: Cross-API validation: DInput axes, XInput slots, HIDAPI bus, browser, WGI
python scripts\verify.py --controllers 2

:: Pretty PnP tree
powershell -c "Get-PnpDevice -Status OK | Where-Object FriendlyName -like '*Game*'"

:: GUI verification
joy.cpl

scripts\verify.py is the tool every README screenshot was produced with. Returns exit 0 if every API agrees the controllers exist and report sane state. See Testing and Verification for what it actually checks per-API.
